# Kinovoice (Киновойс) — all texts

> Kinovoice is an independent publication on film, series and theatre: reviews and essays that grew out of the Telegram channel kino_voice. By Betsy Isakova. All 174 published texts follow, newest first. Short version: https://kinovoice.com/llms.txt

## Minotaur: When Poisoned Air Becomes the Protagonist

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/minotavr-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-11-03 (3 November 2026)
Work: “Minotaur” is a 2026 film directed by Andrey Zvyagintsev.
Tags: Russian cinema, festivals
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/minotavr-2026/

If the phrase “poisoned air” ever needs a visualisation, [*Minotaur*](https://youtu.be/hTHeFP0mcuk?si=UvRbPEE8DxGc2ojd) can safely be cited as the perfect example.

In September 2022, Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov), a businessman in a provincial city, finds himself confounded not only by family trouble (his wife Galina is cheating on him) but also by an order from above: to pick fourteen of his own employees for mobilisation. Making decisions nobody would ever want to make (there is, incidentally, a wonderful scene for this, in which Gleb’s view of the situation is set against those of his businessman friends), the hero barely notices how his own self is changing. Walking with Gleb down this not-so-pleasant but very believable path through the back alleys of a readiness to compromise is, at the very least, gripping; at most, it leaves you stunned.

As soon as the first news about *Minotaur* appeared, I unashamedly read the whole plot on Wikipedia, because I knew that what mattered here was not what exactly would happen, but how. I turned out to be right. This is not just big festival cinema; it is practically a cast of a particular moment in our shared life, the everyday signs of a universal and irreversible transformation sealed inside the frame. And, of course, to sketch the character of what I saw, I want to reach for associations with the classics 👇

First, the film has a scene whose cruelty is comparable, perhaps, only to Korean cinema. The closest match here is Bong Joon-ho’s *Parasite*, where for most of the running time the viewer is weighed down by the bleakest social irony, and then, at the climax, real brutality breaks out on the physical plane. For two hours we watch how the characters came to live like this, and for three minutes we actually see exactly what they have come to.

Second, the urban environment that enters the frame matters a great deal. It so happens that I defended my degree thesis on precisely this subject, “The Representation of the Urban Environment in European Cinema: The Case of Auteur Film of the 1950s–1960s”. It is even funny that back then it hardly occurred to me to look for urbanist subtexts in contemporary cinema, whereas now I would certainly include *Minotaur* in that study as a separate case. For the films of the New Wave it was fundamentally important to achieve documentary realism on screen, which is why the action was taken out onto the streets. Its attention to the details of urban space gives *Minotaur* exactly that: a realism that plunges you into a kind of paralysing déjà vu, down to the typeface on the posters and the shades of the passers-by’s clothes. It is worth adding that in the films of the European New Wave (let us count Italian neorealism and the Soviet Thaw in here too) buildings destroyed in the Second World War flickered through the frame as the backdrop to the mental state of many of the characters. What flickers in the background of the irreversible inner rearrangement of *Minotaur*’s characters we have seen with our own eyes, so from the screen it hits twice as hard.

I would like to watch *Minotaur* again with the ability to pause, rewind and examine the shots: there is more than enough detail to study, from the actors’ subtle facial expressions and the moments when Evgueni Galperine’s singular score emerges and fades away, to the tiniest signs in the background. I hope the chance will come in the near future.

---

## Mirror at the Vnutri Theatre: A Detective Cabaret That Isn’t a Cabaret

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/zerkalo-teatr-vnutri/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-10-27 (27 October 2026)
Work: “Mirror” is a 2026 stage production directed by Savva Savelyev.
Tags: theatre, Moscow
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/zerkalo-teatr-vnutri/

Recently I was lucky enough to get into a production with Savva Savelyev and Pavel Tabakov called [*Mirror*](https://vnutri.space/mirror). It is made by the theatre-space Vnutri, which describes its genre as a detective cabaret, but here I would disagree. It is more of a cabaret with notes of armageddon: when the worst has already happened and all that is left is to say “never mind, let’s waltz”.

The plot is based half on Heinrich Böll’s story “Murke’s Collected Silences” and half on Kurt Vonnegut’s novel *Slaughterhouse-Five*, and, as is not hard to guess, it is devoted to a specific historical event. Here the devastating bombing of Dresden is reckoned with through a chance collision between two of its witnesses from different generations: they share a traumatic background but have completely different truths.

Savva Savelyev and Pavel Tabakov play this story as a two-hander, but their energy is more than enough for the several decades of context the production draws on. A simple situation spins out into an ideological clash of catastrophic proportions, and that does not let you switch off from what is happening for a second. Even though the temptation to look away, as in life, is very strong.

The impression is colossal, so I recommend the production.

---

## Wicker: The Fairy Tale We Deserve

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/pletenyy-muzh-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-10-24 (24 October 2026)
Work: “Wicker” is a 2026 film directed by Alex Huston Fischer, Eleanor Wilson.
Tags: fairy tales, parable
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/pletenyy-muzh-2026/

[*Wicker*](https://youtu.be/leZkEhw37-8?si=eu2TMWzS9gwkgo4p) (released in Russia as *Pletyony muzh*, “The Wicker Husband”) is, literally, the fairy tale we deserve.

This parable about how it is best to live by your own wits has a very compact yet expressive language: in its script, its visuals and its symbolism alike. The medieval world of the little town where the action unfolds is built so painstakingly and inventively that you seem to fall right into it and find yourself in the middle of the street.

What is more, the characters have no names, only their trades: the Basketmaker (Peter Dinklage), the Fisherwoman (Olivia Colman), the Dishwasher and others. The forms of address say a lot about how this society is arranged, too: every woman except the heroine serves as an appendage to her husband, the Tailor’s Wife (or the Healer’s Daughter), the Baker’s Wife, the Innkeeper’s Wife. Nor do their own husbands respect them much, which is hardly surprising.

But what they enjoy most is ganging up on the Fisherwoman: she has no husband, they say, so she is not a complete person. Colman’s heroine is bullied so badly that she goes to the Basketmaker to ask him to weave her a husband (played by Alexander Skarsgård), and that is where the most interesting part begins. The life of the town does not get one bit better from every member of society now living in a traditional marriage, but the Fisherwoman’s life changes forever. The rest of the film is devoted to how other people’s happiness enrages people, and how hard it is to defend yourself against that hatred: one of the wisest statements, and at the same time one of the most modest in its means.

You can see this love and unlove in Russian cinemas from 5 November, courtesy of [@provzglyad](https://t.me/provzglyad).

---

## Yaga: A Supernatural Mystery for a Gloomy Autumn

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/yaga-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-10-23 (23 October 2026)
Work: “Yaga” is a 2026 series directed by David Frazee, Rachel Talalay.
Tags: series, mystery
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/yaga-serial/

The first episodes of the series [*Yaga*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1844) are finally out

This is a very solid, very compact supernatural mystery. For a gloomy autumn it is downright perfect. Private detective Rapp arrives in a remote small town in search of Henry Park, the missing son of a wealthy family, and plunges headlong into the local intrigues. Only nobody is especially eager to help him: not the local police officer Carson, not Professor Katherine, nor the missing Henry’s roommate (who for some reason is his spitting image; both characters are played by Hudson Williams). And then all sorts of supernatural phenomena make themselves known: not a minute’s peace for the characters or for the viewers.

The text of the play, which I had got through in advance, is used to the full. But even better is the part of the action built on top of it, developed by the series’ writers. The two episodes fly by in a single breath, and I hope the rest are made in the same spirit. The IC3PEAK song (the band has been designated a “foreign agent” in Russia) in the neon party scene fits perfectly. Evidently, Russian songs at raves are now a must-have for series on the streaming service Crave.

---

## The Seventh Player: Ted Lasso, Hockey-Style

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/sedmoy-igrok-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-10-22 (22 October 2026)
Work: “The Seventh Player” is a 2026 series directed by Sergey Pikalov.
Tags: series, sport
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/sedmoy-igrok-serial/

I have started watching [*The Seventh Player*](https://youtu.be/DaSEfPMJnp8?si=MgTdWn0NxM8pispP): art imitates ~~life~~, ~~Ted Lasso~~ [the KHL](https://t.me/kino_voice/1822) (Russia’s Kontinental Hockey League), as they say.

Judging by the first episode, the main feeling so far is one of bustle, but one thing is clear: this time Anton Lapenko has mostly been given “himself in the given circumstances” to play rather than one of the stock types (those, admittedly, are handled by the other characters). This is rather interesting, because his character keeps standing out in the plot too, through his “outsider” status, whether in relation to his wealthy family or to his own hockey team. So there is at least one reason to follow the action.

But I very much want to believe that there will be slightly fewer music-video-style scenes further on, because they dilute the pace a great deal, and there are other ways to create atmosphere. For example, the rather well-shot inserts of hockey matches.

---

## Kat Sandler’s Play Yaga: Baba Yaga Without the Stereotypes

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/yaga-pesa/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-10-19 (19 October 2026)
Work: “Yaga” is a 2019 book by Kat Sandler.
Tags: books, plays
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/yaga-pesa/

While waiting for the series [*Yaga*](https://youtu.be/RM4lcJ4yAiA?si=GIH2fmAikEpFrafz) with Hudson Williams. I read the play it is based on and came away thoroughly fulfilled

I adore it when Russian culture is woven into Western works without the crude stereotypes (what we call “cranberry”), and even more so when such things get a screen adaptation.

In Kat Sandler’s play the Baba Yaga we know is not an exotic souvenir on the shelf of Canadian drama but a full-blooded, contemporary heroine who thinks about her own attractiveness, craves the company of handsome men and gives off the kind of woman power you rarely see anywhere. The text has absorbed the morphology of the fairy tale and the standards of contemporary playwriting as if these two traditions had been made for each other.

For anyone planning to watch the supernatural true-crime series from 23 October, it is almost required reading. And for everyone who is simply interested in contemporary literature, I just recommend it highly: in many ways a unique experience)

---

## Half-Life: An Image of Impersonal Danger from the First Episode

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/poluraspad-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-10-16 (16 October 2026)
Work: “Half-Life” is a 2026 series directed by Maxim Sveshnikov.
Tags: series
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/poluraspad-serial/

I do not know what posters could capture the mood of [*Half-Life*](https://youtu.be/nWGrHxr7MY8?is=2LMm3scyCv8ITdiR) from its first episode better than these. A confrontation with an impersonal source of danger that is practically impossible to fight is an image very much in demand.

A story about nuclear tests in the USSR is well served by events unfolding in two eras in parallel. And it is a pleasure that we enter this story through Anna Mikhalkova’s character: you want to believe her and watch this heroine discover the truth.

## The Forest: A Meditative Canvas for Bad Weather

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/les-khranitel-zhizni-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-10-14 (14 October 2026)
Work: “The Forest” is a 2025 film directed by Vladislav Grishin, Irina Shapman.
Tags: documentary
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/les-khranitel-zhizni-2025/

While nature is treating us to not the most pleasant weather, you can enjoy picturesque landscapes in a cinema.

In Russian cinemas from 15 October, [*The Forest*](https://youtu.be/t335XJW4xbo?si=wATMfxMyeU03iDTv) (*Les. Khranitel zhizni*, “The Forest. Keeper of Life”) is a feature-length meditative canvas with the most breathtaking views of woodlands and their inhabitants. There is birdwatching, there is a touch of *V mire zhivotnykh* (“In the Animal World”, the classic Soviet and Russian nature programme), and there is macro photography of things you could not make out with the naked eye even standing in the forest yourself.

The crew made 14 expeditions to capture the primeval forest. The sounds were recorded separately, and the film surprises with them too. All in all, the most calming documentary in a long while)

All screenings are [here](https://ancientforest.ru/#about).

---

## You’ve Got Mail: Autumn Cosiness with Tom Hanks and Meg Ryan

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/vam-pismo-1998/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-10-13 (13 October 2026)
Work: “You’ve Got Mail” is a 1998 film directed by Nora Ephron.
Tags: rewatch, rom-com
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/vam-pismo-1998/

If you increasingly feel like watching something autumnally cosy, let me remind you of **You’ve Got Mail** with Tom Hanks and Meg Ryan.

The story of two bookshop owners who are rivals in real life and anonymous pen friends online has a wonderful, life-affirming style. As a bonus: the aesthetics of analogue devices, now enjoying a modest renaissance among the young, a great script and even touches of the “1998 screenlife” genre. Given how smoothly the film’s atmosphere flows from autumn into Christmas and New Year, it is especially timely for the coming months.

Watching it has some interesting side effects too: compare it with Russian cinema of the late 1990s and about the 1990s, and you may get the impression of a parallel reality. The characters of *You’ve Got Mail* have lactose-free decaf from Starbucks, gyms and internet correspondence, while the characters of [a Russian film from roughly the same period](https://t.me/kino_voice/1718) have New Russians, property scams and domestic disarray amid the capitalism that has suddenly descended on them.

---

## Leviticus: A Modest Horror Film with Taste

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/levit-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-10-12 (12 October 2026)
Work: “Leviticus” is a 2026 film directed by Adrian Chiarella.
Tags: horror
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/levit-2026/

On the subject of [horror films](https://t.me/kino_voice/1820).

I watched [*Leviticus*](https://youtu.be/gfkLVd23T64?si=E4aMUiD7IIHXqq6X) (in Russian it is translated just like that, **Levit**), and it is made modestly but with taste: like a good old straightforward horror flick on a fairly low budget. The plot has a religious community trying to combat teenage infatuation with terror-inducing rites, and, contrary to the ritual’s purpose, an evil spirit takes possession of everyone who has been through the “cleansing”. Worst of all, it appears in the guise of the beloved and tries to kill every time.

What looks especially fresh against the backdrop of today’s fashionable slow-burn horrors is the semi-everyday view of what is going on: some small-town school, some circle of sermon-goers, the stuff of ordinary life; the existential horror behind it still has to be made out, and it is not pushed in your face from the first frame.

The running time is quite modest, but nothing more is needed, because you feel for the characters as human beings: what kind of torment is it when you cannot tell whether the person in front of you is real or their incorporeal murderous double. I am pleased I watched it, and I like the thought that in our world your own feelings are the last thing you should be afraid of.

---

## Race to Monte Carlo: The Escapism of Silver Skates and the Drive of F1

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/bitva-motorov-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-10-11 (11 October 2026)
Work: “Race to Monte Carlo” is a 2026 film directed by Ilya Malanin.
Tags: Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/bitva-motorov-2026/

[*Race to Monte Carlo*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1225) (*Bitva motorov*, “Battle of Motors”) has managed to recapture the unique escapist mood of *Silver Skates* and at the same time (to my mind) to outdo [*F1*](https://t.me/kino_voice/877) in the drive of its racing scenes. And all this with an almost fairy-tale narrative (which here even works to its advantage).

The film about the development and fleeting triumph of the first car built in the Russian Empire has absorbed the best of the Russian and Hollywood traditions. It manages to cross the concept of the American dream with a road movie and an utterly sentimental view of a pre-revolutionary aesthetic that has sunk into oblivion. At the peak of its idealisation the film even lets you forget such basics as class divisions; here everything follows the example of *Silver Skates*. Impossible, but so good. Technically, *Race to Monte Carlo* also stands on very solid ground: the racing scenes are stunning, with a palpable nerve, and the costumes, sets and period cars catch the eye too. The team of supporting characters is written and played brilliantly.

What pulls you in, of course, is the dynamic between Ivan Yankovsky’s and Yura Borisov’s characters: they are the real engines of the picture. The wily, virtuosically brazen motoring enthusiast Andrey Nagel is the main character in the first part of the film, and he honestly balances somewhere between the uncompromising Bokov from *Fisher* and the many-faced Adidas from *The Boy’s Word*. Dmitry Bondarev, in whom an engineer’s passion gradually awakens, is even slightly more interesting to watch: he has contradictions, distrust of the world and an indomitable spirit. This duo is written really well and colourfully, even if it does not quite match the historical facts about Russo-Balt.

There is one weak spot: the central heroine, a motoring enthusiast played by Paulina Andreeva, fits into the inventors’ competitive friendship far too schematically. She appears and disappears like a strictly prescribed plot function and, sadly, never becomes a full-blooded figure (unlike, say, the heroine of *Silver Skates*). Another curious result (whether successful or not is for each viewer to decide) is Emperor Nicholas II: deliberately cute, there is no other word for it, he both supports the automotive inventors and shrugs off the chief antagonist’s denunciations. Unlike the wicked officials who very nearly wrecked Nagel’s entire car production.

All in all, it is worth seeing: this is big cinema, and it can quite rightly be called both an attraction and a sentimental reconstruction of a world lost forever; however you take it, it will impress you either way.

Off to think about the ~~Roman~~ Russian Empire

---

## The KHL as a Series: The “Mic on the Referee” Segment

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/khl-mikrofon-na-sudye/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-10-10 (10 October 2026)
Tags: sport, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/khl-mikrofon-na-sudye/

I keep half an eye on the [KHL](https://hd.kinopoisk.ru/sport/competition/34149/) (Russia’s Kontinental Hockey League; now and then I even root for Torpedo, on the same inexplicable principle that makes me root for Croatia in football).

But what really stuck with me is the **“Mic on the Referee/Player”** segment. That is when all the remarks and quips let fly on the ice become public property (except that the bleeping gets in the way)).

Now that is real mockumentary with a comic bent and an unpredictable plot. On top of that, such interesting behind-the-scenes details sometimes surface that you feel like praising the creators for the detailed work on their fictional world. Now I know, for instance, that at the Volga Arena in Nizhny Novgorod the little gate onto the ice is built so cunningly that not a single member of the officiating crew could get the better of it.

---

## Facts to Take In: Hipsters and 9th Company Have an Identical Ending

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/fakty-dlya-osoznaniya-stilyagi-9-rota/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-10-07 (7 October 2026)
Tags: Russian cinema, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/fakty-dlya-osoznaniya-stilyagi-9-rota/

From the [“facts to take in”](https://t.me/kino_voice/1226) series: **Hipsters** (*Stilyagi*, 2008) and **9th Company** (*9 rota*, 2005) have an absolutely identical ending. And a few more unexpected intersections (with spoilers):

- The finales of the two films are built on an absolutely identical scheme. For the whole film the heroes have been making a sacrifice (the hipsters expressing themselves and losing their place in society, the soldiers in Afghanistan “defending the motherland” and literally dying), and in the end it turns out that nobody needed that sacrifice at all and it was made in vain (it transpires that there are no hipsters in America, and hence no freedom in it either, while the command simply forgot about the 9th Company). But at heart the protagonists of both films are absolutely sure they have won, and the last frames say so outright: both the closing speech of Lyuty, the sole survivor, and the jubilant dance of Shagin’s and Akinshina’s characters in a crowd of other nonconformists from every subsequent era of Russian subcultures.

- The films have the same screenwriter, Yuri Korotkov. This partly explains both the first point and the couple that follow. But you must admit it is remarkable how the same screenwriting scheme works for a war drama and a period dramedy musical.

- Neither film has an unambiguous villain; that role is played by an impersonal system, which in both cases could probably be called by the same name, “the state apparatus”. The indifferent machine catches up with the hipsters and the conscripts alike; there is essentially nobody to hate, only vividly typed heroes to pity, which is very convenient.

- The heroes’ identities are interesting too. Both the soldiers and the hipsters have their names replaced by nicknames. Were our characters to swap places, the monikers Vorobey (“Sparrow”) and Gioconda would fit perfectly into the fashionable crowd, and Bob and Dryn (“Cudgel”) into the barracks. The viewer sees characters that are easy to connect with, while the villain in both films sees a faceless mass that there is no point in addressing by name.

- The figure of a woman whom the film’s heroes accept, but whom society outside the extreme situation the characters live in would condemn. Snow White in *9th Company* and Polza in *Hipsters* break patriarchal taboos and act as symbols rather than fully fledged personalities. Nevertheless, against their background the saintliness of the protagonists, who, once again, are to be pitied for being oppressed by the system, shows up beautifully.

Something to think about.

---

## Nimrods: The Film Green Day Produced

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/nimrody-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-10-04 (4 October 2026)
Work: “Nimrods” is a 2025 film directed by Lee Kirk.
Tags: music, road movie
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/nimrody-2025/

As is only proper, at the end of September I remembered the band Green Day (naturally, because of the line “wake me up when September ends”). And it turns out they have produced a decent film.

The road movie about teenage punks dreaming of making it onto the big stage is called [*Nimrods*](https://youtu.be/5mtbOhpqroo?si=p__bNpwIetYlatK6) (in English slang, “dimwits”). Tommy, Fred and Chad are Green Day fanatics who set off across America fully convinced that the musicians have invited them to open their big New Year’s concert. And although nothing goes to plan, the boys grow up, get to know the world and, as befits a film with a finale in a New Year atmosphere, master some timeless values. There are clichés and conventions in the plot, of course, but they come across more as part of the humour and do not spoil the impression at all.

In short, excellent genre cinema with bits of concert thrown in (you can top up your playlist after watching). All the actors are as natural as can be in their roles, the teenagers and the older generation alike. By a funny coincidence, the small parts include Jenna Fischer and Angela Kinsey, the famous Pam and Angela from *The Office*. It is great when all the elements of a concept come together to winning effect, and this is exactly such a case.

---

## Girlyanda: A Graphic Novel About an Artist with a Claw

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/girlyanda-kniga/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-10-03 (3 October 2026)
Work: “Girlyanda” is a 2024 book by Alexey Khromogin.
Tags: books, comics
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/girlyanda-kniga/

Once again I have been impressed by a graphic novel

I bought **Girlyanda** («Гирлянда», “Garland”) at random, won over by the blurb about the hero, a comics artist whose hand has turned into a claw. Admit it, who has not been there: you are living your life, bothering nobody, and suddenly some important part of you changes forever.

I read it with great pleasure in two sittings: the plot is gripping, and the atmosphere of a snow-covered city before New Year comes as a gift. Best of all, the comic itself is like a box with a false bottom: because the protagonist runs comics-drawing workshops in the story, we as readers also pick up some of the craft, and even get a few reading recommendations.

So I recommend **Girlyanda** too, if only to join in solving the protagonist’s dilemma.

---

## Five Russian Shorts from the Days of Russian-Cypriot Cinema

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/dni-rossiysko-kiprskogo-kino-korotkiy-metr/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-09-27 (27 September 2026)
Tags: festivals, short films
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/dni-rossiysko-kiprskogo-kino-korotkiy-metr/

Yesterday I watched almost the entire short film programme at the [Days of Russian-Cypriot Cinema](https://t.me/kino_voice/1791) festival, and I want to share 5 of the Russian films with you. If you get the chance, watch them too, they are wonderful.

- [*Mama prosila ne vzryvat meteorit*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/13741896/?socialAlias=a2lub192b2ljZQ%3D%3D) (“Mum Asked Me Not to Blow Up the Meteorite”) is a charming story about a boy from a snowbound village who befriends a meteorite and decides to help it gather all the fragments that have broken off. Enchanting magical realism (by now the trademark of the studio Red Pepper Film) and a lead actor who holds your attention 100%, Yaroslav Golovnev.

- [*Kholodny dush*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/13929095/?socialAlias=a2lub192b2ljZQ%3D%3D) (“Cold Shower”) is a compact story about second chances for yourself and for others. The forty-year-old heroine is a single mother who works at the sorting depot of an unnamed online marketplace and, accordingly, is not rolling in money. At work she has a subordinate: a kidult pure and simple, always late but incredibly sweet, with a charming smile, a thermos of fragrant coffee and his signature sandwiches at the ready. How could you not fall in love, especially if it is mutual? But the guy trails problems of his own, and they will have to deal with them together.

- [*Kak my deda provozhali*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/11739404/?socialAlias=a2lub192b2ljZQ%3D%3D) (“How We Saw Grandad Off”) is another Red Pepper Film production, which, incidentally, won the festival’s main award. A family at loggerheads travels to bury the grandfather; since his passing, relations between the generations have gone completely sour. Only a miracle can reconcile the parties to the conflict, and it will be a somewhat unusual one. My sincere admiration for the light pouring through the screen and for the most appetising vatrushki (sweet cheese buns) in contemporary Russian cinema.

- [*Marusya*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/12476676/?socialAlias=a2lub192b2ljZQ%3D%3D): the USSR, shortages, ration cards. Marusya, a thief (an incredible performance by Alexandra Bolshakova), is trying to carry an expensive chandelier out of a flat so she can go on the run to the Black Sea. It turns out that the flat is home to a naive mother with a baby, holy simplicity itself, who does not even understand that the father has abandoned them. Marusya faces a difficult moral choice, and watching it is a real psychological drama.

- [*Vremya kormit golubey*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/8427917/?socialAlias=a2lub192b2ljZQ%3D%3D) (“Time to Feed the Pigeons”) is another short about the wise, the good and the eternal, in which the only thing that threw me was the hero’s nonchalance in the face of expulsion from university, unrealistic by the standards of 2026. To cheer up his grandmother, her student grandson recreates a pigeon-feeding scene beneath her windows and, it seems, achieves his goal

---

## Smaragda: An Unhurried Film That Exceeded Expectations

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/smaragda-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-09-26 (26 September 2026)
Work: “Smaragda” is a 2024 film directed by Emilios Avraam.
Tags: drama, Cyprus
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/smaragda-2024/

[*Smaragda*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1791) turned out to be an unhurried film, but that is where its wisdom lies. All in all, it exceeded my expectations.

After her mother’s death the heroine suddenly finds herself sidelined: a young colleague with a blog and followers is about to be made the presenter of the programme that Smaragda devised from scratch, and her health is throwing up problems. Her personal life is also far from stable and happy. In a state of existential deadlock, Smaragda starts a blog about environmental problems and, in parallel, gets to know herself anew.

The film could be compared to *Fleabag* or *The Worst Person in the World*, and fairly so. At the same time, the Cypriot version stands out for its gentler intonation and its attention to the heroine’s inner world. If you have a taste for films about the philosophy of life, this one is for you.

## Problem Child: Tangible Madness and an Absolute Must-Watch Series

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/trudnyy-rebenok-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-09-25 (25 September 2026); updated: 2026-10-08
Work: “Problem Child” is a 2026 series directed by Vladimir Bolgov, Velimir Rusakov.
Tags: series, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/trudnyy-rebenok-serial/

## 25 September 2026

I am watching [*Problem Child*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1764) with a kind of half-forgotten zest

The series has such a perceptible, tangible air of madness and inadequacy that it plunges you into an unnatural viewer’s comfort. Perhaps it would even be appropriate to call it “ecstasy”: wow, someone on screen has it even more unhinged than in real life. But even in such an upside-down, strange world there is room for love (all ages and social strata really are subject to it), friendship and optimism. And now the story of an injured footballer who moonlights as a tutor to pay for an operation and return to the sport plays in new colours.

 And all the actors are exactly in their places: I will now definitely be following the projects of Gennady Blinov (the footballer-historian) and Boris Deikov (the problem child himself).

A wonderful piece of work, and one with individuality against the background of many comedy series.

## 8 October 2026

I have finished [*Problem Child*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1788), and now I can say with confidence that it is an absolute must-watch series.

Besides what has already been praised in the posts above, something else needs noting. This is a rare case of a series whose pace does not sag or break in the middle of the season (a rarity these days): there is no urge to drop it or skip ahead to the end. Form here is in complete harmony with content, absurdity in both, but very well balanced. A separate bow to the screenwriters for the genuine urge to keep a notebook of quotes while watching.

And the footballer-historian joins my personal collection of characters in the category “you don’t want to be with him, you want to be him”. Stay tuned.

## Gorbushka. The Heart of Russian Rock: Directing in the Solovyov Manner

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/gorbushka-serdtse-russkogo-roka-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-09-23 (23 September 2026)
Work: “Gorbushka. The Heart of Russian Rock” is a 2026 series directed by Timur Fedorov.
Tags: documentary, music
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/gorbushka-serdtse-russkogo-roka-serial/

After watching the documentary concert series [*Gorbushka. The Heart of Russian Rock*](https://youtu.be/F_0ngyPncMI?si=FSDk1DRwY937-UGD), I caught myself thinking that the directing here is of an entirely Solovyov type.

Of course, the connection with the methods of Sergei Solovyov (the director of *Assa*) lies not in direct echoes but purely in the atmosphere: when, within a single work, the hot somehow starts to combine with the blue and the prickly, that is it. A documentary series about the rockers whose prime years were spent at the Gorbunov House of Culture (the Moscow venue known as Gorbushka) is a video memoir, a concert and even a bit of mysticism with a parallel storyline. And as a bonus, a wonderful opportunity to top up your playlist.

If you love documentaries and genuinely Russian rock, I unequivocally recommend it.

## Mayday: I Nearly Switched It Off at Minute 15, and I Would Have Been Wrong

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/meyday-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-09-20 (20 September 2026)
Work: “Mayday” is a 2026 film directed by John Francis Daley, Jonathan Goldstein.
Tags: comedy, action
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/meyday-2026/

I nearly switched this film off at minute 15 (hence the meme, in fact)

[*Mayday*](https://youtu.be/om5Un9X720M?si=neuYff0TZ4oT7Jbo) starts out as a boring, pompous B-grade Hollywood action film, but that is a test of your staying power. Everyone who manages to break through that stage will get a wonderful comedy (at one point at least I laughed out loud).

It is 1987, and Troy (Reynolds), an American reconnaissance pilot who has been shot down, ends up ~~a prisoner~~ a guest of Nikolai (Kenneth Branagh’s character insists on being called Nick). The Soviet citizen turns out to be an ardent fan of America: his home is decorated with the appropriate merch, and his favourite film is *Top Gun* with Tom Cruise **🇺🇸** Helping Troy get home, Nick himself catches fire with the dream of getting asylum in the USA, so he bravely (and just as absurdly) goes through all the stages of escaping from the USSR with his newly acquired friend.

Despite a certain inevitable “cranberry” (crude Russian clichés) and naivety, *Mayday* is good as a reminder that laughing at yourself is sometimes very useful. And if you like it when people in films speak English with a thick Russian accent, watch it without the dubbing.

## Matty Manson’s Razlomy: Prose That Pulled a Fast One on Me

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/razlomy-kniga/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-09-19 (19 September 2026)
Work: “Razlomy” is a 2025 book by Matty Manson.
Tags: books
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/razlomy-kniga/

**Contemporary Russian prose that pulled a fast one on me**

I started reading Matty Manson’s novel [*Razlomy*](https://books.yandex.ru/books/PjwnNnAe) («Разломы», “Fractures”), a sweet urban fantasy about a guy called Vinny who can pass the most intimate questions on to the universe, while he himself has been tormented since the age of 13 by the mystery of his mother’s disappearance. Oh, and he is a bit of a punk too, so it is easy to fall for the “cover” from every side.

Having got through 15% of the text, I, as befits someone with my occupational deformation, began fantasising about a screen adaptation: who would play whom best, among Western actors, naturally.

The neural network and I stumbled upon the information that Matty Manson is the pseudonym of a Russian writer, and that the text, for all the rough edges I had put down precisely to the translation, is originally Russian, some 5 minutes into our search for the best actor for the lead role.

Pluses: now I know about an actor who is a perfect fit for Vinny, by the name of Louis Partridge. Minuses: I feel hellishly deceived.

In short, do not make my mistakes: check the origin of a text before casting your dream cast.

## Tony: A Sweet Film Not to Be Watched on an Empty Stomach

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/toni-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-09-17 (17 September 2026)
Work: “Tony” is a 2026 film directed by Matt Johnson.
Tags: biopic
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/toni-2026/

[*Tony*](https://youtu.be/k1MVnzd2aVc?si=qUHn8CxWS_uZejns) is a sweet, inessential film that is best not watched on an empty stomach.

The story of how the famous chef Anthony Bourdain came to be, played by the negatively charismatic Dominic Sessa, is full of twists that at first glance are well worn: the cocky young man does not get his scholarship, his beloved turns out to have another boyfriend, and on his very first night in a provincial town Tony has his wallet cleaned out (a wallet filled, incidentally, with money stolen from his parents’ house). Life (with the face of Antonio Banderas) diligently (though not to the point of flatlining) douses Tony with icy water so that something may come of the young man, and to some extent this even works as the engine of the plot.

What hooked me was the rapid transformation announced in the trailer: I decided to watch the film to find out how a person who saw himself as a writer turned, over 3 months of holidays, into a cook by vocation.

For all the room the subject gives for unleashing passions on screen, the film is surprisingly sterile: of emotionally engaging scenes there is only one spectacular rush in the kitchen. And it was as if (owing to the predictability of the biopic) there was not much need to worry about Tony’s own fate. The place of the hero you want to root for is taken by his colleague and pal Saul (Leo Woodall), a hail-fellow-well-met type who collects vices and splinters from the door frames of the bedrooms he has managed to visit. Against such a supporting character with a far more dramatic fate, Tony himself loses out.

But the best thing the film demonstrates, both in words and by its own example, is that it may be better to become at least somebody than to remain nobody.

---

## Connor Storrie, Saint Laurent and a Pop-Culture Phenomenon

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/konnor-storri-saint-laurent/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-09-16 (16 September 2026)
Tags: pop culture, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/konnor-storri-saint-laurent/

I love it when someone explores pop-culture phenomena that fascinate (me), and so I got absorbed in a [long-read post by a colleague](https://t.me/shreddingcat/9732)

It is about the Connor Storrie phenomenon in the Saint Laurent advertising campaign. And, I think, one can mentally add his co-star from the series about hockey players, Hudson Williams, who has been shot for Balenciaga. We saw them in the corresponding outfits, by the way, [back at Oscars time](https://t.me/kino_voice/1341).

Still, cinema and the power of fan communities are a great thing, at times influencing the world veeery tangibly. Even the example of these fashion houses shows how, from the 1990s to the present day, the policy of “models will be the face of the brand” has given way to “the face of the brand will be people who carry a cultural trail and a certain ideology behind them”. And which other public figures can be as rich in context as actors?

What is especially sobering is the answer to the question “Why does a high-fashion brand need the hero of teenage daydreams and the cause of girlish tears, if his audience is not even particularly solvent?”. I kept wondering, and now, thanks to the reading, I have realised that a whole strategy is hiding behind it.

## Coyote vs. Acme: A Successful Mix of Animation and Corporate Critique

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/khitryy-koyot-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-09-09 (9 September 2026)
Work: “Coyote vs. Acme” is a 2026 film directed by Dave Green.
Tags: animation, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/khitryy-koyot-2026/

[*Coyote vs. Acme*](https://youtu.be/QEHesDZSqoY?si=Rw8wUjQh_S78VFcD) turned out to be the most successful possible mix of unexpected elements: animation and live action, cultural clichés about Albuquerque (thank you, Vince Gilligan) and a critique of corporations.

The plot about a cartoon character who sets out to defend justice (and his tasty dinner) with the help of a human lawyer looks far more interesting on screen than it sounds in a synopsis. The film is the sweetest thing, practically for all ages, with humour that is not primitive yet not bloodthirsty either, and with wonderful casting hits (this is the funniest John Cena I have ever seen). And also a touching story of enmity behind which friendship was actually hiding (I have no occupational deformations whatsoever)

Because the action takes place in Albuquerque, and the lawyer hero is very fond of flashy advertising, I kept wanting to imagine Saul Goodman as played by Bob Odenkirk in his place) But even without that, *Coyote vs. Acme* is mesmerising: behind its apparent simplicity the film hides great charm. In Russian cinemas from tomorrow, and I strongly recommend going and having a great time.

## The 2x2 Idents by the Artists of Prostye Veshchi

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/zastavki-2x2-prostye-veschi/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-09-04 (4 September 2026)
Tags: animation, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/zastavki-2x2-prostye-veschi/

An off-topic post about a very humane initiative

The TV channel 2x2 (Russia’s animation channel), together with artists with mental disabilities from the design bureau [Prostye Veshchi](https://prostieveschi.ru/about/) (“Simple Things”, an inclusive workshop in St Petersburg), has created television idents: five artists came up with characters and stories, and 2x2 digitised them and made animated idents, which have been on air on the channel since 1 September.

The result is bright and unique, and it is cool that such things make it onto the telly at a time when it is getting harder and harder to find anything interesting there. And drawings like these, by the way, can not only be seen on screen but also bought as souvenirs in the Prostye Veshchi shop: I personally got stuck on the [page](https://shop.prostieveschi.ru/veschi-s-printami/) with notebooks and postcards.

## CTRL+FEST 2.0 Asks “What Next?”: Films That Look for the Answer

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ctrl-fest-2-0-chto-dalshe/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-09-03 (3 September 2026)
Tags: festivals, list
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ctrl-fest-2-0-chto-dalshe/

The [CTRL+FEST 2.0](https://t.me/ctrl_fest) festival asks the question “What next?”, and I, as in any unclear situation, decided to think about which films would help find the answer. Many films of recent years fit; they are different and at times contradict one another, but it is in argument that truth is born, so I think that is for the best. The conflict that can be written out for each of the films also hides the answer to the question “What next?”

- **Everything Everywhere All at Once** (2021): when every branch of reality is laid out before you, yet it is so hard to choose your own

- ***Rag Union*** («Тряпичный союз», *Tryapichny soyuz*, 2014): when the future is made up of pushing one thing and having another fall

- ***Mezhsezonye*** («Межсезонье», “Off Season”, 2021): when the search for the right answer turns into a tragedy

- ***Proekt “Konets sveta”*** («Проект „Конец света“», “Project Doomsday”, 2026): when complete solitude means frightening freedom

- ***Acid*** («Кислота», 2018): when your whole life lies before you, but you do not understand what you can give it, apart from an iPhone charger

- ***The Dog of Many Tomorrows*** («Космическая собака Лида», *Kosmicheskaya sobaka Lida*, 2026): when all the answers were already in your thoughts, and you only needed a little time to find them

- ***Ya rugayus*** («Я ругаюсь», “I Swear”, 2025): when the best way to bring your future closer is to fight for it to happen at all

## Hard to Be a God: A First Episode Without the Bombast, and a Finale Worth Reaching

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/trudno-byt-bogom-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-09-02 (2 September 2026); updated: 2026-10-18
Work: “Hard to Be a God” is a 2026 series directed by Dmitry Tyurin.
Tags: series, Strugatsky
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/trudno-byt-bogom-serial/

## 2 September 2026

The first episode of **Hard to Be a God** (*Trudno byt bogom*) has an absolutely wonderful aura: none of the knock-you-off-your-feet bombast that is traditional for Russian fantasy.

This interpretation of the Strugatskys does not claim to be the fundamental, final truth; on the contrary, you can tell it was made by contemporaries for contemporary viewers. Sergey Bezrukov’s Don Condor every now and then lets slip the smirk of Belov from *Brigada*. Nikita Kologrivy, too, does what he does well, and in the very first episode he is already squabbling with the local king in the raised tones of Koshchey from *The Boy’s Word*.

And so, in small details and shades of intonation, every actor is, to my mind, 100% in the right place: Viktoria Isakova, Irina Pautova, Lev Zulkarnaev, Ravshana Kurkova, Alexander Demidov and many, many others. The audience giggled approvingly when screenwriter Andrey Zolotarev, playing the treasurer, nodded with great decorum in a small scene of the first episode. I wonder whether his character will get a big story arc?)

A particular pleasure was Aleksandar Radojičić as Don Rumata, the protagonist through whose eyes we begin our acquaintance with the world of Arkanar. Unlike the actors listed above, he carries no fixed associations for the mass audience, and that is great, because it means we cannot predict his character: a genuine intrigue. Besides, in real life Aleksandar has the sweetest Serbian accent, and the one thing I did not manage to work out while watching was whether he had been dubbed over entirely, or whether a slight accent had been kept as a sign that the hero, even by the standards of the setting, has arrived from some very, very distant land. To my mind, it would be great to convey the hero’s otherness through the actor’s natural accent.

Also, colleagues at Wink (the Russian streaming service) have made a very informative (and entertaining) [long read on the universe of *Hard to Be a God*](https://xn--90aagb7bchcbmvfi0jqa.xn--p1ai/): you can take a quiz to find out which Observer you are and leaf through the characters’ dossiers. Alongside watching the series (which, as you have gathered, I plan to keep doing), I will be reading the Strugatskys’ novel and watching Aleksei German’s feature-length version: I want to immerse myself fully in this metaverse.

## 18 October 2026

Getting to the finale of [*Hard to Be a God*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1754) turned out to be harder than I thought, but it was all worth it.

First, the difficulties: in my view, from somewhere around the middle the series becomes cramped in its own cluttered world. The rhythm falters, the episodes become unevenly packed, and so viewer engagement suffers too (mine, at any rate).

On the other hand, Don Rumata as played by Aleksandar Radojičić was a pleasure. He is detached enough for an Observer and at the same time sincerely interested in gaining the experience of mortals. This both saves him and lets him down; here everything depends on how you feel about the finale. In my opinion, it never hurts to remember at what price the passage from dark times to light is won.

---

## Chudo: A Graphic Novel About an Angel in Yekaterinburg

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/chudo-kniga/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-08-30 (30 August 2026)
Work: “Chudo” is a 2026 book by Lyosha Zavoyskaya.
Tags: books, comics
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/chudo-kniga/

If you want to lift your mood, look at the world with renewed love and give your soul a rest, you will need [*Chudo*](https://books.yandex.ru/comicbooks/UlIzF76S?utm_campaign=users_referral&amp;utm_medium=referral&amp;utm_source=direct_link) («Чудо», “Miracle”).

This is a small graphic novel (or comic, as you like) about the adventures of an angel who has descended from the heavens to Yekaterinburg. He longs to see the world of people, and the guides he gets are the spirited Masha and her kind-hearted younger brother Tima. But the most important thing in this comic is the small components that add up to an utterly inimitable whole:

- A unique style unlike anything else: the golden glow of the angel’s wings, the lights of the night city and the flickering windows of high-rise blocks break through the screen (or the paper). If the notion of “dopamine” can be applied to comics, then it applies to *Chudo*.

- A fresh take on the well-established plot of a heavenly being visiting Earth. We have seen it in the film *Moy paren — angel* (“My Boyfriend Is an Angel”), in the series *Good Omens* and in many other places. But the adaptation to the ways of a contemporary Russian metropolis, with moments from the life of young people, news on the television, jokes about working in catering and a father who has left the family, feels utterly incomparable.

- The infectious kindness of what happens, which never slides into a cloying moral about Christian values. I do not know how the author created such an effect, but the plot requires no involvement whatsoever in terms of faith or other sensitive matters: what takes shape before us is simply the story of one acquaintance with Earth and the verdict of a hero who has seen humanity in all its manifestations.

And I have already added *Chudo* to my list of dream adaptations.

---

## Big Pharma: The Pleasure of Visual Language

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/bolshaya-farma-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-08-28 (28 August 2026)
Work: “Big Pharma” is a 2026 series directed by Danil Chashchin.
Tags: series, thriller
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/bolshaya-farma-serial/

I have started [*Big Pharma*](https://youtu.be/D2WYEJ30rZo?si=zWO7pxdbwh3BD0eE), and I am getting real, sincere pleasure from the visual language of this series.

Cinematographer Batyr Morgachev uses a fisheye lens here, and wide-angle perspective, and swirling bokeh (that blurred background around Goroshko that seems to curl in motion). You cannot take your eyes off it, in short.

All this, plus the actors’ well-aimed performances, compensates me for a slight sense of contrivance over how richly the main characters live: by every indication a no-name researcher who spent a couple of decades working on a single drug, and his plastic-surgeon son, whose prosperity one believes in, of course, but not to that extent. Nevertheless, I will definitely keep watching: this is an extremely gripping pharmaceutical thriller.

---

## OPG: Yuri Chursin as Conscience

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/opg-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-08-25 (25 August 2026)
Work: “Organized Criminal Group” is a 2026 series directed by Pyotr Buslov.
Tags: series, crime
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/opg-serial/

I have started watching the series [*OPG*](https://youtu.be/75cy3k0rDQY?si=l_D1GYz-JzhrPFiU) («ОПГ», “Organized Criminal Group”), drawn by Yuri Chursin as the Conscience of the protagonist, who in turn is played by Pyotr Buslov.

His character, nicknamed Vorkuta, comes out of prison after a sentence of some 20 years, and a clingy Conscience trails after him. As a result, an incorporeal substance with the face of Yuri Chursin makes the former racketeer apologise to all his victims from the 1990s. The premise is interesting, but on the details I have a couple of observations:

**1️⃣** First, I cannot shake off the thought that this very much resembles the central idea of Yura Borisov’s character in the film *Captain Volkonogov Escaped*. There he wanted to apologise to the surviving relatives of the repressed. It will be interesting to see how a similar character motivation unfolds in comic circumstances and a 1990s setting.

**2️⃣** Second, the filming location genuinely bothers me: for the cityscapes of the fictional town of Dalnemorsk, where *OPG* takes place, they for some reason chose a highly recognisable square in Moscow’s Kitay-Gorod, with a view of buildings in an unmistakably Moscow style, hardly associated with provincial seaside towns. Somehow this immediately hits your ability to trust what is happening on screen, unfortunately.

But I am genuinely delighted by Chursin’s transformations: as Conscience (that is, a subject invisible to everyone except his “owner”) he keeps transforming, and every time he does it with invention. By the second episode I already wanted a spin-off with Conscience, as he plays it, as the main character. It distantly recalls (today is my day for finding intersections) Evgeny Tkachuk’s work in the recent [*The Dog of Many Tomorrows*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1372) (*Kosmicheskaya sobaka Lida*, “Lida the Space Dog”), where it was also done with great invention and real sweep.

---

## April X: A Neon Thriller with Connor Storrie

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kod-sna-2025/

My personal summer blockbuster season continues, because **April X** (released in Russia as *Kod sna*, “Dream Code”) is about to hit cinemas.

This is a neon psychological thriller with Connor Storrie ([the man turned a Russian accent into a whole trend](https://t.me/kino_voice/1213), how can you not love him), who, judging by the trailer, is in for all sorts of scrapes. What is most interesting, the film comes out here 2 weeks earlier than in American cinemas. If only we could get an early look at season 2 of *Heated Rivalry* like that.

## What the New Spider-Man and The Odyssey Have in Common

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/chelovek-pauk-i-odisseya/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-08-21 (21 August 2026)
Tags: blockbuster, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/chelovek-pauk-i-odisseya/

What do [the new *Spider-Man*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1690) and [*The Odyssey*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1666) have in common?

It is remarkable how these two summer blockbusters actually echo each other. In **The Odyssey** the hero has forgotten himself and, roughly speaking, where he was going. In **Spider-Man** it is the other way round: everyone around has forgotten the hero, and because of that he now does not know where to turn. By and large, these are two dimensions of one and the same phenomenon, differing only in the outward or inward expression of the personal crisis we see on screen.

And Tom Holland (not only him, as you can see from the meme, but that is not the point right now) has had the chance, in the guise of his characters, to stand both on the outside of the protagonist’s suffering (Telemachus, the son of Odysseus, who tries somehow to cope with the world while his father remembers his place) and on the inside (Peter Parker himself). The actor really got two roles from the series “choose your type of existential crisis”, and both, fortunately, look convincing and three-dimensional, as shown by a contemporary and for contemporaries.

So it turns out that the biggest blockbusters of 2026 put at their centre heroes who are not so much fighting evil as trying to define themselves anew, regain a sense of belonging and understand where to go next.
*The existential crisis has officially become the plot of mass cinema, apparently because it has stopped being something purely personal*.

---

## Minions & Monsters: Unexpectedly Cinephile Entertainment

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/minony-i-monstry-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-08-19 (19 August 2026)
Work: “Minions & Monsters” is a 2026 film directed by Pierre Coffin.
Tags: animation
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/minony-i-monstry-2026/

[*Minions & Monsters*](https://youtu.be/V-O-uBaHk3c?si=_26y1Bj5o3K1WPww) unexpectedly turned out to be very cinephile entertainment.

The first thing to know: the trailer for the feature about the yellow henchmen of evil gives an impression of a completely different plot from the one you are going to see. I did not expect much from the trailer, and what I got was a genuine multi-genre production drama about the Minions making a film.

I see little point in writing much about the plot: this is the case where you just need to catch the Minions’ vibe, ride this attraction and catch all the cinematic references to Charlie Chaplin, Buster Keaton and anything you associate with 1920s Hollywood. And a bit of backstory of the Minions themselves from the beginning of time is extremely entertaining to learn too: it is a very pleasant buddy-movie part of the whole film)

It remains to work out what the hares from *Restlessness* are doing in a film about the Minions.

## Olivia Wilde’s The Invite: Watch Without Expectations, and Mind How the Characters Are Dressed

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/priglashenie-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-08-16 (16 August 2026); updated: 2026-08-17
Work: “The Invite” is a 2026 film directed by Olivia Wilde.
Tags: dramedy, costumes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/priglashenie-2026/

## 16 August 2026

The film [*The Invite*](https://youtu.be/OJ19I9q_hOQ?si=emKmsv1_YOeCZUYU) is best watched without firmly built expectations.

There are many surprises inside this dramedy staged like a chamber play. Joe and Angela, a long-married couple whose relationship has been battered by life, played by Seth Rogen and Olivia Wilde (who also directed the film), have long since stopped communicating in any form other than quarrels. Joe, a music teacher, is unhappy with his job, his students and his daily routine, while Angela, a housewife, is looking for new acquaintances and suddenly invites over the neighbours who frankly drive him mad because they make noise at night 🔞

It sounds like the standard setup for a comedy about a couple rebuilding their relationship after one decisive encounter, but *The Invite* is in fact nothing of the kind. Practically a televised play with four characters, it is supplied with classical music as a background with stunning precision, and abounds in shifts of emotional register and play with the visual side.

A separate achievement of the film is the neighbour couple played by Penélope Cruz and Edward Norton. As a duo they have stunning chemistry, but each on their own has a simply magnetic energy. I especially like how Cruz’s character, next to Norton, comes across as a kind of Tyler Durden: she instantly sees through the psychology of whoever she is talking to and manipulates them masterfully. One of the best female characters I have seen lately, and one of the coolest acting ensembles overall.

## 17 August 2026

By the way, pay particular attention to how the characters of [*The Invite* ](https://t.me/kino_voice/1723) are dressed

The hosts, Joe and Angela, wear clothes in dull pastel tones (washed-out mint and faded denim), which individually go with the interior of the flat but do not harmonise with each other at all. Indeed, the characters themselves have long been ill-matched, suffering from the boredom of their life.

We see a completely different combination in the guests: Pina and Hawk are dressed to match each other. Both wear black tops, which emphasise their deep connection and at the same time their mysteriousness (and they did arrive with rather mysterious vibes, it must be said).

The costume designer Arianne Phillips [said](https://www.wmagazine.com/fashion/the-invite-costumes-olivia-wilde-arianne-phillips-interview) that she deliberately made Joe’s and Angela’s costumes clash in shade: it is an important characteristic of their relationship. She described the black of the guest couple as a symbol of togetherness and mutual chemistry. And the simple silhouettes were chosen to save viewers from premature conclusions about the characters.

---

## Danelia’s Heads and Tails: If Brother Were a Rom-Com

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/orel-i-reshka-1995/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-08-13 (13 August 2026)
Work: “Heads and Tails” is a 1995 film directed by Georgiy Daneliya.
Tags: rewatch, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/orel-i-reshka-1995/

If *Brother* had been a rom-com with a happy ending, the result would have been [*Heads and Tails*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/40866). It is a great stroke of luck that Georgiy Daneliya really did make it, in 1995.

Plot-wise it is all simple: Oleg Chagin (Kirill Pirogov, who, incidentally, rose to fame in *Brother 2*) returns to Moscow from a shift job in the North to win his beloved back from the husband she has suddenly acquired. In Moscow, naturally, nobody is waiting for him, except for a fateful encounter with Zina Prishchepkina, a simple canteen worker played by a veeery young Polina Kutepova. Then begin the adventures of the “just an ordinary Tuesday in Russia” variety: the hero accidentally saves a stranger’s life, meets a New Russian (an unrecognisable Leonid Yarmolnik), instantly becomes his friend, and then falls victim to Gypsies, capitalism and hasty conclusions.

The most valuable thing in the film is the inimitable aura of an era at the turn of the millennium: one richly represented in cinema, yet here not coated in the usual clichés but shot as if through the eyes of a witness following the fate of an ordinary contemporary. The landscapes of 1990s Moscow are mesmerising too: the Oktyabr cinema alone flashes through the frame a dozen times, as if to remind us that in thirty years everything in the city has changed, and nothing.

But the main thing is Kirill Pirogov’s Chagin: a true hidden treasure in the line of generational heroes like Kostik from *The Pokrovsky Gate*, Bananan from *Assa*, Ivan from *The Courier* and Danila from *Brother*. Chagin is lost, cynical and cunning in moderation, yet not at all cruel, not mean, and he has not lost his humanity. He is, of course, a protagonist with a full set of negative qualities, but he switches them on, as if on purpose, only with good intentions.

---

## Obsession: The Year’s Most Talked-About Horror Turns Out to Be a Comedy

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/obsessiya-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-08-09 (9 August 2026)
Work: “Obsession” is a 2025 film directed by Curry Barker.
Tags: horror, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/obsessiya-2025/

During the first half of [*Obsession*](https://youtu.be/0NK6s9o3hkE?si=AyntY76tkq4X4rT9) I laughed practically every five minutes. The awkwardness of Bear’s attempts at social activity is exaggerated to the point where it looks like an entirely comedic device.

But once the horror component unfolds, the impression it leaves is, of course, indelible. Director Curry Barker creates terror with a minimal set of means; what triggers you most are the unnatural, instantaneous leaps of emotion in the characters. Inde Navarrette in particular does something blood-chilling using nothing but her facial expressions. Even when here and there you notice a mannequin standing in for a human figure with CGI (the film has a modest budget), it is still outweighed by the shock you have already been through.

The very concept of the body being alienated from the mind (as in *Get Out*) leaves you numb. And the theme, of course, is a burning one: both that love is blind and that you cannot force someone to love you. An unequivocal recommendation to watch (just not over dinner).

---

## Spider-Man: Brand New Day: Feeling on a Par with a Superhero

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/chelovek-pauk-novyy-den-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-08-03 (3 August 2026)
Work: “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” is a 2026 film directed by Destin Daniel Cretton.
Tags: superheroes, blockbuster
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/chelovek-pauk-novyy-den-2026/

[*Spider-Man: Brand New Day*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1687) lets every viewer feel on a par with a superhero.

Doing so could not be easier, because in the new instalment Peter Parker appears as someone starting over from scratch, slightly burnt out and, like any young adult, confused. It seems the friendly neighbour could not have been any different in 2026: this new sincerity in Tom Holland’s portrayal is winning at the very least, and at most it reboots the franchise perfectly. Let me remind you that after the previous instalment, as a result of Doctor Strange’s spell, everyone in the world (even those closest to the hero) forgot Peter Parker.

The adventures of Spider-Man in a world where he loses not only his external but also his internal supports look more than plausible. The most varied special effects are, of course, in place and at their best, but Parker’s flights between skyscrapers look convincing not only thanks to the cool graphics. Holland has made his Spider-Man not just a “neighbour” but a true contemporary, who learns to find support within himself and to give it to others, even when it seems the critical point has come. But he does his superheroing: turning enemies into friends, emptiness into connections, and all of it to a cool soundtrack.

Maybe, in 2026, that is the main superpower.

## Monsters, Inc.: The Speech Quirks That Dubbing Hides

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/korporatsiya-monstrov-2001/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-07-28 (28 July 2026)
Work: “Monsters, Inc.” is a 2001 film directed by Pete Docter, David Silverman, Lee Unkrich.
Tags: animation, dubbing, rewatch
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/korporatsiya-monstrov-2001/

Healing my psyche after [this](https://t.me/kino_voice/1671) took a rewatch of ~~Heated Rivalry~~ **Monsters, Inc.** in the original. [As usual](https://t.me/kino_voice/1218), I tracked the quirks of speech that the dubbing hides from us:

- The most meme-worthy pet names of Wazowski and his beloved, which recently went viral as a trend, sound in Russian like “Zmeyusik-lapusik” and “Kruglik-bublik” (roughly “snakey-sweetie” and “roundy-bagel”). In English they are, respectively, Schmoopsie-poo and Googley Bear (sometimes Googley-woogley). This seems to be a case where the dubbing won)

- The little girl Boo was voiced by the three-year-old daughter of one of the voice actors, so in the original this little heroine sounds literally like a real child.

- And the next two points are for the most well-watched. Roz, the obnoxious administrator who torments Wazowski with bureaucratic nitpicking, when she reveals her true role, talks exactly like the fixer Mike Ehrmantraut from *Better Call Saul*/*Breaking Bad*. His famous “That's what happens next” matches the animated heroine right down to the intonation, and that is astonishing.

- The main villain, the purple lizard Randall, in one scene (comically enough, in the locker room) gives off the most brutal Rozanov vibes from *Heated Rivalry*. If you have watched the series, you will not be able to miss the similarity of intonation in the phrase “Aha, sure” with its villainously blunt mockery. The character was wonderfully voiced by Steve Buscemi)
