## Disclosure Day: A Spielberg Thriller with a Fantastically Bad Script

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/den-razoblacheniya-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-07-27 (27 July 2026)
Work: “Disclosure Day” is a 2026 film directed by Steven Spielberg.
Tags: science fiction, thriller
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/den-razoblacheniya-2026/

**Disclosure Day** turned my day off into a day of disappointment.

Steven Spielberg’s thriller with a fantastically bad script, and with Emily Blunt and Josh O’Connor, literally traumatised me.

In the first half of the film about two humans chosen by an alien intelligence who are trying to come to terms with their gift, there was nothing particularly suspicious. A few genre conventions, solemn faces, thoughts of saving the planet, if not the entire universe: standard stuff. The bend-over-backwards move of having Blunt’s heroine speak Russian with the appropriate accent is credited too, it actually perked me up ([I love that sort of thing](https://t.me/kino_voice/1213)).

But in the second half some kind of phantasmagorical absurdity began: a spectacle devoid of logic, credibility and common sense. The kindness of the plot or sweet nostalgia does not explain it. Specifically, the problems are these:

- It turns out that the characters began preparing for the appearance of the gifted Margaret (Blunt) even before they knew who would turn out to be the bearer of alien abilities at all. For the whole film they build a set that completely copies the heroine’s house and childhood bedroom, and then, with the most ingenuous look, are surprised to meet her.

- The collective antagonist that tormented the gifted pair for the whole film ultimately found its zen, so that the finale could unfold in “whatever will be, will be” mode, while the main villain sank into heavy thoughts about the fate of humanity.

- In the finale the heroes put classified footage of the aliens on air, and the broadcast is instantly picked up by channels in every state, and then around the world (there are shots of everyone in Russia glued to the screen). It is so true to life that in 2026 the world is still united by television. But do not worry, the authors have not forgotten about neural networks: one of the producers of one of the broadcasts in one of the states declared with an air of importance that the footage received was definitely not AI. You can literally see with the naked eye that the aliens in the footage are the real thing.

- The main characters, a fragile weather presenter and a lanky IT guy, managed to hold on for a considerable time to the bonnet of a mangled car being dragged along the rails at full speed by a train, and then also to jump onto a carriage while dodging an oncoming train. Not a single item of clothing torn, not a single wound, dislocation or bruise sustained: sleight of hand and no cheating. I understand that the film is science fiction, but any science fiction must be grounded in some rules of its screen world, not give the authors a free hand for complete nonsense.

- The alien device can do everything the script needs at any given moment and plugs any plot hole. The gadget lets you enter another person’s mind, take on anyone’s appearance and even generate electricity, in case the TV studio suddenly loses power (of course, the world has to learn the truth about the aliens from the television).

At best, while watching *Disclosure Day* I found it hysterically funny. But on reflection I have been indignant for three days now.

---

## The Odyssey: The Quintessence of Nolan’s Directorial Signature

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/odisseya-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-07-26 (26 July 2026); updated: 2026-07-30
Work: “The Odyssey” is a 2026 film directed by Christopher Nolan.
Tags: blockbuster, adaptation
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/odisseya-2026/

## 26 July 2026

**The Odyssey is my new favourite Christopher Nolan film.**

*Getting ahead of myself, I will headline this post with the thought that this seems to be the quintessence of Nolan’s directorial signature: all the Nolan themes (from the search for an unreachable home to responsibility for genius), the formal and structural devices with asynchronous narration and leaps in time, the actors’ appearances, are all here in peak form, the best possible. Surpassing the degree of perfection of each of these components of success is now within the power of, perhaps, only Nolan himself in his next work.*

First and foremost, this is a practically perfect screen adaptation of the familiar stories of ancient Greek folklore: the Cyclops, the Trojan horse, the giant Laestrygonians, Circe who turns sailors into pigs. Each of these stories is realised on screen so painstakingly and with such respect for its legendary status that for this reason alone I am ready to urge everyone to see this film. None of the stories with these creatures is some empty scare for the sake of a spike of adrenaline in the audience or an insert in the form of a spectacular attraction. They look, as befits elements of Homer’s *Odyssey*, monumental to the point of awe. I had never imagined a Cyclops looking like that, or the process of turning into pigs happening like that, because I could never have imagined these phenomena being so realistic, so inseparable from the elements of the world familiar to us. I simply fell in love with the way Nolan realised this and stitched it into the fabric of a spectacular blockbuster.

**\*️⃣** Incidentally, it is important to clarify that I took all the news about *The Odyssey* during filming and in the run-up to the premiere with a certain scepticism. Some of Nolan’s works (*Tenet*, for example) remained in my memory as a pretentious attempt to build a film on formal devices without particularly meaningful content, and the fear that the same would happen with *The Odyssey* was great. But all my sceptical thoughts were shattered by the magnificence of what I saw.

Do not be afraid of the three-hour running time (the pace of events ideally lets that time fly by unnoticed), of miscasting (there is none) or of the film’s convoluted structure: the balance of all the parts makes the picture truly outstanding and a must-see.

## 30 July 2026

What else makes [*The Odyssey*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1666) interesting is its gallery of characters and the key ideas they embody (and which lend themselves beautifully to memes).

 **1️⃣**Odysseus as played by Matt Damon is not shown as a trickster or a sly fox with a dash of comedy, as one might have expected looking back at the original text. Moreover, he is practically reduced to the “little man” who happens to live in a historic era (as if there were any reason to dwell on that subject in 2026), partly thanks to Damon’s type, since he has often had to play “ordinary guys”. The result is a hero utterly close to our perception, who, guided by the laws of his time (it happens to the best of us), made the decision to create the Trojan horse, and only later understood that there is something higher than the mores of an era. And the years the hero spent wandering in search of home, or simply in oblivion, can be interpreted in different ways, from PTSD to a liminal purgatory in which Odysseus pays for his moral crime. Even the memes about *The Odyssey* come with stills from *Oppenheimer*, where the hero himself regretted what he had invented.

**2️⃣** It is appropriate here to mention Athena as played by Zendaya: she acts as the materialisation of that timeless law of, if one may put it so, humanism, which Odysseus neglected. The shots of her silent condemnation have become memes about an extra ice cream eaten or hours spent scrolling the feed precisely because everyone knows disapproval of their own actions on various scales. So nothing human is alien to the hero of the ancient Greek poem, and that is one of the secrets of the film’s success.

**3️⃣** The memes about Penelope, the bow and the suitors feasting on Ithaca cover, if only superficially, the second most important plot vertical of *The Odyssey*. In my view, the film gives it slightly less attention than it could have, but the priorities are still set correctly. While someone is trying to return home, someone else gets to watch that home literally cease to exist and fill up with people who should not be there. Both funny, as the memes suggest, and sad beyond belief.

---

## Pluribus and Heated Rivalry: The Parallel Release of Two Series as a Phenomenon

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/pluribus-heated-rivalry-paralleli/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-07-24 (24 July 2026)
Tags: series, analysis
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/pluribus-heated-rivalry-paralleli/

Naive parallels you did not need.

It seems that we as a society have not reflected enough on the fact that the parallel release of the series [*Pluribus*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1179) and [*Heated Rivalry*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1205) is a phenomenon in itself.

**Pluribus** showed a universe where the heroine, a writer, had created a series of stunningly popular fantasy novels whose main characters were in a conventional relationship, while she herself considered her work mediocre and hypocritical, because she could not count on success for the unconventional romantic line she really wanted to describe. She had to go on writing, to please the fandom, about the kind of love that suited the readers.

In reality, in parallel with the release of this series, the whole world was also watching **Heated Rivalry**, the screen adaptation of precisely such a novel, in whose case the writer did not bet on traditional mores and wrote as she felt. Need I point out that a certain popularity (to put it mildly) is what both the series and the book got in the end?

*And what if Carol Sturka from Pluribus had written the novel she always wanted, without looking over her shoulder at public taste? Would that have worked, in the end, as a butterfly effect towards a turn into the branch of reality where no armageddon happens?* Think about it.

One way or another, it is good that the apocalypse happens in the universe where creativity is limited by prejudice. And for our reality, apparently, all is not yet lost.

---

## Restlessness: The Heroes Find Themselves in Something Like a Quantum Purgatory

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/nepokoy-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-07-20 (20 July 2026); updated: 2026-08-07
Work: “Restlessness” is a 2025 film directed by Leonid Shmelkov.
Tags: animation, interview
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/nepokoy-2025/

## 20 July 2026

A great rarity: behind this stylish poster hides a no less intricately composed film, [*Restlessness*](https://youtu.be/3Qiu-KRJsMw?si=_BSi1e_hxAMYkxnI) (*Nepokoy*).

The plot of this adult animation is unpretentious precisely because quite early on it dissolves in favour of a controlled chaos of events, whose interpretation is left to the viewer’s discretion.

Yasha and Bernard are driving together to an unnamed distant destination and decide to spend the night on the way at an ordinary, moderately shabby roadside hotel called the Rosa. And there everything turns out to be stranger than strange.

Perhaps, without going into the details of what happens, it would be fair to say that the heroes have found themselves in something like a quantum purgatory. The hotel has a Madame, who is receptionist, cook, chambermaid and entertainer in one: she makes breakfasts from the dishes of roughly every cuisine in the world, hosts concerts, film clubs and all sorts of garden games. Only none of this gives the new guests any pleasure, because leaving the hotel proves impossible, first physically and then mentally.

What the hotel will be for you, and what the numerous metaphorical turns of the plot will turn into, is a matter of associations, imagination, viewing experience (if you wish, you will see Lynchian absurdity, and if you wish, a Wes Anderson aesthetic) and of the desire to reflect: *Restlessness* gives you full scope for that. For myself, I formulated what I saw as an extended visualisation of the opposite of what Pushkin wrote in the lines *“there is no happiness in the world, but there is peace and freedom”*. When there is everything for happiness but no possibility of making an independent decision in its favour, restlessness begins.

And this specific *Restlessness* can be experienced in cinemas (and only in cinemas; no release on streaming platforms has been announced) from 30 July.

## 7 August 2026

After [this interview](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4013087/) I wanted to rewatch [*Restlessness*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1648).

Director Leonid Shmelkov talks about the concept of this feature-length animation in such a way that you literally discover some things anew. It was pleasant to find that I had defined the essence of the pink hares and the annoying runners who flash on screen more than once exactly as was intended.

---

## Cold: An Immersion That Knocks You Off Your Feet

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kholod-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-07-16 (16 July 2026); updated: 2026-09-22
Work: “Cold” is a 2026 series directed by Aleksey Kazakov.
Tags: series, interview
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kholod-serial/

## 16 July 2026

From today you can watch [*Cold*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1629) (*Kholod*), a chilling series with Lyubov Aksyonova.

When I watched the first episode, I literally lost track of time: from about the fifth minute I was simply clutching my head, trying not to start voicing the scale of the plot catastrophe out loud in unprintable language. The sheer number of misfortunes that befall Zhenya, Aksyonova’s heroine, at times really makes you forget to breathe. The very case where, while watching a series, you are not once tempted to check your phone.

At the same time Zhenya is so resilient, enduring and patient that it is hard to deny her sympathy, and the desire to root for her is the main motivation to watch to the end. Every scene shows very directly what kind of real deprivation is at stake (moral and physical), without sparing the viewer and without trying, as it were, to “hide” the uncomfortable moments of the story outside the frame. A series of rare sincerity about the powerlessness of the little man before the unjust blows of fate.

## 6 August 2026

In a recent interview with Sobchak (the Russian TV journalist), Lyubov Aksyonova told a story that is hard to forget: her father spent 4 years in a penal colony and then proved his innocence in court. She was 19. Now she plays Zhenya in [*Cold*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1643), a drama from Ivi, START and Wink (Russian streaming services) about a woman unjustly convicted over a car accident. When you know this, you look at the role quite differently.

Today my [interview](https://theblueprint.ru/culture/specials/cold-interview) with Lyubov Aksyonova, Linda Lapiņš and Alexandra Babaskina came out in The Blueprint. We talked about trauma, how it breaks you, makes you grow up and sometimes becomes a source of strength, and about how to stay human through all these trials.

Inside there is a lot that the trailer will not tell you: why Aksyonova, for the first time in her career, drew up a detailed map of her character and why the early Zhenya went by the code name “Snegurochka” (the Snow Maiden); Lapiņš’s real story of a girl whose fate seemed predetermined but which ended at Yale University; and why Sasha Babaskina is sure that children are sometimes stronger than adults.

The piece turned out insanely beautiful, not only in its ideas but visually: special love to the photographer Maxim Tarakanov and the whole team

As always, I picked out the quote that is key for me; it was voiced by Lyubov Aksyonova ⤵️

> *Cold* is a story about how, even from the most terrible ordeal, a person always has the chance to come out towards love and to lean on it. Love can turn out to be stronger than the desire to destroy. And only love can really defeat death. And that, probably, is the most important thing for me.

By the way, after the conversation with the actresses the following episodes look different: you begin to notice how Zhenya changes her body language, the rhythm of her speech and even her breathing from one period to the next. I checked it myself.

You can read the piece [at the link](https://theblueprint.ru/culture/specials/cold-interview).

## 15 September 2026

I deliberately saved up more episodes of [*Cold*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1643) to watch them in one go, and I was not wrong.

The series, and Lyubov Aksyonova’s performance in particular, has an immersive effect that somehow knocks you off your feet. I lost my sense of connection with reality during the first two episodes, and I lost it again watching all the following episodes back to back.

All thanks to what I would call “the aura of a thick novel”. This series is nothing like the typical alternation of events and consequences for various characters. *Cold* gives the impression of a vast canvas woven from a multitude of threads in different shades. First, the “threads” are never lost, even if they may meet again many years later. Second, among them there is anything you like except black and white. Third, while this “canvas” is being woven, it is worth stocking up on patience, just like the heroine, Zhenya. And the “embroidery” is so dense that you feel a physical urge to “reread” the series even before the finale. I am really looking forward to the last episode.

## 22 September 2026

Wrapping up the conversation about [*Cold*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1772)

I took part [in a poll by colleagues from Kinopoisk](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4013398): we exchanged opinions on the series’ finale. I am pleased, which shows in my rating of 9/10 too, but what seems especially important to me is the gap left for the viewer’s hope in the closing frames. What matters is not even that Aksyonova’s heroine had some choice and some decision was made, but rather the reminder that after the most terrible ordeals a person retains some power over themselves, even if the outside world cannot be controlled. Lyubov [told me about this in our interview](https://t.me/kino_voice/1698), and it is great that exactly this is felt by the end of the viewing.

I separately recommend reading my colleagues’ opinions: each of us took a liking to (or, conversely, remembered with a negative context) something different. And I invite you to the comments; I am sure there is plenty to discuss ⬇️

---

## The Holy Boy: When the Village Would Be Better Off Without Its Righteous Man

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/dolina-ulybok-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-07-13 (13 July 2026)
Work: “The Holy Boy” is a 2025 film directed by Paolo Strippoli.
Tags: horror, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/dolina-ulybok-2025/

In cinemas now: [*The Holy Boy*](https://youtu.be/G7DFSS3WGH0?si=x8BHvR6czpg-vqMD) (*La valle dei sorrisi*, released in Russia as *Dolina ulybok*, “The Valley of Smiles”), an Italian horror drama about a strange town where everyone is far too happy.

The plot develops around Sergio, a PE teacher withdrawn after the loss of someone close (we are kept starved of specifics about the loss for a very long time), who comes to the town of Remis for 3 months as a substitute. At first glance he notices the suspiciously elevated mood all around, and then finds out for certain: the town has its own saint, who heals those suffering from grief after losing loved ones. The miraculous abilities belong to Matteo, a 15-year-old schoolboy, who gradually takes over the status of protagonist.

*The Holy Boy* seems to be the case where, contrary to the proverb (the Russian saying has it that no village stands without a righteous man), the village would be better off without its righteous man. And the problem is not Matteo himself but how the locals treat him: their consumerism is what serves as the trigger of the catastrophe. The script, incidentally, lets you focus your attention on the most varied aspects, from the difficulties of growing up and the problems of parenthood to a condemnation of the current trend for non-toxic communication, processed traumas and all the rest. At times, admittedly, so much is left unsaid that it starts to resemble plot holes, but that is a question of one’s personal readiness for small abstractions.

Incidentally, before the screening you should bear in mind that a couple of moments will be missing: these days not all of the film’s scenes meet the requirements for showing on the big screen, but it is good that on the whole it has made it to us.

In Venice, at any rate, *The Holy Boy* received the award of the Federation of Italian Film Clubs. So there is something to discuss there after watching.

## Raz malchishka, dva malchishka: Short in Length, but Very Palpable Reading

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/raz-malchishka-dva-malchishka-kniga/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-07-04 (4 July 2026)
Work: “Raz malchishka, dva malchishka” is a 2025 book by Asya Demishkevich.
Tags: books, horror
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/raz-malchishka-dva-malchishka-kniga/

I do not very often like anything from contemporary literary fiction in Russian, but recently, on a recommendation, I read Asya Demishkevich’s novel [*Raz malchishka, dva malchishka*](https://books.yandex.ru/books/iVnOelfS?utm_campaign=users_referral&amp;utm_medium=referral&amp;utm_source=direct_link) («Раз мальчишка, два мальчишка», “One Boy, Two Boys”) practically in one breath, and now I am going to recommend it to you.

I do not know how to characterise its genre more precisely: it is a coming-of-age novel, folk horror and topical allegorical absurdity all at once. Thirteen-year-old Andrey is sent off to the army by his wicked stepmother (the morphology of the fairy tale crops up often in this text, do not be surprised), and there everything is somehow strange: the squad includes a couple of dead men, there are no barracks at all, and in their place iron bedsteads stand in a bare field under the open sky.

The further adventures of the “recruits” are more interesting to read than to learn from a retelling, so here I will limit myself to general raptures. Demishkevich’s style is contemporary in the best sense of the word, and this shows not in attempts to mimic the plausible speech of a Russian teenager! I am talking about the complete removal of the boundaries between the reader and what is happening, which are usually, conventionally, represented precisely by the author’s style. The words seem to narrate and comment on the events for the reader all by themselves (and there is plenty in those events to think about and to laugh at). And the ending, in my view, for all its unexpectedness, is more than logical. Short in length, but very palpable in its impressions.

---

## You Don’t Mess with the Zohan: One of the Best Sessions of Restorative Escapism

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ne-shutite-s-zokhanom-2008/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-06-27 (27 June 2026)
Work: “You Don’t Mess with the Zohan” is a 2008 film directed by Dennis Dugan.
Tags: comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ne-shutite-s-zokhanom-2008/

I would never have thought that one of the best sessions of restorative escapism for me would be watching **You Don’t Mess with the Zohan**.

The plot about a counter-terrorist (Adam Sandler) who has grown tired of fighting and faked his own death to start a new life may seem one-layered. Perhaps its strength lies precisely in laying out all the between-the-lines meanings in plain view, so that each viewer picks the main ones according to their own inclination. And yes, the hummus jokes won me over. Yes, I watched it in the original, so I fell for the accents too ([apologise](https://t.me/kino_voice/1213)). Yes, the humour in the film is on the dark side and belongs rather to the “borderline good taste” category (if you have seen *Borat*, it is comparable). All this is paid off by one gigantic “but”, which those who have seen it will probably name easily, and those who have not (I envy you now) will surely be able to note while watching.

For all its frivolity, this is a film-cum-social utopia about what one would so like to see in the world but which is so impossible to achieve. Everyone does what they love. Disagreements are in the past. The sharpest remarks addressed to one’s neighbour are labelled in advance as jokes (and invite mutual ribbing). I do not know how this film passed me by in its day, but it found me, perhaps, at the best moment, and I hope it will brighten one of your evenings.

---

## Pasha: A Handcrafted Island of Calm in a World of Adrenaline Content

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/pasha-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-06-20 (20 June 2026); updated: 2026-08-04
Work: “Pasha” is a 2026 series directed by Anton Kolomeets, Evgeniya Tamakhina.
Tags: series, dramedy, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/pasha-serial/

## 20 June 2026

Once again a team in merch (I want some!!): Amediateka (a Russian streaming service) presents the series **Pasha** from my [list](https://t.me/kino_voice/1543) of things to look forward to.

Judging by the first episode, this is a very touching, sparkling dramedy with gentle humour and intonation. Pasha, a Muscovite who is half Uzbek by ethnicity (and therefore runs into every stereotype), is trying to find somewhere to live for 10 days, because his mother’s friend has settled into his own flat with a child who has chickenpox (and Pasha, as luck would have it, never had it). So the hero literally and figuratively cannot find a home in his native city.

As the creators said, Askar Ilyasov is present in every scene of the series. And I will add that he sets the tone and mood of everything that happens, and that creates something inimitable. The premiere is on 10 July, and I cannot wait.

## 14 July 2026

I carried on watching [*Pasha*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1590) after the first episode at Pilot (the Russian series festival in Ivanovo), and got exactly what I expected.

The series has an intonation rare these days, that of a kind of lyrical comedy where nothing especially funny seems to happen, sometimes even the opposite, something sad, and yet every so often you smile. Simply because life goes on, the sun peeks through the clouds, the neighbours act up and the relatives are toxic. Life does not end there, after all.

I will also keep watching closely because Askar Ilyasov promised something special in the seventh episode. Given that every episode of *Pasha* looks like a handcrafted island of calm in a world of adrenaline content, I am inclined to trust that advice.

## 4 August 2026

I watched all the episodes of [*Pasha*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1641) in one go and had the loveliest evening.

Askar Ilyasov promised that something special awaited us in episode 7, and he did not deceive us: it is the peak of the season in conviction, sincerity and the absence of any sense of a boundary between the two sides of the screen. But personally I was most moved by episode 6, whether it was the images of a Moscow school in the 2000s that touched a nerve, or the rare chance that materialised before little Pasha to replay a dysfunctional scenario, this time with a happy outcome (in the best traditions of contemporary psychology).

In any case, I highly recommend watching *Pasha*: the value lies not only in the image of the protagonist but in the scattering of types surrounding him. Every supporting character is genuinely distinctive and interesting; they are all, to borrow a line from children’s prose, “alive and glowing”. A rare feeling for contemporary series.

## Pilot 2026: Independent Projects I Want to See in Full

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/pilot-2026-nezavisimye-proekty/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-06-18 (18 June 2026); updated: 2026-06-20
Tags: festivals, series, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/pilot-2026-nezavisimye-proekty/

## 18 June 2026

The block of independent projects at Pilot (the Russian series festival in Ivanovo) is over, and here are the projects I hope we will see in full in the future:

**GBU “Zhizn”** («ГБУ „Жизнь“», “State Institution ‘Life’”)

As the project’s team put it, “we tell the story of traditional values in a non-traditional way”. The series will be devoted to an unusual funeral home that tries to make even the part of life connected with death life-affirming. A soft, blackish (naturally) but very likeable comedy.

***Volshebnaya pyl*** («Волшебная пыль», “Magic Dust”)

A talented chemist (Yulia Volkova) loses her job and suddenly discovers that her neighbour is cooking up something suspicious. Having wrecked the neighbour’s home-cosmetics business with her vigilance, the woman is plotting something.

***Vverkh za mechtoy*** («Вверх за мечтой», “Up After the Dream”)

A romantic comedy with Polina Denisova and Grisha Vernik. An underrated producer is forced to work with an arrogant showman (and former classmate at that), but their enmity gradually gives way to passion. The “from hatred to love” mechanism works brilliantly in cinema, and I have known one of the producers, Liza Bulatova, since school, so I believe in this story.

***Privet, Karolinka*** («Привет, Каролинка», “Hi, Karolinka”)

A children’s adventure fantasy about a girl who investigates the mysterious disappearance of her grandmother with the help of a magic piece of chalk. The project’s highlight is that the main villain is played by the stylist Alexander Rogov. The spiritual heir of *Lyubopytnaya Varvara* (“Curious Varvara”, the children’s detective series), which means a bid for a quality children’s series.

## 19 June 2026

The morning begins with independent projects: today it is science fiction, aliens and mockumentary.

*Shisha*

A project about a regional evil spirit who lives in the age of social networks and decides to relaunch its villainous brand to avoid the closure of the “Agency of Dirty Tricks”. For this, “Kolkhoz Production” is brought in. A little raw (which is absolutely normal for the pilot of an independent project), but already a very charming spiritual heir of *What We Do in the Shadows* and *The Magic District* (*Volshebny uchastok*).

*Kosmos nash* (“Space Is Ours”)

A blogger who films so-called contactees (people who have made contact with aliens) reaches a million subscribers and suddenly loses his dog. Instead he acquires a suspicious female fan with the manners of an alien. Also a pilot that is likeable at the level of its concept and has every chance of success after some polishing.

## 20 June 2026

Today’s block of independent projects pleased with youth themes:

***Kod 102*** («Код 102», “Code 102”)

Possibly the strongest independent project of this year. A vibey neon series about young musicians from Ufa who are trying to break through and realise their dream. The project has distinctive features: the colour of Bashkortostan and Ufa, the participation of local performers, and an excellent cast: Chingiz Garaev, Arseny Kasperovich, Pyotr Skvortsov and other cool artists.

***#Ne\_moya\_zhizn*** («#Не\_моя\_жизнь», “#Not_My_Life”)

A story about the destructive influence of social networks on our lives, told through teenage characters. A high-school girl who dreams of becoming a blogger accidentally finds a phone and starts posting videos from it. After that everything goes uphill for her, but as soon as the owner demands the phone back, the situation stops being pleasant.

***Tozhe mne lyubov*** («Тоже мне любовь», “Call That Love”)

A drama about different types of relationships: between romantic partners, between sisters, with oneself. All the relationships, naturally, are unhealthy. It looks very much in the spirit of the recent [*Half Man*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1489).

---

## Living Anew: The Series That Came Out Suspiciously Quietly

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/zhizn-zanovo-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-06-18 (18 June 2026); updated: 2026-11-04
Work: “Living Anew” is a 2026 series directed by Aleksandr Boguslavskiy.
Tags: series, streaming
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/zhizn-zanovo-serial/

## 18 June 2026

**Living Anew** (*Zhizn zanovo*), which was among the things I was [looking forward to](https://t.me/kino_voice/1543) with interest, has fully lived up to expectations.

The time-travel comedy looks like a very gripping, solid piece of work. Alexander Yatsenko, in the role of an ambulance doctor tired of life and of his own inadequacy, is very convincing, as *Arrhythmia* showed, and this series uses that advantage 100%. The humour here is charming and unhackneyed, so watching is a great pleasure.

As a result of an MRI machine breaking down, the hero from our time is transported to 2002, and the panorama of St Petersburg in the 2000s, shown to the music of Glukoza (the Russian pop singer), simply takes your breath away. The cinema is showing *Progulka* (“The Stroll”), and every student has a pager on their belt. And the hero himself finds himself in that time with all the knowledge of his 40 years, which he puts to use in his own way.

A super project, which I will await impatiently and will definitely watch to the end.

## 4 November 2026

The series [*Living Anew*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1558) came out on the streaming platforms suspiciously quietly, and I, as I had planned since Pilot (the Russian series festival), am continuing to watch it.

Everything is done attractively, rhythmically (perfect for watching many episodes in a row!) and without the dreary clichés inherent in the time-travel genre. Not without some confusion in its moral compass, but Dima the doctor (Alexander Yatsenko/Anton Shavrin) in 2002 tirelessly extricates himself from one mishap after another, trying meanwhile not to incur the notorious butterfly effect, and he does it rather wittily. A compliment to the script and the costume designers: the wardrobe of Lenya, the protagonist’s best friend, is so stylish that you want to steal the whole lot for personal use in 2026.

The main advantage, which reveals itself after a few episodes, is the perfect casting of the characters in their youth and in adulthood. Anton Shavrin (the young version of Yatsenko) wonderfully conveys the state of a forty-year-old doctor locked in the body of an 18-year-old student, a real find of the series. Robert Zakharyan, who plays Artyom Tkachenko’s character from 2002, is altogether a most successful comic type; I hope he will reveal himself further in that capacity. And I very much like the heroines in their youth: Alisa and Kristina are played by Elizaveta Ishchenko and Margarita Dyachenkova (whom I have been following for a long time, because we have known each other since school), and each has an elusive intonation carried over from her adult version (Karina Razumovskaya and Elena Podkaminskaya respectively).

I have a few final episodes left for dessert, and I am stretching them out as best I can.

---

## Luca: Incredible Beauty, Both in Image and in Meaning

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/luka-2021/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-06-09 (9 June 2026)
Work: “Luca” is a 2021 film directed by Enrico Casarosa.
Tags: animation, rewatch
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/luka-2021/

*Silenzio Bruno!*

The part of my brain responsible for the calendar arrival of the holidays ordered me to rewatch Pixar’s **Luca**. I have things to share:

- The film is very underrated. Incredible beauty, both in image and in meaning. It was worth rewatching if only for the thought: people capable of accepting us even as sea monsters (read: as ourselves) do exist!

- Actually, after the first viewing I did not remember that Luca himself is also a sea monster. I was sure he had merely made friends with a sea monster)) The Mandela effect has never been so personal.

- Respect for how the film shows boys growing up: through friendship, vulnerability, curiosity and the right to be strange. Luca and Alberto grow up not because they become tougher, but because they learn to hear themselves and each other. For a healthy coming-of-age, it is just the thing.

- This is one of the few Pixar works that do not flaunt their “adult side”, like, for example, both [*Inside Out*](https://t.me/kino_voice/140) films or *Soul* (with all due respect). Here, on the contrary, they play a game with the adult viewer to the very end called “interpret it however you like”. This is not unambiguous depression or the afterlife; here, go and work out what it even means to be a sea monster?

- I have poured on the honey; now time not to forget the minus. The finale, to my taste, is made mostly in favour of pedagogical considerations (and therefore boring and blurred). One can argue about what the freedom the heroes strove for so hard actually is, and what their friendship meant to each of them. But in terms of meaning the film rather loses out from such a “something for everyone” decision. It is good that the picture’s merits outweigh this with room to spare.

---

## The History of Concrete: John Wilson Turns His Gaze Right Under His Feet

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/istoriya-betona-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-06-04 (4 June 2026)
Work: “The History of Concrete” is a 2026 film directed by John Wilson.
Tags: documentary, festivals
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/istoriya-betona-2026/

Starting today is the [Beat Film Festival](https://beatfilmfestival.ru/schedule) (the Moscow documentary festival), which has a most interesting programme this year (including [on Kinopoisk](https://t.me/beatfest/5408), Russia’s largest film database and streaming service, so you can watch right at home).

I managed to see in advance the film [*The History of Concrete*](https://beatfilmfestival.ru/movies/istoriya-betona) by John Wilson, the creator of the absurdist HBO show *How To with John Wilson*. The director continues to observe the contradictory everyday life of New York, now turning his gaze right under his feet, to concrete, in whose history we as humanity take insufficient interest.

He makes this choice in the midst of a creative crisis, after his collaboration with a major streaming service has come to an end (the inner workings of creativity get into the frame here too, which we always appreciate). Together with John we find ourselves at a screenwriting masterclass and learn the secrets of making “soap” that succeeds with the mass audience (*oh God, I felt ill at how the ingredients overlapped with* [Heated Rivalry](https://t.me/kino_voice/1213) *point by point, but I pretended not to see or hear*). The director decides to follow the soap-makers’ instructions and to shoot his history of concrete by precisely these principles.

Among the documentary observations are shots from the distinctive corporate life of the concrete industry and rambling conversations with strangers that at times startle the ear (a couple of interlocutors told the director that “there isn’t too much concrete in cities, the problem is that there are too many people in cities”). Towards the end the film transforms altogether into a philosophical reflection on the fragility of human nature in our thoroughly material world. In short, you will definitely not be left without discoveries after watching: do not miss it if you like looking at the world from a new angle. And I will be back with other gems from the programme.

---

## Which Moped with Chrome-plated Handlebars…: Word-Juggling Beyond All Limits

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/malenkiy-moped-s-khromirovannym-rulem-kniga/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-06-01 (1 June 2026)
Work: “Which Moped with Chrome-plated Handlebars at the Back of the Yard?” is a 1966 book by Georges Perec.
Tags: books
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/malenkiy-moped-s-khromirovannym-rulem-kniga/

A book break

Seizing the opportunity, I brought back into my life the long-forgotten pleasure of reading a book (a paper one!!) on the beach. The text I chose, however, was not carefree but, on the contrary, one hiding existential horror under a thick layer of post-irony (and who are we to forget about cognitive dissonance on a day off?)

**Which Moped with Chrome-plated Handlebars at the Back of the Yard?** is a novella by Georges Perec balancing on the edge of unbearable lightness and unliftable absurdity. This author’s mastery of literary word-juggling is beyond all limits; I am off to read all his other texts now. In this regard, by the way, it would be right to mention the novella’s translator into Russian, Vladislav Kirichenko, as well: this seems to be a case where the text only gained from the translation.

The novella’s plot is simple: a company of Parisian party-going intellectuals who sit in cafés for days on end help a pal wriggle out of being called up for the Algerian War. Well, France had one of those in the 1950s and 1960s, when the action takes place, and they liked to send conscripts there. And so, in the leapfrog of endless banter and cynical haggling with the circumstances at hand, the heroes live through an adventure of a moral kind that is, in a good way, chilling (though the author diligently shields us from this). The events themselves, in essence, are not that important, but how they are written about is precisely the main reason the book is worth reading.

---

## After Fisher: A Dense Start with Familiar (Bar One) Types

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/posle-fishera-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-05-28 (28 May 2026); updated: 2026-06-29
Work: “Posle Fishera” is a 2026 series directed by Olga Frenkel.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, mystery
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/posle-fishera-serial/

## 28 May 2026

[*Posle Fishera*](https://youtu.be/XAhopBYx78w?si=fEpcyXL-k_2bBB_P) («После Фишера», “After Fisher”, the continuation of the hit crime series *Fisher*) has a very dense start with familiar (bar one) character types.

In place of Bokov there is the angry investigator Belova, played by Yulia Snigir. There is also an excessively cheerful second investigator, Terekhov (Alexander Petrov), who at first strongly resembles Yatsenko’s character in the first seasons. But the forest girl, played by Polina Gukhman, is something completely new in this universe. This literally wild figure is, perhaps, now the main source of interest in the coming season. And it is simply perfect casting, a find.

The plot premise, about a murder that leads to the investigation of a whole chain of similar crimes, is clear; that too is a fairly classic component here. The distinctiveness comes largely from the forest landscapes and the internal feuding of the detectives themselves, which is already intriguing and motivates you to keep watching. I am wishing for the same screenwriting finds [in terms of speech](https://t.me/kino_voice/631) that made the second season such a joy)

Incidentally, respect for the cover of Mumiy Troll’s song “Eto po lyubvi” (“It’s for Love”) in the opening credits: usually I am not thrilled by reworkings, but this one is spot on.

## 8 June 2026

And [*Posle Fishera*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1501) has really picked up speed in the second episode.

What is especially pleasing is how all the plot branches are gathering into one big, intricately woven chain: there were some fears that the whole thing might fall apart, but now they will not come true) And, by the way, although the series slightly lacks the “charm” of the 1990s and 2000s familiar from the previous seasons, the root of all the problems is still hidden in exactly that era: the flashbacks to 2006 are now into their second episode, and 1993 comes up in conversations too. The gold standard, in short, is being observed.

And some sort of chemistry has started to appear between the two sleuths. In the first episode there was no sense of a mutual hatred sufficiently motivating for solving cases. But it has appeared, and I hope it continues in the same spirit.

## 29 June 2026

Three episodes before the end of the season, [*Posle Fishera*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1541) leaves a certain scope for the viewer’s reflections.

The detective intrigue has grown stronger (as have the professional relations between Snigir’s and Petrov’s characters), and Tonka, played by Polina Gukhman, has come into her own too. And, most unexpectedly, a rightful place among the supporting characters has been taken by Belova’s daughter (Taisya Kalinina), who earlier seemed merely a fleeting detail of the investigator’s life. Now her influence on the situation has a noticeable effect on the storylines of almost all the characters.

I am even tormented by the thought: will the next plot twist be the moment when Belova has to choose between her own daughter and her newly acquired one (in the person of Tonka)? The script clearly still has room to unfold, so I do not rule out that development either.

---

## I Love You Phillip Morris: From Sly Frenzy to Penitent Melancholy

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ya-lyublyu-tebya-filipp-morris-2009/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-05-25 (25 May 2026)
Work: “I Love You Phillip Morris” is a 2009 film directed by Glenn Ficarra, John Requa.
Tags: comedy, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ya-lyublyu-tebya-filipp-morris-2009/

*I watched a film that only I and its creators remember*.

It is the dramedy **I Love You Phillip Morris** with Jim Carrey and Ewan McGregor. When you first see this film, you think: why has STS (the Russian TV channel) never shown it? It has Jim Carrey in it, doesn’t it?

But half an hour into watching you understand everything (though this aspect, naturally, is not the main one at all).

The picture is unusually constructed: from the very beginning there is no colossal task or danger facing the hero. We simply watch him try to adapt to a world in which even just living quietly in his own way takes effort, never mind reaching any heights (though he strives for those too).

In vibe it is to some extent like **Better Call Saul** and **Liar Liar** with the same Carrey. That is, before us is the most charming trickster, who still pays for every deft manoeuvre with bitter tears. And so we rush about together with the hero from sly frenzy to penitent melancholy, which always works as the most gripping attraction.

Notably, the picture has no firm ending: the hero seems fated to keep wriggling like this all his life. So the drama in this dramedy, in my view, certainly outweighs the comedy (which is always convincing)

---

## The Drama: A Vivid Film About Broken Tolerance

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/vot-eto-drama-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-05-16 (16 May 2026)
Work: “The Drama” is a 2026 film directed by Kristoffer Borgli.
Tags: drama, rom-com
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/vot-eto-drama-2026/

[*The Drama*](https://youtu.be/6zmKcUa4Xxk?si=1GDxOxemZpXz_RDH) was for me a stunningly vivid film about broken tolerance. And also absolute cinema of artistic exaggeration.

The anti-rom-com with Zendaya and Robert Pattinson has a lot of everything with the prefix “over”. Over-reaction to the heroine’s confession of the worst deed of her life (paradoxically, it is not even a deed but thoughts). Over-concentration of infuriating traits in the newlyweds’ best friend as played by Alana Haim: her character is constructed deliberately for the audience to hate, and I do not even know how to watch *Licorice Pizza* now with the same actress in the lead. Over-susceptibility of Pattinson’s character to the opinions of those around him: I am sure that if he and his bride had had that conversation in private, rather than to the drunken hooting of friends who themselves instigated this exchange of confessions, everything would have gone far more peacefully.

And the most inside-out thing is the context of the action. In a world where everyone is capable of forgiving deeds from cyberbullying to domestic sadism on hearing merely a clarification of the age at which the misdeed was committed (like, 15 years old, no sense yet), it proves impossible to accept the existence of thoughts about something worse than one’s own mischief. Director Kristoffer Borgli shows how hard it turns out to be, in the age of universal tolerance, to show tolerance precisely towards dissent from the social norm (even if it was never backed up by actions). Worse still is watching a groom who, under pressure from society, is ready to renounce “the love of his life” in one fell swoop. No comment.

Conclusions? The film is an excellent social horror. The main characters would have been helped by the proverb “let bygones be bygones” (the Russian version runs: whoever brings up the past loses an eye).

---

## The Hustler: Everything Is Stunning, but the Ending Slightly Disappoints

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kommersant-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-05-15 (15 May 2026)
Work: “The Hustler” is a 2026 film directed by Fedor Kravchuk, Nikita Kravchuk.
Tags: Russian cinema, drama, crime
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kommersant-2026/

In the film [*The Hustler*](https://youtu.be/Bltzllpag7Y?si=s517AoiBZWCOh4tz) (*Kommersant*) everything is stunning, but the ending slightly disappoints (me)

There is a lot that is cool in the story of a banking bigwig who, through a combination of not the most pleasant circumstances, ends up in prison.

**1️⃣** First, every 15 minutes (literally) a new calamity comes crashing down on Alexander Petrov’s character: arrest, prison, betrayal and onwards to worse. This looks not only gripping but realistic: there are situations in life that you cannot shake off for years, because they only grow with every attempt to resolve them.

**2️⃣** Second, the acting, artistic and visual parts work simply perfectly for the script: convincing enough, and at the same time cinematic enough not to turn it all into a mockumentary.

**3️⃣** Third, as a separate point I want to draw attention to the character played by Husky (the rapper), Slava the *smotryashchiy* (the inmate who runs the cell block). The last time I saw such a distinctive hit on the gangster type, right down to the intonation, was Ruzil Minekaev in *The Boy’s Word*.

As for the finale. I will not spoil it, but the idea that the hero supposedly chose the right path in life and did not fall below human dignity strikes me as inconsistent. In the second half of the film he literally kicks a prison-cell enemy senseless, because the situation and the basic notion of self-defence demanded it. Was that not a spiritual fall and the most genuine revenge? So the protagonist does know how to show “reciprocity” towards his enemies? Yet towards the business partner who cheated him out of money and several lost years of his life, mercy, apparently, got activated. In short, the resolution is beautiful, but it definitely does not match the realism of the rest of the picture.

P.S.: A thought keeps nagging at me. At the end the protagonist says that he never saw his former friend again, and at the decisive moment of their showdown on the outside Slava the smotryashchiy seemed to meet him halfway in an absurd impulse not to kill. It is quite likely that off screen the fate of the “friend” was decided after all, just not before Andrey’s eyes.

---

## The Devil Wears Prada: Minus One Point for Andy for Lacking Journalistic Curiosity

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/dyavol-nosit-prada-2006/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-05-10 (10 May 2026)
Work: “The Devil Wears Prada” is a 2006 film directed by David Frankel.
Tags: rewatch, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/dyavol-nosit-prada-2006/

I spent yesterday evening rewatching **The Devil Wears Prada**, so today I am ~~studying the brand’s website~~ have some observations to share. There will definitely be spoilers below, so if for some reason you want to avoid them while reading about a 20-year-old film, be careful.

- The fact that Andy (Anne Hathaway) came to apply for a job at a fashion glossy having prepared nothing but her brilliant CV with a note about editing the university newspaper is either a sign of a lost approach to hiring or the heroine’s glaring irresponsibility. If the former, then we, it turns out, have lost the chance to get by on professional skills alone, without also elbowing our way to expertise in the subject of a particular medium. If the latter, then Andy simply approached the matter unprofessionally. Just as any self-respecting journalist prepares for an interview with a particular subject, building the conversation around that person, so, when coming to work at a fashion glossy, it would have been natural to brush up on the basics in order to learn the surname Gabbana. Here Andy gets minus one point from me for lacking basic journalistic curiosity.

- I also felt like going over Andy’s personal life from the point of view of logic. If the attraction to the veteran journalist has already become mutual, why run away from him, slamming the door (and, let us admit, losing a certain circle of career privileges)? If she wants to return to the relationship with her original boyfriend while getting rid of the irregular hours, why take a job in New York rather than go with him to Boston? The film handles the romantic aspect far more schematically than the career one: the heroine’s companions turn literally into symbols either of career temptations and intrigues (Christian the journalist) or of simplicity and naivety outside the glossy world (Nate the boyfriend). What will happen to the heroine’s personal life in the second part with such schematisation is frightening to think about.

- Surprisingly enough, the most interesting characters in the sequel for me will be Emily and Nigel. They are contradictory, both to a certain extent villainously charismatic and, on the whole, deeper than either Andy or Miranda. In essence, it is they who personify the world of glossy magazines in the film, embodying its pluses and minuses.

- No questions for Miranda Priestly. That is all.

---

## Kniga Utkina: A Text as Many-Sided as Its Hero

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kniga-utkina-my-tut-zhizn-zhivem-kniga/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-05-07 (7 May 2026)
Work: “Kniga Utkina: My tut zhizn zhivyom” is a 2026 book by Stanislav Gridasov (compiler).
Tags: books, sport
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kniga-utkina-my-tut-zhizn-zhivem-kniga/

Hello to everyone whose night went better than mine (I have been unable to fly out of Vnukovo airport since midnight, but that is a whole other story).

What is saving me is the half-autobiography, half-biopic of Vasily Utkin (the legendary Russian sports commentator) called [*Kniga Utkina: My tut zhizn zhivyom*](https://books.yandex.ru/books/hAVI33lR) («Книга Уткина: Мы тут жизнь живем», “The Utkin Book: We Live Life Here”). A read completely motley in structure and style, which combines tales from the master’s life, testimony to the birth of sports journalism in the 1990s, and utterly charming details of Utkin’s biography through the eyes of his comrades-in-arms. In short, the text has turned out many-sided, like its hero, and extremely inspiring for great deeds.

One detail clouded my delight, and that is the production of the audio version of *Kniga Utkina*. I am very sceptical about audiobooks and almost never listen to them, because there is always something I do not like. Here I decided (inspired, apparently, by Vasily’s openness) to listen, and was instantly let down. The beginning of each chapter is dressed up with a peculiar jingle combining jaunty music in the style of the *Uralskie Pelmeni* opening theme (the Russian TV comedy show) with stock sounds of fans shouting. And this is completely (with all respect to both ingredients) out of keeping with the spirit of the work. The book presents Utkin as a subtle, passionate and witty man who, by misfortune, left us far too early. So hearing such a “playful” compère’s introduction before, say, a philosophical chapter by Yuri Saprykin not only throws off any mood but is simply inappropriate(

So I highly recommend the book, only not to listen to it but precisely to read it.

---

## Half Man: The Finale Is Worth Watching for One Scene and One Character

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/half-man-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-04-30 (30 April 2026); updated: 2026-05-31
Work: “Half Man” is a 2026 series directed by Alexandra Brodski, Eshref Reybrouck.
Tags: series, drama, thriller
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/half-man-serial/

## 30 April 2026

*\*she spent two days thinking how to write about this series\**

[*Half Man*](https://youtu.be/egkRy1U94tA?si=i7wxU7hOzcE0Fsfr) hits the viewer’s nerves at full swing with a heap of hints and not a single interpretation, which is to say with an uncertainty heavier than some tortures. The series about the difficult relationship of two, in essence, stepbrothers looks far more striking than it sounds in a retelling, precisely because of the ambiguity of both main characters. How each of them perceives the other is quite a puzzle.

Richard Gadd, the writer and producer of this story, who previously impressed everyone with [*Baby Reindeer*,](https://t.me/kino_voice/115) has undergone a colossal change of image. Now he is not the “doormat” type but, on the contrary, Ruben, a brutal guy radiating an aura of danger within a kilometre’s radius. For everyone, that is, except Niall, the brother who appeared by force of circumstance, with a far more modest physical and moral make-up. It is to him, incidentally, that the reindeer nickname has stuck (one Richard apparently has no intention of giving up in his projects). The story of the heroes’ relationship develops from adolescence towards a specific moment in adult life, which looks like the most chilling episode of the first instalment.

*Half Man* can be called a coming-of-age story, a drama about toxic masculinity and even a psychological thriller. Most important of all is the speed with which the series seizes your attention, leaving no chance of declining to watch the second episode.

## 6 May 2026

From the second episode of [*Half Man*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1447) one gets the clear impression that this could have been a very funny comedy of misunderstandings, were it not for the utter realism of the consequences of all the heroes’ actions. In essence, that very step from comedy to tragedy, which *Half Man* takes in the direction of the latter.

Most of the screen time, as in the previous episode, goes to the young versions of the heroes, Mitchell Robertson (Niall) and Stuart Campbell (Ruben), and they, of course, deliver the strongest work. They are joined by the young incarnation of another important character, Albie,  played by Bilal Hasna. I think we will 100% see some of these names in the coming awards season.

As for the famous discomfort in viewing, for which the series has already made a name for itself, it arises in fragments, sometimes giving way to moments that are even too bright. All the more painful to descend this rollercoaster back into the hell of uncontrollable catastrophe that engulfs the heroes time after time. And, it must be noted, 70% of the anxiety is down simply to the figure (not the words, not even the actions) of Richard Gadd, the adult version of Ruben: he turns your stomach worse than any cruelty shown on screen.

## 11 May 2026

The midpoint of the [*Half Man*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1464) season is marked by the most powerful episode (possibly of the whole season). And by a no less impressive cliffhanger at the end of the episode. In short, the psychological thriller we deserve.

As was bound to happen, the conflict that at first seemed absolutely black and white has gone into shades of grey. Of all the parties, only Albie seems unconditionally unambiguous, and even that, as the series has already taught us, with the proviso “for now”.

And now we also have an idea of how the taking of a single decision can be made into one big 50-minute doubt, complicated by a rising sense of guilt. It fits very well into the series’ high concept about the influence of preceding years on one specific day in the future.

## 19 May 2026

Interesting things happen with Richard Gadd’s series.

In [*Baby Reindeer*](https://t.me/kino_voice/115) an important part of the plot hinged on how the life of a victim of traumatic events is subsequently built around the original catastrophe, and at what price healing happens (and not always, at that).

In [*Half Man*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1476), on the contrary, judging by the fourth episode, they are beginning to hint to us: are we not fixating too much on our trauma? Maybe we should stop replaying how someone hurt and insulted us, and instead get on with our lives? Because years later the difference between the one who found the strength to move on and the one who decided to stay in the victim’s costume is colossal. Both heroes, who considered themselves victims for many long years, end up living radically different lives, and it is impossible to watch this without emotion. Especially relevant when confronting global crises that traumatise everyone.

What a curious circle the moral of the fable has made from 2024 to 2026, though.

## 31 May 2026

The final episode of [*Half Man*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1489) is worth watching for one scene and one character (who does not even take part in it).

The couple of revealed moments from the past played, by and large, no role in moving the plot. We already knew whom Niall was marrying, and we had already seen that Ruben was at the wedding without his family. The fatal outcome of the fight in the shed was shown back in episode 5, so that circumstance could hardly surprise either.

One specific moment closed the whole chain of absurd self-harm to one’s own life and others’. The last conversation between Ruben and Niall in prison, through a wall of clear plastic, is a stunningly concise expression of both heroes’ nervous breakdown. Their entire fate over a couple of decades comes down to a brief enumeration of facts that are hard to say and to hear without laughing at the absurdity. It all resembles some sad joke.

And then I [remembered](https://t.me/kino_voice/1505) which “joke” would fit here. There is nothing worse than building your life on an attempt to guess what the other person is thinking (even if that desire is caused by past trauma). There is nothing funnier or more senseless than years and decades spent in that mode. One hero managed to break out of the vicious circle: Albie. His life and health were broken, he was literally trampled physically and morally. And here is this man, 20 years later, as if nothing had happened, smiling, meeting people halfway, ready to give people chances. I am sure that off screen he lived full years thanks to honesty with himself and to demanding that honesty from those around him (rather than trying to “guess for himself”). For me, perhaps, it is precisely this character who will remain the main one in the story.

---

## Project Hail Mary: Mass-Market Cinema with Taste and Humanity

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/proekt-konets-sveta-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-04-24 (24 April 2026)
Work: “Project Hail Mary” is a 2026 film directed by Phil Lord, Christopher Miller.
Tags: science fiction, adaptation
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/proekt-konets-sveta-2026/

I have got round to [*Project Hail Mary*,](https://youtu.be/m08TxIsFTRI?si=1Sprxcx5D8tQfoOo) (released in Russia as *Proekt “Konets sveta”*, “Project Doomsday”) and it is a genuinely, cosmically cool film

The story of a teacher who ends up on a space mission against his will is good in many ways: stunning cinematography and graphics, a lovely Ryan Gosling (I do not like all his roles, but this one is right on target), a convincing script without an excess of melodrama or a slide into overly black humour. By the way, it is also a great adaptation of the novel of the same name by Andy Weir (the author previously wrote *The Martian*; space is his forte). In short, a practically perfect example of mass-market cinema made very skilfully, but with taste and humanity.

And about the latter I want to write separately. It is obvious, probably, that the film immediately invites comparison with *Interstellar*: in scale, in its concerns, in the overlaps of the plot. But *Interstellar*, in my view, is simply an anti-advertisement for the space science-fiction genre compared with *Project*. The film with Gosling does not build a wall between the action and the viewer out of grandeur and ambition that one must look at exclusively from below and with reverence. The detail of *Project*, unlike *Interstellar*, does not require homework on analysing what you have seen in order to understand and remember at least something. And this, surprisingly, does not make the script flat or predictable; on the contrary, it helps you engage and get greater pleasure from watching.

So think about that, as they say. And do watch *Project Hail Mary*, it is worth it)

---

## Who Is Behind the Underground?: A Doc About Pasha Tekhnik Without Romanticising Its Hero

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/pasha-tekhnik-za-kem-stoit-andegraund-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-04-17 (17 April 2026)
Work: “Pasha Tekhnik: Who Is Behind the Underground?” is a 2026 film directed by Vladislav Kuznetsov.
Tags: documentary, music
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/pasha-tekhnik-za-kem-stoit-andegraund-2026/

Yesterday I went to a screening of [the documentary about Pasha Tekhnik](https://youtu.be/Nkr89DLuvM0?si=Ti2_wAgEFPEIlMYL) (the Russian underground rapper) with the great subtitle “Who Is Behind the Underground?”. Right there in the title the emphasis is declared to be on the personality of the man and his relationship with a particular segment of culture, and the picture is structured exactly that way.

I am not the most immersed in Tekhnik’s work, so I went with great research interest. It must be said that the film does look like the perfect guide for everyone who either was not aware of the nuances or simply wanted to recall once more how it all began.

With documentary biographies there is always the fear of running into romanticisation, excessive sentimentality or, God forbid, a tedious idealisation of the hero. In the doc about Tekhnik none of that occurred: it resembles the story of an ordinary man who stumbled somewhere, somehow fell out with the law, in some ways turned out weaker than life requires. You want to trust his story, because this is not some artist who headed for the stage from childhood and then performed perfectly all his life without once deviating from the stage gloss. If there were good moments, they are shown as such, and if there was something low, devoid of beauty and dignity, that ended up on screen too, because it is honest.

The music journalist Nikolai Redkin described the phenomenon of this artist perfectly accurately, and at the same time rather paradoxically, by saying that Tekhnik is “the Yuri Nikulin of the lower internet of the 2010s” (Nikulin being the beloved Soviet clown and comic actor). As for me, throughout the screening I kept thinking that Tekhnik’s biography somehow unexpectedly rhymes with Dostoevsky’s famous line: “*Man is a mystery. It must be solved, and if you spend your whole life solving it, do not say you have wasted your time*”. It seems we all tried a little, and it was definitely not in vain.

---

## The Black Countess: A Mix of the Aesthetics of Of Freaks and Men and Kholop

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/chernaya-grafinya-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-03-29 (29 March 2026); updated: 2026-05-04
Work: “Chyornaya grafinya” is a 2026 series directed by Ilya Kulikov, Ivan Korvin.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, supernatural
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/chernaya-grafinya-serial/

## 29 March 2026

After the screening of **The Black Countess** (*Chyornaya grafinya*) at Original+ (the Russian series showcase) I honestly hoped that a couple of episodes would come out at once on premiere day on Okko (the Russian streaming service). The first episode, though incredibly packed, breaks off at the most interesting point. Here is what I [wrote](https://t.me/kino_voice/1366) about the plot:

> The present day. In a richly decorated country estate a play is being vigorously rehearsed. The director, Timur (Yuri Chursin), never tires of reminding the actors that the client has paid a million dollars. The sole spectator (Kirill Käro) arrives, and he is impressed neither by the simple-hearted joy of the actress playing the “niece”, nor by the society talk in the style of 19th-century plays, nor even by the voyeuristic crack in the wall of the room allotted to him, which allows him to spy on the ladies’ bathing. The fire in his eyes appears only after one of the actors really dies. The gun turned out to be loaded with a live round, and the carefully rehearsed shot proved fatal. The strangeness does not end there: first the frightened troupe discovers that the satellite phone (the only means of communication in a deliberately created offline space) is broken, and then learns that the mansion where the show is taking place is cursed. According to legend, it once belonged to a countess who, having gone mad after her husband’s death, tormented the peasants until they walled her up in the building. Since then, so the tale goes, only death and disease dwell there

But only one episode came out, and that, of course, is the best way to win the viewer’s impatience for the second. Most interesting of all is how the mix of the aesthetics of *Of Freaks and Men* (Alexei Balabanov’s 1998 film) and *Kholop* (the 2019 hit comedy about a rich man re-educated in a staged 19th century) will develop. What we have is seemingly a colossal handmade performance for one man, and seemingly a bad dream about captives bound by a vicious mutual guarantee.

## 15 April 2026

I am continuing to watch [*The Black Countess*,](https://t.me/kino_voice/1378) and by the end of the third episode, of course, an expectation arises of some new mechanism to keep the intrigue going.

We have already seen dead characters, and the surviving ones’ hypotheses do not look plausible at all. A certain feeling of going round in circles arises, which I hope will be broken by the events of the next episode, because the story has very great potential.

Incidentally, in terms of immersion in the backstage of an actor’s life, *The Black Countess* distantly resembles *Aktrisy* (“Actresses”), another project about the fate of actors, only not at all mystical and firmly tied to the present day. It remains to guess which way *The Black Countess* will lean more.

The character posters give away nicely who will last longer than the others in this meat grinder.

## 4 May 2026

The deeper into the forest, the less I understand what is going on in [*The Black Countess*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1403) at all.

The killings of characters have stopped being the main engine of the plot, replaced by a sorting through of suspects. This already gives the proceedings a new angle for the closing episodes, but at the same time, together with the other ingredients, it completely blurs the genre of the series. In other words, it knocks the ground out from under the viewer’s feet. In some respects that is even good, but there are nuances.

The Black Countess, the legend of whose fate has been recounted more than once during the series, has acquired a storyline of her own. Now we see, as it were retrospectively, a visualisation of her whole story with her husband, children and peasants. And this repetition seems to slow down noticeably the storylines of the present-day characters (though only a few of them are left). The purpose of this duplication of the legend on screen is not entirely clear, but I will very much hope that in the end it pays off worthily.

---

## The Dog of Many Tomorrows: The Celebration of Cinema We Were Missing

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kosmicheskaya-sobaka-lida-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-03-26 (26 March 2026)
Work: “The Dog of Many Tomorrows” is a 2026 film directed by Evgeny Sangadzhiev.
Tags: Russian cinema, science fiction, family
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kosmicheskaya-sobaka-lida-2026/

In Russian cinemas from today: [*The Dog of Many Tomorrows*](https://youtu.be/j1VeIolxYfU?si=IK6Kb0isEJE5DzLB) (*Kosmicheskaya sobaka Lida*, “Lida the Space Dog”), an absolute and unconditional celebration of cinema, which we were [missing.](https://t.me/kino_voice/s/120)

The plot is simple in retelling; this, as they say, has to be seen. Igor is 13, and what he misses most is his cosmonaut father, who, however, on yet another birthday merely sends him Lida, a dog that has been in space and was very nearly written off for experiments. At first the boy is not fond of the dog, but, on learning of his stepfather’s plan to send him to a cadet school, he runs away from home together with the four-legged one.

This is where the space dog’s superpowers come to light, allowing the boy literally to glimpse the future and choose his real self from the multitude of versions in the multiverse. All the adult variations of Igor, from a portly beggar to a brazen get-rich-quick guru, are embodied by Evgeny Tkachuk, stunning and inimitable, reborn on screen dozens of times in two hours. He has Brendan Fraser’s *The Whale* in him, and Doc from *Back to the Future*, and who knows who else; in a word, complete majesty.

Surely at the mention of “multiverses” something like *Everything Everywhere All at Once* came to mind, and that is an absolutely correct association. Only in *The Dog of Many Tomorrows* the dynamics of fantastical madness are joined by the atmosphere of the 2000s so dear to the heart, a soundtrack from Delfin to Korol i Shut (Russian rock acts of the era) and, in essence, a story about making contact with one’s eternal inner child. Sangadzhiev has managed to combine a coming-of-age film, science fiction and a road movie, working out some unprecedented genre in the process. Everyone will make their own discovery, for which the film is definitely worth seeing.

## Wuthering Heights: As If a Rose Had Been Wrapped in Plastic Film

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/grozovoy-pereval-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-03-23 (23 March 2026)
Work: “Wuthering Heights” is a 2026 film directed by Emerald Fennell.
Tags: drama, adaptation
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/grozovoy-pereval-2026/

I watched **Wuthering Heights**. I understand everything, but this I did not understand.

The film turned out somehow emotionally out of reach. For the entire running time they insistently try to plunge us into the sensual abyss of Catherine and Heathcliff, promising, among other things, untold eroticism, but it does not work, not one bit. Some invisible barrier gets in the way, built out of the impossibility of believing either in the heroes’ feelings or in the drama around them. As if a rose had been wrapped in plastic film and presented in the expectation of hearing admiration for its scent.

At first glance it is completely impossible to grasp how a film with such a cast, such elaborate costumes, such inventive camerawork and, after all, such an outstanding literary source could come out so wrapped up in itself. But 2 days after finishing it, I dare suggest that the reason lies specifically in Emerald Fennell’s directorial vision.

It is no secret that, in terms of script, the picture contains only one of the novel’s fragments, and even that one altered to suit the filmmaker’s design. And here lies the answer: perhaps the story Fennell decided to tell simply turned out weak. We have all seen enough toxic co-dependent relationships, and there is no new lens here. The love scenes, since the promo put the emphasis on them, cannot be called revolutionary either. During the viewing I literally let slip out loud that a more interesting reflection of this side of the relationship can be seen in one contemporary Russian series, and I will write that here.

In a word, the new *Wuthering Heights* lacked the divine spark.

---

## Onegin. I Wasn’t Finished: The Classics Have Been Taught to Really Rock

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/onegin-ya-ne-dogovorila-teatr/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-03-21 (21 March 2026)
Work: “Onegin. Ya ne dogovorila” is a 2026 stage production directed by Natasha Shurganova.
Tags: theatre
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/onegin-ya-ne-dogovorila-teatr/

*Onegin. Ya ne dogovorila* («Онегин. Я не договорила», “Onegin. I Wasn’t Finished”) at the Moscow theatre [a39](https://t.me/a39theatre) is a total knockout.

Zoomer actors are absolutely the best thing that could have happened to theatre in the 21st century. And they, it seems, have done the best thing that could have happened to *Eugene Onegin* at the present moment. The classic text went through deconstruction and came together again, newly relevant and comprehensible to everyone.

The “bodily commentary”, as announced in the production’s subtitle, was there too. The utterly mind-blowing techno, to the accompaniment of which the characters and relationships of Zhenya, Tanya, Olya and Vova (yes, exactly like that: the diminutives of Eugene, Tatyana, Olga and Vladimir) unfolded, sweeps away any scepticism without trace. Because the classics have been taught to really rock. Just consider the 2 women of mature years who were googling Sydney Sweeney with interest during one of the monologues.

I watch all of a39’s premieres, and usually leave more or less satisfied. But *Onegin* is an absolute revelation even against the background of the other cool things at this theatre. Every time I am impressed by the boldness and innovation of these guys, and I recommend them to you with all my heart.
