## A Private Life: A Mystery That Is Hard to Watch in Full Seriousness

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/chastnaya-zhizn-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-03-03 (3 March 2026)
Work: “A Private Life” is a 2025 film directed by Rebecca Zlotowski.
Tags: mystery, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/chastnaya-zhizn-2025/

The ironic mystery [*A Private Life*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1297) will be hard to watch if you take everything in full seriousness. Elena Malysheva (the Russian TV doctor and presenter) demonstrated this by her own example at the film’s premiere; I am attaching her mini-analysis (watch it only if you are not afraid of spoilers).

The role of a slightly obsessive psychotherapist with an utterly unempathetic attitude to her own life suits Jodie Foster very well. Following her is not easy, and it is harder still to empathise, or at least not to be driven mad, but all this speaks in favour of the heroine’s depth. In the fictional universe of the mystery she is surrounded by no less many-sided personalities. My favourite is the ex-husband, who is such a green flag in every respect that he still has every chance of getting rid of the unpleasant prefix “ex” in his status!

In general, in terms of genre I would also class the film as a comedy of the absurd: many of the heroine’s decisions speak for this, as does the brisk rhythm with which they succeed one another. The most interesting thing about the picture is discussing it after watching, and that is always valuable. The hero of the discussion at the premiere, by the way, I officially consider to be Egor Moskvitin (the film critic): an imperturbability one wants to aspire to. Thanks to him and to colleagues from [@provzglyad](https://t.me/provzglyad) for this evening.

## Olga Kromer’s Kazhdy atom: A Hidden Treasure with a Strange Epilogue

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kazhdyy-atom-kniga/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-02-23 (23 February 2026)
Work: “Kazhdy atom” is a 2023 book by Olga Kromer.
Tags: books, historical novel
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kazhdyy-atom-kniga/

A book break

[Two books](https://t.me/kino_voice/1284) in parallel reading were not enough for me, and I started a third, and it was the one I finished fastest.

I am talking about Olga Kromer’s novel [*Kazhdy atom*](https://books.yandex.ru/books/f5m79nAg) («Каждый атом», “Every Atom”): a plot packaged as young adult about a 16-year-old Soviet lad in 1937 (I suspect the hero’s further adventures can roughly be guessed). In the broad sense the book turns into a detailed description of the process of replacing an idealised worldview with a realistic one. Despite the coming-of-age framework, it is written very vividly, interestingly regardless of age, and even (something I always especially value) cinematically, which is why it genuinely draws you in. The small things of everyday life, of the heroes’ daily existence, of the city and its transport are described in detail.

Appearing in a cameo, for example, is Pavel Filonov, the painter who entered the history of art as the theorist of analytical art, so historical accuracy is all in order there. It would be interesting if he were played by, say, Yura Borisov.

I would even call the novel a hidden treasure, were it not for one “but”. An epilogue that completely crosses out the heroes’ entire journey. In my view, what the author chose to end the book with turns all its fresh merits into an incredible truism. This is perhaps the rare case where I would sooner prefer an open ending (and I cannot stand open endings) to what is offered as the conclusion of the plot. So I highly recommend this book, but advise being prepared for a strange epilogue.

---

## Hamnet: A Film That Plunges You into the Silence of Total Submission to All-Powerful Art

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/khamnet-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-02-12 (12 February 2026)
Work: “Hamnet” is a 2025 film directed by Chloé Zhao.
Tags: drama, adaptation
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/khamnet-2025/

[*Hamnet*](https://youtu.be/xYcgQMxQwmk?si=2Mc0purezlb4R6tJ) is a film that plunges you into the silence of total submission to all-powerful art.

Chloé Zhao’s film is uneven, in places faltering in pace, but it leads very linearly to one key scene. I would even say, to a visual image of catharsis, which in this case we can not only feel but also see.

Also unique is the ease with which one manages to look “behind the scenes” of creativity, and here Akhmatova’s famous line about poems growing “from what rubbish” acquires, before the viewer’s eyes, the grandeur and fate of ancient tragedy. But that is not all that can be found in the film: a small romantic story awaits you (with *Romeo and Juliet* vibes to it), a family comedy (the brightest frames of the film) and a slightly mystical line about the witch-like nature of Jessie Buckley’s heroine.

To some extent, by the way, both Agnes and William, as played by Paul Mescal, are healers. Agnes follows nature’s recipes for healing in the physical sense; William is a sorcerer of word, stage and image. A perfect match of the characters as a couple and a perfect match of the elements in the film.

## Get Back On Your Feet: A Dramedy That Cannot Be Denied Realism and Sincerity

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/vstat-na-nogi-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-02-05 (5 February 2026); updated: 2026-03-20
Work: “Get Back On Your Feet” is a 2026 series directed by Pavel Timofeev.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, dramedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/vstat-na-nogi-serial/

## 5 February 2026

I was really looking forward to the release of the series [*Get Back On Your Feet*](https://youtu.be/8APSRYcGHE0?si=UByTqt_HIG6u4rlz) (*Vstat na nogi*), and every second of the wait was worth it

The story of a man who returns to his home town after 20 years in prison and gets to know his daughter, who is in a wheelchair, all over again may sound from the description like some grim social drama. But in this case it is nothing of the kind. *Get Back On Your Feet* is an excellent dramedy that at the same time cannot be denied realism, conviction and sincerity towards the viewer. There is a vivid atmosphere, perfectly chosen music and lively lines in the dialogue. And most importantly, the chance to recognise a little piece of yourself in every one of the characters.

Gosha Kutsenko (Stary, just out of prison) and Mila Ershova (the strong-spirited Olya) deliver stunning performances. Thanks to their tense interaction on screen, after just 2 episodes you understand what a gigantic echo the affairs of the long-gone 1990s and 2000s have in our time. On the one hand, there are awkward jokes about almond milk (“what, do they milk almonds?”); on the other, mutilated family photo albums and entire destinies. And such an approach is no less important and serious a reckoning with that era than the numerous series set directly in the “wild 90s”.

Separately I want to note how the character posters are done. It is as if someone (fate/the universe/God, take your pick) is looking down on each hero from above, assessing how the hero will use the chance that has come their way. For some it is a chance at freedom, for some at love, and for some even at a new life. It is pleasing when the global concept of a series is so painstakingly reflected in the details of the promo.

## 27 February 2026

[*Get Back On Your Feet*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1268) has passed its midpoint, and episode 5 cements the series’ reputation as the most finely constructed content since the start of 2026.

It is astonishing how a story about a former convict, thieving taxi drivers and a not very empathetic coffee-shop owner can turn into a circle of mutual help and mutual forgiveness, where people begin to understand one another and rescue cats. It is incredible what a combination of light and sorrow is packed into the modest little plot strand about Sanka the barista, who rescues Olya when her wheelchair gets stuck in the mud. After watching this episode, living becomes a little less frightening, which means none of it is in vain.

And of course, all along I was racking my brains over where the cats were, if the place is announced as a “Kotofeynya” (a cat café)?! Thank you, two cats were shown at once, quota met)

## 20 March 2026

Between festival series I managed to take in the finale of [*Get Back On Your Feet*.](https://t.me/kino_voice/1326)

It corresponds perfectly to the concept of “simple and with taste”. And it does so with such talent that one wants to appoint simplicity, rather than brevity, the sister of talent.

The resolution of the final problem with the spiteful woman played by Alexandrova turns out to be so humane and simple-hearted that it is even surprising. How little is sometimes needed for a happy ending and catharsis. All the more realistic, then, looks the imperfection of the resolution of the conflicts around Olya and Roma’s relationship. There is no point waiting for a final solution to all problems, otherwise you may never start living.

## Rag Union: A Half-Forgotten but Heart-Warming Film

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/tryapichnyy-soyuz-2015/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-01-31 (31 January 2026)
Work: “Rag Union” is a 2015 film directed by Mikhail Mestetskiy.
Tags: Russian cinema, comedy, flashback
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/tryapichnyy-soyuz-2015/

I am picking up the \#KinoFlashback relay from Olya Belik’s [KinoKotik](https://t.me/kinokotik/11859) (thank you) to tell you about a slightly forgotten but heart-warming film.

I thought for a long time and in the end decided to choose Mikhail Mestetskiy’s [*Rag Union*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/742198/) (*Tryapichny soyuz*). A film from 2014, not that old, but by my feeling not nearly watched enough by everyone)

Here we have a young Ivan Yankovsky, Alexander Pal and Pavel Chinaryov, quite unlike how we are used to seeing them. They play three charismatic rebels who make up a cell of actionist artists. By chance they meet Vanya (Vasily Butkevich), an ordinary lad who, thrilled with his new pals, is eager to take part in all their schemes (anything is better than advertising gravestones).

Judging by the events of the film, it turns out that the life of actionists is pretty eventful, and not always with art. So there is room here for a comedy of the absurd, wonderful black humour, a rom-com (with the appearance of female company) and the pithy motto “*Push one thing and another falls*”, which you want to take into your life after watching (which, in fact, I did).

In short, the atmosphere of a summer adventure whose reality you doubt for the rest of your life is guaranteed.

I pass the nostalgic relay on to the channels [Sedmoe Iskusstvo](https://t.me/s/sedmoeiskysstvo) and [Bloknotik o kino](https://t.me/s/kinobloknotik): I am sure your film flashbacks will be impressive.

## The Viral Potential of Sport in Cinema and the Cannibalisation of Attention

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/virusnyy-potentsial-sporta-v-kino/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-01-27 (27 January 2026)
Tags: series, sport, industry
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/virusnyy-potentsial-sporta-v-kino/

On the viral potential of sport in cinema and the cannibalisation of attention

I cannot help comparing [*Heated Rivalry*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1243) with [*Marty Supreme*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1240) in terms of viral potential through the display of sport. In both, the focus is on athletes, they attend international competitions, and this gives rise to many spectacular scenes of actual sporting contests. Both works have a kind of public resonance: the hockey story created a fully fledged new fandom, while the plot about a ping-pong player is already shaping Oscar expectations for Timothée Chalamet.

And yet in the case of *Heated Rivalry* we see a universal craze for hockey: growth in ticket sales for hockey games (Bloomberg [writes](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-01-21/heated-rivalry-tv-series-draws-casual-fans-to-nhl-hockey-games?utm_source=chatgpt.com) of growth of more than 20%), growth in sign-ups for hockey clubs and other external effects noticeable from online trends. With *Marty Supreme*, though, there is practically no such effect, even though ping-pong was aestheticised there as much as possible (just recall the film’s orange promo in honour of the hero’s branded balls). There is, of course, growth in ticket sales for ping-pong matches, also by more than 20%, as the Guardian [claims](https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/jan/24/ping-pong-american-revival-marty-supreme-table-tennis), but this is completely baffling on intuitive assumptions.

Of course, the works are of fundamentally different genres, never mind that one is a series and the other a film. But it seems to me that had *Marty* not come out exactly at the peak of the whole world finishing *Heated Rivalry*, our feeds would have been filled with the aesthetics of table tennis rather than hockey)

---

## Marty Supreme: A Comic Hymn to the Fake-It-Until-You-Make-It Approach

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/marti-velikolepnyy-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-01-25 (25 January 2026)
Work: “Marty Supreme” is a 2025 film directed by Josh Safdie.
Tags: drama, sport
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/marti-velikolepnyy-2025/

[*Marty Supreme*,](https://youtu.be/67nRr6DubE0?si=ZIqRfpmQusE3a7SR) it seems to me, is not one of those films that try to please the viewer. Paradoxical as that is, given the adrenaline pace, the snowball of events and the panoramic historical context.

First and foremost this film is a rather comic hymn to the fake it until you make it approach, that is, “pretend until you achieve it”. Its living embodiment is Marty Mauser himself, as played by Timothée Chalamet. A hero, let us say it plainly, who does not inspire much sympathy, both because of his brazen character and because of certain things the plot leaves unsaid (the reasons for his acute hatred of his mother remained a mystery to me). And however much one would like to believe in the inevitable success of the approach in question, the most satisfying thing here is the resolution the hero arrives at. Does he win? Yes, but not at all the way he counted on.

As for the acting of Chalamet, to whom everyone is predicting an Oscar for the role of Marty: in my humble view, it is not such an outstanding performance as to claim the statuette. It is an impressive but not overwhelming role, if you leave aside the actor’s 6 years of learning table tennis and the deliberate worsening of his eyesight for the sake of convincing prescription glasses on screen. The trouble is that this escapes the eye of a viewer who may be completely outside the context of actors’ preparation for roles. And what happens in the film does not have such a fundamental effect.

Still, that does not make the story any less well worked out or any less provocative of discussion after watching, which is the main thing.

---

## A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms: The Sweetest Piece of the Game of Thrones Universe

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/rytsar-semi-korolevstv-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-01-21 (21 January 2026); updated: 2026-02-24
Work: “A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms” is a 2026 series directed by Owen Harris, Sarah Adina Smith, Andrea Harkin.
Tags: series, fantasy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/rytsar-semi-korolevstv-serial/

## 21 January 2026

The sweetest piece of the *Game of Thrones* universe has been found!

Such are my impressions after the first episode of [*A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms*](https://youtu.be/IvGDPA9SbFE?si=l_FFQL-NFU_MSrSh). In the course of one episode this story both charms and marks out its genre and tonal boundaries from the main franchise: everything here is somehow brighter, more naive, yet at the same time more accessible. Convincing and without unnecessary drama, as they say.

Dunk, a hedge knight (meaning he does not serve one lord but hires himself out to different ones, a kind of medieval freelancer), starts his path in the world of knights from scratch after the death of the old man he served as squire. At the very first inn he meets his future squire, Egg, a very stubborn but devoted boy. From that moment on, the proceedings steer into a charming buddy movie that holds your attention through two opposite extremes. All of it, incidentally, takes place 100 years before Daenerys’s fight for the throne, so Targaryens will turn up somewhere too.

Dunk (Peter Claffey) is one of the most unaffected heroes I have seen in contemporary series. His character works really well for trust in what is happening, and at the same time for lowering the pomposity, and that is a real find for Martin’s universe, where until now practically everything happened with a very straight face. And here it is the irony that wins you over most of all: it turns out to be appropriate even in the cruel Middle Ages)

## 29 January 2026

And [*A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1235) continues to delight.

The second episode altogether creates the impression of a great family dramedy in a fantasy setting (well, if you forget the first scene). Between Duncan and Egg a very cool, complementary bond has taken shape, in which the child is sometimes wiser than the adult, and the adult more unaffected than the child. All this creates a great viewing experience: it seems to be made for adults, yet with a warmth and humour that we often get only in the children’s content segment.

But although there is none of the stuffy arrogance of the other parts of the *Game of Thrones* universe, the pace is still quite slow. 2 of the season’s 6 episodes have passed, and our protagonist still has not started taking part in the tournament. They take a long time harnessing the horses, but after [*House of the Dragon*](https://t.me/kino_voice/170) we are used to it.

## 3 February 2026

The finale of the third episode of [*A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1235) is greatness in its purest form!

One scene pays off both the slow pace of the first episodes and the apparent toothlessness of what was happening. The plot twist revealing Egg’s origins also lands perfectly in the middle of the season: 3 episodes still lie ahead, and that is exactly the right amount of time to reveal the character in a new capacity.

Separately I want to praise the showrunners for the slow build-up within this particular episode: from an absolute buddy movie there was a smooth and hypnotic transition to palace intrigue. And here, as they say, watch the hands: in the final minute of the episode every glance, shift of intonation and gesture matters. I rewatched this scene about 4 times and, of course, am now eagerly awaiting the continuation (and I am also sorely tempted to run a couple of chapters ahead of the series in the book)

## 7 February 2026

Thanks to the Super Bowl, HBO decided to release the new episode of [*A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1264) a couple of days early (so that the game would not steal the viewers’ attention))

As for the content of the episode, it is simply a raw nerve 35 minutes long. The protagonist’s nightmare (in the literal and figurative senses), where absolutely unsolvable problems arise one after another on the snowball principle (true to life, on the whole).

But while watching, of course, you admire the staging of this escalating plot 1000%. Peter Claffey’s acting range is revealed brilliantly: we have seen him embarrassed, cheerful, upset, and now this palette has gained the shade of a genuinely wounded knight who no longer resembles the awkward peasant of the previous episodes. Before us is no longer a boy but a man, as the saying goes. And watching him is a great stroke of viewer’s luck.

## 18 February 2026

One of the episodes of [*A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1276), by the fine tradition of HBO projects, was bound to lead us away from the main plot, introducing us to the hero’s past or to entirely new characters.

That episode turned out to be the fifth, combining both Duncan’s biography and a wonderful battle scene. The device that allowed these events to run in parallel is in some ways already familiar: recall how in *Game of Thrones*, at the Battle of the Blackwater, Tyrion fell down and missed everything. Only there it looked more like budget-saving, whereas in *A Knight* it is a clever way of handling the modest running time of an episode and the viewer’s attention.

Nevertheless, never before have I wanted so much for a season finale to run a couple of hours)

## 24 February 2026

The finale of [*A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1295) leaves a feeling of complete harmony from what you have watched.

The six episodes of the first season are a wonderful example of the combination of buddy movie, gripping action, drama in measured doses and calibrated humour. This leaves the viewer (no matter how much they are into the lore of the *Game of Thrones* universe) practically no chance of getting bored or, God forbid, leaving dissatisfied. An exemplary miniseries that will obviously take its place among the best of 2026.

It is especially heartening that the series has already been renewed for a second season, which will come out in 2027. Add it to your watchlists and finish reading Martin’s source text)

## Shrek in the Original: Every Character Has Their Own Accent

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/shrek-2001/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-01-15 (15 January 2026)
Work: “Shrek” is a 2001 film directed by Andrew Adamson, Vicky Jenson.
Tags: animation, rewatch, dubbing
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/shrek-2001/

After this [revelation](https://t.me/kino_voice/1182), over the holidays *Shrek* was rewatched in the original, and it turns out that every character there has their own accent! I noticed this from how differently they pronounce the word “donkey”, and after that my linguistic investigation could not be stopped.

First of all, of course, Shrek: he has, surprisingly for us, a Scottish accent. Mike Myers, the original voice actor, wanted in this way to give him a working-class association. Initially the character, like Myers himself, had a Canadian accent, but at the last moment all the lines were re-recorded. Incidentally, in the original Shrek sounds nothing like the Russian dubbing we are used to. He is less peculiar and less matey than in Russian; to my taste, the character even pales a little as a result

Next, Donkey. In the original he has Eddie Murphy’s accent, American colloquial, so-called African-American Vernacular English. In the Russian dubbing, again, this colloquialism does not seem to come across; rather, Donkey just seems like a party-going dude)

Fiona has the golden mean, which is logical. As a representative of two worlds at once, she speaks with a Californian accent. It is associated with progressive young people, sometimes subcultural ones, which in the case of Fiona and her transformations is almost true)

Our favourite son of Snow White and a dwarf, Lord Farquaad, speaks pure British English. Here it really does him no credit: such an accent is chosen only to underline the character’s arrogance and inappropriate pride.

Bonus: in the first *Shrek* there is a scene of a meeting with Robin Hood in the forest. This noble outlaw speaks with a pronounced French accent, even though he belongs firmly to British folklore. I await your theories, because no sane explanation has been found.

---

## Sentimental Value: A Film About the Healing Powers of Art

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/sentimentalnaya-tsennost-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-01-11 (11 January 2026)
Work: “Sentimental Value” is a 2025 film directed by Joachim Trier.
Tags: drama, festival films
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/sentimentalnaya-tsennost-2025/

[*Sentimental Value*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1104) coincided nicely with the melancholy at the end of the New Year holidays.

However many themes the film raises, for me it is first and foremost about the healing powers of art. And the paradox of the picture is that it is easy to connect with every character, no matter how empathetic (or not so empathetic) a person you are.

When the elder daughter, Nora, resentful since childhood towards the father who left the family and in the end a depressive person, finds something salvific in going on stage and reading the script, you understand her. When the younger daughter, Agnes, has the strength to understand both her sister and her father, you share her impulse 100%. When the feckless father and somewhat less feckless director Gustav himself rushes between a fatherhood already lost forever and a life in art that is not yet hopeless, it is hard to condemn him. Such a variety of empathies lets you look at yourself as if in a mirror with many facets: in some you look better, in others worse, but invariably honestly. And the finale, in my opinion, is a rare case where the concept of “hope” has been transferred to the screen in full, and for that alone it is worth getting to.

The film is harmed just a tiny bit by its deliberate touches of melodrama. Like Gustav briefly ending up in hospital, or Agnes’s fleeting reluctance to approve her son’s participation in the film. I am not inclined to justify manipulative devices, though of course they do have a place. But for the subtleties listed above, as well as the episode with the story of a whole family told as if from the point of view of the house, I am grateful to the film in the end.

---

## Buratino: A Children’s Blockbuster with a Charming Italian Accent

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/buratino-2026/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2026-01-03 (3 January 2026)
Work: “The Golden Key: A New Pinocchio Story” is a 2026 film directed by Igor Voloshin.
Tags: Russian cinema, fairy tales, family
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/buratino-2026/

What is good about [*Buratino*,](https://youtu.be/wbNkmDCZS94?si=CNZw3QUpPerYPRTs) (the Russian Pinocchio; international title *The Golden Key: A New Pinocchio Story*) is its individual finds.

First, the children’s blockbuster is made with a charming Italian accent: all the inscriptions, signs and some of the musical numbers are in that melodious language, and an emotional “Basta!” keeps slipping into the characters’ speech (and no, this is not an attempt to summon Vasily Vakulenko, the rapper known as Basta). Karabas Barabas’s actors, for instance, perform not just anything but Italian commedia dell’arte! It made me want to rewatch the Italian-style New Year special of *Evening Urgant* (the Russian late-night show).

Second, every single acting performance is very successful. And although each “human” character does not get much screen time as such, every appearance of the characters, from Papa Carlo and Harlequin to Alice the Fox and Duremar, is vivid and distinctive. In my view, that is quite a rarity, especially in the fairy-tale genre.

Third, the picture is focused on one central theme: finding yourself in a world where you are different. Director Igor Voloshin’s fairy tale clearly transmits from the screen: be you a log or a cockroach, the main thing is not to listen to ill-wishers and to go your own way, guided by sincere motives and the support of friends. A message that is therapeutic, at the very least, for adults and children alike)

## No Other Choice: Everything We Love Korean Cinema For

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/metod-isklyucheniya-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-12-30 (30 December 2025)
Work: “No Other Choice” is a 2025 film directed by Park Chan-wook.
Tags: Korean cinema, black comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/metod-isklyucheniya-2025/

Among the things left unwatched in the pre-New Year bustle, [*No Other Choice*](https://youtu.be/MRgxBgJyu6k?si=o0BgzHHDwwDlXcNe) (released in Russia as *Metod isklyucheniya*, “Process of Elimination”) definitely deserves attention.

This is a black comedy by Park Chan-wook in which everything we love Korean cinema for works 100%. A manager laid off by his company because of automation after decades of work tries with all his might to get back his job and his full life with his family in his own house (something that could very well happen to any of us in the near future).

Since we are dealing with a Korean film, there is ultra-violence here, and a critique of capitalism and social inequality, and a moral dilemma left for the viewers to ponder. The protagonist, his own antagonist, as played by Lee Byung-hun, hypnotically steals your attention for all 2 hours, making you take every choice together with him. And a finale unexpected for this type of hero, which can be characterised neither as a happy ending nor as a tragedy, makes the film unforgettable in the best sense.

Screenings can still be found in cinemas, and in early January the picture will appear on streaming platforms. The case where a film, from its poster (I could not choose, both are so beautiful) to its inner details, makes a great impression.

## Luc Besson’s Dracula: The Last Romantic and a Fly in the Ointment in the Finale

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/drakula-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-12-24 (24 December 2025)
Work: “Dracula” is a 2025 film directed by Luc Besson.
Tags: adaptation, melodrama, gothic
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/drakula-2025/

I had long wanted to see Luc Besson’s [*Dracula*](https://youtu.be/9ZV0TaSpiG8?si=fyI48zRgiX8L_AGS), and on balance I am more pleased than not, but there is a catch)

In terms of intrigue, atmosphere and the adaptation of the established Dracula plot, the film works really well. Caleb Landry Jones is simply beyond all praise; I believed every one of his glances, gestures and shades of smile, and I am already planning to watch *Dogman* with him too. I very much like the idea of the eternal search for the one and only love and that romantic “I love you so much I can’t live”, which in other settings might look false, but not here. And it turns out to be a very pleasant surprise exactly how the plot arrives at the classic story of Dracula and another man’s bride: it refreshes the story as a whole beautifully.

But there is a fly in the ointment. With great faith in the character I followed Dracula as a rebel, the last romantic, even a punk of his time. You could even say I rooted for him with sporting interest. And the finale, in the form it takes in the film, will most likely disappoint a viewer with my attitude. And here it is not even a matter of taste but a problem of logic and of the motivation of a hero who seemed fairly stable and purposeful but towards the end succumbed to some impulse not very well worked out in terms of the script. I would not say the whole impression is crossed out, but philosophical questions about the overall idea of the film do arise.

## Volchok: An Adventurous Road Buddy Movie in the Interiors of the Late Russian Empire

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/volchok-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-12-19 (19 December 2025)
Work: “Volchok” is a 2025 film directed by Konstantin Smirnov.
Tags: Russian cinema, adventure, historical
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/volchok-2025/

I see criminally few good reviews of the film [*Volchok*](https://youtu.be/nTPxko3_V8M?si=nY_Hr5hxNPhPjxFq), and yet, mind you, it is an adventurous road buddy movie with Evgeny Tkachuk in the interiors of the late Russian Empire.

The plot sounds simple: an orphaned rich heir, after his father’s death, sets off to seek protection from a family friend in Nizhny Novgorod and hires the bare-knuckle fighter Volchok to help him. But do not rush to class the picture among the typical representatives of the genre. The plot here grows surprisingly actively with nuances, twists of self-serving family ties and criminal turns. In the second half of the film, when you already want to breathe out, the action dashingly performs new twist after new twist, as if stopping had never been in the plans. The same can be said of the finale: at least several storylines flow out of it, enough for a sequel.

Besides the wonderful Evgeny Tkachuk as good with fists, the cast also includes Daniil Vorobyov as a slippery relative and Sergei Makovetsky at the highest point of his ambiguous charisma. The young Mark-Malik Murashkin copes beautifully with his role too; it is surprising that I had somehow missed all his previous work. And the film is extremely successful in terms of craft as well: it is sturdily put together, just like Volchok-Tkachuk himself. The period setting, the costumes, the sets that are huge on a city scale and the camera flying over it all simply do not let you switch off from what is happening even for a minute. You want to examine everything and admire it, as if travelling together with the heroes.

A very finely calibrated and handsome genre piece, in short, so how could I not recommend it)

---

## One Battle After Another: A Film Not at All Close to Me

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/bitva-za-bitvoy-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-11-24 (24 November 2025)
Work: “One Battle After Another” is a 2025 film directed by Paul Thomas Anderson.
Tags: world cinema, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/bitva-za-bitvoy-2025/

[*One Battle After Another*](https://youtu.be/kQUPdVxZNPk?si=RZpYgM9QRvwrSQsm) is a film not at all close to me. At the same time, all its ambitions for the coming Oscars, like its overall message, are obvious.

For the most part I do not understand the characters or their motivation, but even less do I understand a world in which the heroine seizes military bases yet for a long time remains completely unpunished, and afterwards calmly becomes a mother and, having plunged into postnatal depression, returns to her revolutionary cause. What the police and related agencies are busy with in the universe of the film remains a mystery that turns a perfectly realistic film into some kind of science fiction. I naturally sympathise with the girl, but that does not remove the questions.

As for the elements with claims to awards: here, of course, there is wonderful acting from absolutely every performer, a distinctive soundtrack and cinematography. For me the main trouble with the picture is the incoherence of all its merits, because of which the film seems to fall apart into pieces that do not inspire trust.

The main idea, about the impossibility of ending violence by violent means, is, frankly, as old as the hills. But a topical reading is added by the final scene with Sean Penn’s character, which is done, perhaps, more elegantly and intelligibly than anything else in the picture, and that is already good.

## Cashier: Four Heroines at Opposite Poles of Controlling Their Lives

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/obnalschik-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-11-19 (19 November 2025); updated: 2026-01-07
Work: “Cashier” is a 2025 series directed by Boris Akopov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, crime
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/obnalschik-serial/

## 19 November 2025

So far [*Cashier*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1071) (*Obnalshchik*, “The Cash-Out Man”) looks to me like the sum of *Daring* (*Likhie*: crime in the Far East and Elena Nikolaeva as the mother of the family) and *Na avtomate* (“On Autopilot”, Boris Akopov’s previous project, where young people were also drawn into criminal adventures). But this does the series no harm at all!

Among other things, it has become clear why the poster puts such emphasis on the hand of Alexander Yatsenko’s character (those who have already seen the first episode will understand me). On the whole, the plot develops fairly quietly, yet grippingly, and, of course, wins you over. The criminal world here is heavily disguised as ordinary life, which is understandable: after all, this is not the 1990s but the 2010s, even if not the calmest of times. Besides, it is interesting to see what the theme of young people who have got their hands on easy money will lead to: the brothers in *Na avtomate* were also balancing before exactly that kind of moral choice.

## 10 December 2025

[*Cashier*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1094) has very competently picked up speed by the end of episode 5.

What is especially striking is the opposite poles at which the 4 main heroines stand when it comes to controlling their own lives and the lives of those around them. Two of them, Olga (Elena Nikolaeva) and Alyona (Sofya Lopunova), are not their own mistresses at all. Their life is the shadow of plans that the characters of Alexander Yatsenko and Fyodor Kudryashov are trying to carry out, and complete ignorance of what is going on at all.

Meanwhile the crime bosses Mama (Olga Tumaykina) and Katya (Elena Nesterova) are their reverse projection. The whole town is in their power, and any lie, if it happens at all, is cruelly punished. Not at all the situation the heroes’ beloveds find themselves in, with noodles hanging blatantly from their ears.

Perhaps one can even see a growth trajectory in this: maybe the current crime queens of Vostochny were once in that position too, and it was from exactly this point that they grew to the scale we are shown.

In Boris Akopov’s stories there is always something hidden deeper than it seems at first glance, so I have great faith in the female storylines.

## 7 January 2026

I have finished [*Cashier*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1143) and am, of course, impressed not so much by the finale as by the development of one particular heroine, Olga as played by Elena Nikolaeva.

In the middle of the season I wrote that she has no control over her life at all. Towards the end there was a 180-degree turn: weakness became her strength, an insinuating weapon with a gentle intonation. While her husband and son, the characters of Alexander Yatsenko and Fyodor Kudryashov, who lost none of their conviction, acted according to external circumstances and other people’s orders, she simply took the situation into her own hands.

To think she drove her guard (whose task was to kill the heroine a couple of hours later) to self-destruct! I am delighted: Boris Akopov came up with a heroine who outclassed all the gangsters of the Far East in a single scene. Maybe she is not much of a psychologist, but as a moral annihilator she worked at full capacity)

---

## Die My Love: A Film That Deeply Empathetic Viewers Will Like

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/umri-moya-lyubov-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-11-14 (14 November 2025)
Work: “Die My Love” is a 2025 film directed by Lynne Ramsay.
Tags: world cinema, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/umri-moya-lyubov-2025/

[*Die My Love*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1077) is a film that deeply empathetic viewers will like. Less empathetic ones too, luckily: there is Robert Pattinson’s character, who will be baffled in parallel.

The plot, let me remind you, is about a young couple who move from New York to the back of beyond in order to love and create there (he wants to make a music album, she to write a book). Instead, the lovers find themselves in the thickets of a mental split brought on both by the changes in their life with the arrival of a child and by their own unfulfilment. The catalyst of the mental madness is Grace, played by Jennifer Lawrence, who copes incomparably with the image of a young woman in postnatal depression, and not only that.

The specific plot twists need no retelling, because the picture exists rather at the level of sensations, visual images and blurred feelings. Lynne Ramsay’s direction conveys this, balancing perfectly on the edge between the reality and the unreality of the artistic world she has created. As a viewer I concentrated on the heroine, and understood her, as they say, from A to Z. The impossibility of articulating what is going on in your soul, together with the awareness that, because of external factors, you are every second drifting further from the image of yourself familiar to your loved ones: this is exactly what watching Grace over the course of the film lets you understand without words. The stills I chose for this post are about the same thing: outwardly Grace seems part of some causeless celebration of life, while inwardly she is a piece of confetti forgotten on the floor that once sparkled in the lights of the party.

Separately, I was won over by the scene of the wrecking of the bathroom, which is at once like a claustrophobic horror, a black comedy and an audiovisual attraction whose events you even slightly want to join. So watching on the big screen is recommended: from 27 November, courtesy of [@provzglyad](https://t.me/provzglyad)

## Pluribus: The End of the World as a Chance to Achieve at Least Something in Your Own Eyes

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/pluribus-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-11-09 (9 November 2025); updated: 2025-12-27
Work: “Pluribus” is a 2025 series directed by Gordon Smith, Vince Gilligan.
Tags: series, science fiction, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/pluribus-serial/

## 9 November 2025

I have watched the first episodes of [*Pluribus*](https://youtu.be/a6lzvWby9UE?si=KUNaXOPF7IBpFwfh), the science-fiction drama from Vince Gilligan (*Breaking Bad*, *Better Call Saul*) about a virus that turns the minds of all surviving people into a single whole. Except for the writer Carol, the heroine played by Rhea Seehorn, and a dozen or so other earthlings from different countries.

This is a vivid story that provokes complex emotions and questions about what you would do in the heroine’s place. That is precisely why the impeccable way it is all shot recedes into the background, its calibrated technique not eclipsing the moral dilemma.

After two episodes I am still mulling it over. Analogies come flooding in, from Covid and utopian hopes for ChatGPT to NPCs from video games and the trend for eco-friendly communication. This is exactly what makes the story many-layered and ambiguous, first of all thanks to its unpredictability, which is quite rare and, of course, motivates you to keep watching. It is separately interesting how the heroine’s desire to✨save the world✨ (in the traditions of American cinema) actually serves to compensate for her complexes about her inability to create a book that meets her own high standards. The end of the world becomes a chance to achieve at least something in her own eyes, and for that, of course, one can rise up against the entire world.

It is curious how Vince Gilligan, known first and foremost for the story of a man who, having fallen ill, begins a new life, has arrived at the story of a woman around whom the whole world has fallen ill, and who has no plans whatsoever to begin a new life)

## 15 November 2025

Episode 3 of [*Pluribus*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1070)

This is the first of the episodes whose script was not written by Vince Gilligan, and I was prepared for the previous pace to be gone. But not to that extent) Although, let us remember, *Breaking Bad* and *Better Call Saul* also wound up on their way to greatness quite slowly.

It seems that the series, like the representatives of the collective mind in the plot, has gone into energy-saving mode and the redistribution of resources for some future, as yet not entirely clear, goals.

Nor, incidentally, are the possible ways of continuing the story obvious. It is as if everything has stalled, and Carol asks none of the questions whose answers we viewers would very much like to know.

On the other hand, I have begun to enjoy the slightly absurd comedy we are being served. Showing the hundreds of people needed to run a supermarket where the “self-reliant and independent” heroine will buy everything for herself is funny and, moreover, very sobering for everyone on this side of the screen as to how everyday life is actually arranged.

## 22 November 2025

Episode 4 of [*Pluribus*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1085) flies by in an instant (and reminds you how pleasant it is to binge Vince Gilligan’s series).

It seems that the measure of cruelty the new collective world is prepared to go to was taken in the first 3 episodes. Now it is Carol’s turn, and she, it seems, has no intention of making allowances, either for herself or for the representatives of the new race. The unpredictability of her decisions and of the surrounding world’s reactions to them remains at the same level, and that is pleasant to watch. Especially considering the very legible humour at the expense of neural networks, famous for their neutral, meaningless answers)

I hope the second half of the season will give more understanding of the goals of the heroine and of the “uninfected” like her. But it is already clear that a second and even a third season are unavoidable.

## 28 November 2025

Episode 5 of [*Pluribus*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1109) on the whole almost fits into a quote from *A Clockwork Orange*: *“to have a glass of milk and do a bit of the old ultraviolence”* (only, naturally, with a “not”).

The story greatly benefits from going beyond the consequences of the apocalypse that has already happened and moving into unexplored territory. The second half of the season is exactly the time to do it. In particular, Carol’s investigation into the collective mind’s representatives’ love of milk seems set to spill over (pun not intended) into one of the season’s main plot twists, which will give impetus to future events.

Incidentally, I do not know whether it is intended or arises situationally, but the heroine’s attempts to lead the ranks of the scattered “survivors” are shown rather comically (and she reflects on this herself, too). There is no point waiting for a turning point when the series finally steps towards comedy or, on the contrary, loses all irony about the absurdity going on. As *Better Call Saul* and *Breaking Bad* taught us, Vince Gilligan combines all this superbly (I, at any rate, laughed without restraint at the moment with the drone that could not carry off the bag of rubbish).

## 16 December 2025

Episode 7 (the most uneventful at first glance) of [*Pluribus*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1138) could be labelled “sleeping-pill” content.

Were it not for a couple of genuinely sharp moments that demonstrate which of the heroes is prepared for what in this new world! If I ever have to explain the meaning of the term “slow burner”, I will probably refer to precisely this episode. Vince Gilligan is magnificent at this, as we remember from the first season of *Better Call Saul*, which was slow from beginning to end.

Here too nothing happens, yet in the background there are shifts of tectonic plates by the standards of plot and character development. The example of Carol and Manousos contrasts stagnation and regression with movement and overcoming oneself. The difference in motivations immediately becomes obvious: for whom it really was important to save the world, and for whom to become needed by someone in this new world. And from here on, obviously, the most interesting thing is to follow what endings the characters with such starting points will arrive at.

## 23 December 2025

What about [*Pluribus*?](https://t.me/kino_voice/1155)

It is unexpected (though understandable from the point of view of the series’ creators) that the meeting between Manousos and Carol is being put off for so long. Were it not for a couple of striking tendencies in these characters’ behaviour, episode 8 could even be called filler, for the exceptional self-containment of the two characters’ storylines.

But what obviously awaits us is an impressive season resolution with a meeting that should justify the need to wait for the continuation. Probably in the second season the struggle between methods of adapting to the new life will continue and will be even fiercer than Carol’s revolt at the very beginning. It is impressive how long the series’ authors manage to sustain the ambiguity of the new world order: another successful example of grey morality that contains arguments both for the infected and against them.

## 27 December 2025

The finale of [*Pluribus*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1165) is as imposing as an atomic bomb.

This is one of those episodes for which all the slow and uneventful episodes of the season were worth watching. In the finale, in a modest 50 minutes, everything is turned upside down twice, and in the density of its moral flip-flops it is simply an unsurpassed level.

Once again it turns out that man is an alien to man, even under the conditions of the end of the world. And where the line lies that cancels out cultural contrasts, we learn only in the last frames.

Episode 9 of *Pluribus* has the second-highest rating of the season on IMDb, 8.5 (against 9 for the pilot), and that is a good sign. I will await the second season with moderate impatience)

---

## The Magic District, Season 2: The Very Fairy Tale Adults Are Missing

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/volshebnyy-uchastok-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-11-06 (6 November 2025); updated: 2025-12-28
Work: “The Magic District” is a 2023 series directed by Stepan Gordeev.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, comedy, fantasy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/volshebnyy-uchastok-serial/

## 6 November 2025

One of the best viewing sensations is to start the second season of a series having only just finished the first.

That is what I did with [*The Magic District*,](https://okko.tv/serial/volshebnyjj-uchastok) (*Volshebny uchastok*) having got acquainted with its universe right on the eve of the sequel’s premiere on Okko (the Russian streaming service). It was the best decision: from the first frame you do not want to climb out of the story for a minute, and the season finale gave no chance to relax at all. How pleasant it turned out not to have to wait 2 years for the continuation.

It would have been worth it in any case, though. The second season not only takes over all the merits of the first but multiplies them with interest. Lyokha Popov used to be simply funny in the Perm way; now he is also immortal, with all the gags that follow from it. The Gnome used to be simply a foul-mouthed dwarf (hard to believe, but he is my totem character one hundred percent); now he is not a gnome at all and not even foul-mouthed (and even cooler in his vocabulary, which I will be adding to my lexicon). There used to be the familiar Moscow; now there is a fairy-tale international St Petersburg (with jokes about mushrooms and salt, of which there is never too much (of the jokes)).

There is plenty to admire beyond the plot and the acting. In place are the fairy-tale looks of the characters, stunningly worked out by Anna Bashtova, the rhythmic direction of Stepan Gordeev, the coolest music and the charming atmosphere of the very fairy tale that adults are missing. Falling in love with this project is the best range of emotions you can experience at the end of 2025.

P.S.: As it happens, I also had the rare experience of watching *The Magic District* and *Realnye patsany* (“Real Lads”, the long-running Perm sitcom) in parallel, but I will write about that separately some time.

## 8 December 2025

And in [*The Magic District*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1050) everything is as fairy-tale as ever

I returned to watching after a couple of weeks and was very glad to see in episode 5 no fewer than two cool female characters: the Mermaid played by Valentina Mazunina (with the characteristic intonation of Valya from *Realnye patsany*) and a cameo by Anna Semenovich (in the plot, the singer has been captured by the wicked owner of a wish-granting pike). Once again I was reminded that the charm of the series lies, among other things, in little treats like these in the form of charismatic episodic characters)

I keep waiting to see how the story will approach New Year: after all, the last episode of the season is scheduled for 25 December, and the New Year mood will not create itself! I believe the authors have taken care of it: look, the pike, which is traditionally caught through a hole in the ice, was pulled out of the water in the middle of summer, so maybe some other winter folklore will come our way too.

P.S.: The wisdom tooth that utters those very wisdoms in the voice of Losyash (the moose from the animated series *Smeshariki*) is the peak. The whole episode I waited for it to say “my fairy-tale friend!”

## 28 December 2025

However detached [*The Magic District*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1139) may be from New Year themes, the series still managed to create a naively festive atmosphere for the season finale. The keys to success are these:

- Of course, there was no doing without ubiquitous New Year promo. It suits the series, as you can see from the poster.

- Perhaps Ilya Sobolev’s [greeting](https://t.me/mc2_prod/1884) “Happy New Year”, which was heard at the premiere, meant the new year of 1996 in the story, announced in the finale, rather than the literal holiday, as one might have thought. Well, the final change of era is more of a “Happy Old New Year!” (And yes, the 90s do not annoy me)

- We love and value New Year films precisely for their naive, life-affirming happy endings. There is one here, and in my opinion it is quite acceptable, if hasty by the standards of the action accelerating towards the resolution. One would like to hope that the wait for the next season will not drag on either)

## Peculiarities of the National Hunt: Digital Detox and Anti-Stress

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/osobennosti-natsionalnoy-okhoty-1995/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-11-03 (3 November 2025)
Work: “Peculiarities of the National Hunt” is a 1995 film directed by Aleksandr Rogozhkin.
Tags: rewatch, Russian cinema, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/osobennosti-natsionalnoy-okhoty-1995/

Well, here’s to the classics!

In October I was also studying the universe of Aleksandr Rogozhkin’s films: the three parts of *Peculiarities of the National Hunt* (in one of the films, of the National Fishing). I had seen fragments of these films on television long ago, but only now did I get round to watching them properly from start to finish. And not in vain: it was one of the best weekends of the month! If I were asked to name films synonymous with the words “digital detox” and “anti-stress”, I would choose these.

These anecdotes about the timeless face of the Russian soul, filmed with the utmost seriousness, surprisingly combine utterly carnivalesque humour with deeply existential philosophy. It is precisely in this paradox that some irrefutable sense of involvement in what happens on screen is born: both in terms of the fun shared with the characters and in terms of the general attitude to the absurdity of life. For this inimitable feeling you want to rewatch and rethink the films, plunging anew into a world without ranks or cares that flares up and fades somewhere on hunting trips in the forest (and also out of self-interest: to memorise for future use all the general’s pithy toasts, each beginning with the fundamental “Well…”)

## You Drive Me Crazy: The Feeling of Captivating Love Bottled in Film

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/svodish-s-uma-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-29 (29 October 2025)
Work: “You Drive Me Crazy” is a 2025 film directed by Darya Lebedeva.
Tags: Russian cinema, rom-com, science fiction
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/svodish-s-uma-2025/

If you had no cinema plans for the coming evenings, urgently plan a trip to [*You Drive Me Crazy*.](https://youtu.be/39T_q4gt7HE?si=g9iPXzTNF-iuOeUm) (*Svodish s uma*) It is definitely worth catching.

I saw the film yesterday evening, and it is simply a find for any viewer. Director [Darya Lebedeva](https://t.me/lebedevadao) has made a stunning feature debut combining a convincing plot, the coolest performances from Mila Ershova and Yuri Nasonov, romance and humour in harmonious proportions, and a love of cinema that you feel through the screen. I have so many raptures that I will lay them out point by point (the film’s **rating of 8.5** on Kinopoisk will not let me lie)

- A fantastical element has never suited a romantic comedy so well, perhaps, since *Palm Springs*. The story of a guy and a girl who live in the same flat in different versions of the universe but see each other in the mirror and fall in love fits so well into the logic of the world of *You Drive Me Crazy* that no questions about it arise whatsoever. It is just as convincing as the plot of *Piter FM* (the 2006 St Petersburg rom-com) about two strangers who talk only by phone but can never manage to meet. The setting, by the way, is the same fateful St Petersburg, and it is very beautiful here. So even if you are on the side of realism, boldly decide to watch.

- After watching, I spent the whole evening and this morning discussing the details of what I had seen and decoding them. I have not plunged into analysing a film after watching like this for a long time, so you must take your favourite conversation partners to the screening. Everything matters here: the eccentric glasses of the hero, Vanya, Alisa’s fringe, the jokes about *Twilight* and cocktail recipes, the changed locks on the doors and the stickers stuck on the mirrors. The film is somewhat like an engaging quest that you are invited to complete with extremely likeable characters, who, incidentally, become better in the process, infecting the viewer with the same aspiration.

- From the moment you leave the auditorium your soul demands an immediate rewatch, and that is quite rare. You want to stretch *You Drive Me Crazy* out, prolong it, repeat it and not let it go. To convey the feeling, I will draw a parallel with Ray Bradbury’s *Dandelion Wine*. There he had “summer caught and bottled”, and here we have the feeling of captivating love and sincere closeness between two slightly lost people who deserve happiness, caught and bottled in film. How good that the film will most likely be released on the platform Start (the Russian streaming service), which is listed in the credits, and the chance to touch this story will always be there.

---

## Comeback: The Air of an Era That Breathes Genuine Youth Through the Screen

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kambek-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-11 (11 October 2025); updated: 2025-11-16
Work: “Comeback” is a 2025 series directed by Dinar Garipov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, 2000s
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kambek-serial/

## 11 October 2025

I have got round to [*Comeback*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/series/6605654/) (*Kambek*), an ultra-atmospheric series with Alexander Petrov as a homeless man who has lost his memory.

The action takes place in the 2000s, and the air of the era literally breathes through the screen with some kind of genuine youth. This atmosphere is intensified by the teenage protagonists: strong, brave, wise in their own way. And it is all scored with tracks by Mujuice, who always reaches right to the depths of the soul. And the plot, of course, from episode to episode emphasises something unhackneyed about friendship, kindness to one’s neighbour and to oneself. Simple and tasteful.

Watching it, I felt things long forgotten since [*Mir! Druzhba! Zhvachka!*,](https://t.me/kino_voice/13) (“Peace! Friendship! Bubblegum!”, the 1990s-set series) so I am with this series to the end.

## 18 October 2025

I continue to ~~watch~~ adore [*Comeback*](https://t.me/kino_voice/997)

The fourth episode of the series is a perfect example of a situation where the vertical plot of an episode complements the overall horizontal structure of the story so organically that it is even hard to separate them. Gratitude to the creators and to [@russian_c0de](https://t.me/russian_c0de) for such craftsmanship, of course.

The series is at its midpoint and is very competently gaining momentum. The [record](https://t.me/kinopoisk_Industry/5558) viewing figures say so eloquently. Such demand, it seems to me, can be explained by interest in the chosen era. We all, to one degree or another (especially younger viewers), came out of the 2000s, out of that culture, that reference point in our worldview and sense of self. And recalling one’s relative youth is always absorbing.

## 20 October 2025

I am separately enjoying the aesthetics of the school the heroes of [*Comeback*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1013) attend

For me these are home landscapes. The main value is that it is an *ordinary* school (even if that came about only because of the period: in 2004 all schools were like that). I studied at exactly this type of school, and my eye rejoices at the familiar layout of the classrooms with those peeling wooden chairs (which forever snagged your tights, the girls will understand me), the worn linoleum, the wooden shelving, the wide windowsills and the chaotic plants on them. The canteen is a little bigger than in the still from the series, but with the same serving line of metal vessels with red lettering. In my last years of school, the chalkboards were replaced by whiteboards and then partly by electronic ones, but everything around remained as it was)

These days you hardly ever see such schools on screen, certainly not in stories about our time: everywhere there is bound to be a swimming pool, a canteen with a buffet like a hotel, and ultra-fashionable renovations. Such schools really do exist, but schools of the old type exist and operate in parallel (I went to mine last year, and the authenticity is intact). And it is very pleasant to recognise on screen a piece of one’s personal youth, which, it turns out, can even serve as a film set.

## 31 October 2025

In the sixth episode of [*Comeback*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1013) many storylines are very neatly written off, precisely to place the emphasis on the new input in the form of Alexey Chadov’s mysterious character. Obviously it is he who will be one of the main protagonists in the two final episodes, and for that a little extra artistic and running-time space is needed.

Separately pleasing is the quotation of a scene from the film *Brother*. If you remember, at a certain point Danila there tried to stand up for Sveta, the tram driver, against her husband, who was beating her. Having neutralised the man, Danila asked her to leave with him, but she stayed with her spouse, who was suffering from a bullet in his leg and would obviously go on beating her. The same thing, almost frame for frame, was repeated in *Comeback*, and, one might say, has already reached the level of an archetypal plot.

By the way, I am watching the series very attentively in order to record every episode in a Kinopoisk [feature](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4011978/); if you find yourself pondering the details, drop in.

## 16 November 2025

And the best adornment of the finale of [*Comeback*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1043) is the [news](https://t.me/kinopoisk_soon/20435) of a second season of the series.

In the last episode the concentration of events reached an off-the-scale level, but, pleasingly, not one of the storylines suffered for it. Though I preferred the first half of the story, where, first, the kids seemed to still have everything ahead of them (😭), and second, there was enough time to reflect on each event. But the last episodes have their own drive too, combined with the feeling of a departing era, of a great adventure and the carefree early 2000s.

What will I expect from season 2? Updated images of the kids (in particular, the development of Dasha’s affairs of the heart with various candidates and with Petya, who vanished as suddenly as he appeared). A non-glossy look of the late 00’s, in the series’ tradition, naturally. And the normalisation of Kompot’s life: showing the hardships of a homeless man’s life is half the job; far harder is to reflect honestly the difficulties of his socialisation and of overcoming the stigma trailing from his former status.

It is cool that the project has deservedly got a continuation, and one really does want to wait for it.

---

## Above Eternal Rest: A Difficult Film You Want to Keep Thinking About

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/nad-vechnym-pokoem-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-08 (8 October 2025)
Work: “Above Eternal Rest” is a 2025 film directed by Svetlana Proskurina.
Tags: Russian cinema, festivals, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/nad-vechnym-pokoem-2025/

The final film of the competition programme, Svetlana Proskurina’s *Above Eternal Rest* (*Nad vechnym pokoem*), very much mirrors [*My Son*,](https://t.me/kino_voice/943) which we watched first. This premiere has every right to be called a contemporary *Cargo 200* (Alexei Balabanov’s film) mixed with *Crime and Punishment*. Only, whereas before evil was committed shamelessly in an open room, now it is hidden under the floorboards, with people going mad from complicity, from landing in a “random hell”, as the director put it, and that is something else.

The story of a mother and son bound by one terrible secret does not let you take your eyes off the everydayness of murder in the name of salvation, not even a crime, that word sounds too formal here. At the same time it is hard to condemn Rita, the heroine played by Masha Leonova: she is not a villainess, not a killer and not a bad person. She too is a victim. And understanding this true state of affairs in the story is what weighs on the viewer most of all.

A difficult film that you want to keep thinking and reasoning about. Masha Leonova is a wonderful actress whom one would like to see in such subtle roles more often. She showed a heroine who to the very end makes you doubt whether she has gone mad, or turned savage from indifference, or coldly calculated her deed. Possibly the best female role of the festival.

---

## Yura Was Here: A Film About Beautiful People, Beauty of the Soul and Love for One’s Neighbour

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/zdes-byl-yura-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-08 (8 October 2025)
Work: “Yura Was Here” is a 2025 film directed by Sergey Malkin.
Tags: Russian cinema, festivals, music
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/zdes-byl-yura-2025/

*Yura Was Here* (*Zdes byl Yura*) is an unimaginably beautiful film about beautiful people, beauty of the soul and love for one’s neighbour, which saves first of all the one who loves. Do not think this is some sentimental sweetness: on the contrary, the film is punk, dynamic, out of the ordinary.

Onto the heads of the heroes, young musicians, lands Yura (Konstantin Khabensky), the uncle of one of the guys, who because of a birth injury can neither speak nor live independently at all. To the heroes’ difficulties with their neighbour in a communal flat and their attempts to break onto the big stage is added the care of a relative who at first seems to be needed by nobody. In time it is he who becomes the most important person for all the participants in the story.

The artistic world of the film is filled with music, colours and details that bring everything to life. I recognised in the frame, for instance, the cool café Chifanka in Moscow’s Kitay-Gorod)

I cannot help confessing my love for the songs of the band Kick Chill as performed by Kuzma Kotrelev; the creators promise to release a separate soundtrack. This, in my opinion, is the hit of the film festival, as the song “Allo, Marina” from the film *God rozhdeniya* (“Year of Birth”) once was. Things are fine with references here too: at the moment the candles on the cake are lit, for example, someone says the phrase “Everyone out of the Gloom”, for which Khabensky’s character from *Night Watch* is famous.

I will go and watch it a second time as soon as it is in cinemas: from 5 February, courtesy of [@bosforpictures](https://t.me/bosforpictures) and [@volgafilms](https://t.me/volgafilms).

## Tied Up: A Cinematic Celebration of Animation, Sincerity and Kindness

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/na-vybros-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-07 (7 October 2025)
Work: “Tied Up” is a 2025 film directed by Konstantin Bronzit.
Tags: animation, Russian cinema, festivals
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/na-vybros-2025/

Konstantin Bronzit’s *Tied Up* (*Na vybros*, “For the Dump”) is a real cinematic celebration of animation, sincerity and kindness. In the spirit of Pixar, but with a native soul.

The story of things thrown out onto the rubbish heap which, just like people, want to be needed and useful, touches you so much precisely because this thought is close to anyone. They desperately try to reach a paradise, even if a rubbish-dump one, and how can you not understand them?

The animated film gives the feeling of a true dramedy, provoking laughter and tears at the same time. The humour is built on paradox, so it works without fail. Just consider the joke by the rat that feeds on books, to the effect that Pasternak is a bit bland. At times it even feels like a dystopia in the spirit of Pelevin, but only in its positive manifestations.

Konstantin Bronzit, who worked on the film for 5 years, modestly laughs it off: it is only a children’s cartoon, he says) But the message about the eco-friendly treatment not only of rubbish but, first and foremost, of living people is unmistakable.

In cinemas from 20 November, an unequivocal recommandation.

---

## Transparent Lands: A Film That Demands Heightened Attention from the Viewer

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/prozrachnye-zemli-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-07 (7 October 2025)
Work: “Transparent Lands” is a 2025 film directed by Dmitry Davydov.
Tags: Russian cinema, festivals, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/prozrachnye-zemli-2025/

*Transparent Lands* (*Prozrachnye zemli*) is a film that demands heightened attention from the viewer, if not a second viewing.

The story of three old men living in solitude in a traditional village (outstanding work by the production designers), as if outside time, unfolds practically without words. They while away the time with tea, the banya (steam bath) and cupping jars, and hunting, until they fish out of the pond a man frozen to the state of glass. In the hut he thaws, comes back to life and even starts baking bread, presenting it to the old men as a real miracle (and motivating a wonderful scene of celebration in the snowy night). Only after his disappearance does the life of the village’s inhabitants change.

Contrary to its title, the film cannot be called transparent. It starts a discussion of the fear of death, the preservation of memory and the philosophy of life. Director Dmitry Davydov gradually leads us into the world of a dying village, showing the process of its passage into a space of transparent memories, where the whole village circles in the eternal round dance of the ancestors, no longer belonging to our world, just like the life reflected in the picture.

---

## Scenes of Friendly Ties: An Atmosphere Film Woven from Fragments of Friendship

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kartiny-druzheskikh-svyazey-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-06 (6 October 2025)
Work: “Scenes of Friendly Ties” is a 2025 film directed by Sonya Rayzman.
Tags: Russian cinema, festivals, dramedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kartiny-druzheskikh-svyazey-2025/

*Scenes of Friendly Ties* (*Kartiny druzheskikh svyazey*) is an atmosphere film woven from fragments of friendship and the leisure of film-industry pals. I would call it “fan service for insiders”, with local memes about the woes of film people, the Lev Zulkarnaev type and the specifics of theatre schools)

The plot about the departure of one of the friends (Alexander Pal) serves as a background rather than an engine of the plot, and the pals’ professional conflicts turn out to be more interesting. In this respect the picture sometimes falls apart into episodic sketches, which, however, is no great problem, because each of them is like a small dramedy, complete independently of the main line.

The only thing that raises questions is the scene with the cat. The thing is, the film begins with him being put down (morally devastating for Maria Karpova’s heroine and for all the viewers), although no illness is stated. Later we see a flashback of how the cat was found while the heroes were studying at theatre school, and that was not so many years ago, so the picture acquires an even more paradoxical meaning. It is clear that the cat’s death is a metaphor for the end of the heroes’ relationship, but a very cruel one.

---

## Fire Boy: An Uneven Film, but Alive and Striving Towards the Light

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ognennyy-malchik-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-06 (6 October 2025)
Work: “Fire Boy” is a 2025 film directed by Nadezhda Mikhalkova.
Tags: Russian cinema, festivals, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ognennyy-malchik-2025/

Nadya Mikhalkova’s *Fire Boy* (*Ognenny malchik*) is an uneven film, but alive and striving towards the light.

The story of the feelings of a young man before whose eyes a person accidentally burned to death (that very “fire boy”) grips the attention on several themes at once. There is the lack of contact with his mother (comically consonant with the lack of mobile reception for most of the film), the danger of everyday indifference, and a search for himself with a touch of mysticism. In this respect Denis Kosikov paradoxically precisely conveys every facet of his hero’s state. I can say the same of Bogdan Goloshchuk, a most vivid actor whose character appears briefly at the very beginning in order to set the tone of the whole film at once.

I find a lot in common between the themes of *Fire Boy* and Alexander Gorchilin’s *Acid*, which stated a similar problem of indifference and a subsequent attempt to forgive oneself with the pithy phrase “if you want to jump, jump”. And that is why the film, despite its rough edges nearer the finale,  rather hit home with me.

---

## Fireworks in the Afternoon: The Very Film Worth Travelling to Festivals For

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/feyerverki-dnem-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-05 (5 October 2025)
Work: “Fireworks in the Afternoon” is a 2025 film directed by Nina Volova.
Tags: Russian cinema, festivals, dramedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/feyerverki-dnem-2025/

*Fireworks in the Afternoon* (*Feyerverki dnyom*) is the very film worth travelling to festivals for. Alive, sparkling and elusively beautiful, like those very fireworks set off in the afternoon.

An airy, realistic story about three sisters trying to save the family nest from being sold is an extremely successful feature debut by Nina Volova. A drama on the edge of non-stop laughter and bitter tears, it has also managed to absorb the mood of Chekhov’s texts, both *Three Sisters* and *The Cherry Orchard*.

At the same time the film steps with one foot into the territory of a conversation about the mysterious Russian soul: the estranged gaze is provided by Wang Bing’s character, a Chinese entrepreneur who is at first very calculating. His gaze largely creates the comic sensation of examining yourself in a mirror, but a good-natured one, open to the new.

The team was applauded for about 10 minutes; I filmed a couple of moments. It is so far the best film I have seen in the programme, and I will very much look forward to its release so I can show it to everyone.
