## Lermontov: A Journey Through Time to What Does Not Change with Time

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/lermontov-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-05 (5 October 2025); updated: 2025-10-16
Work: “Lermontov” is a 2025 film directed by Bakur Bakuradze.
Tags: Russian cinema, biopic, festivals
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/lermontov-2025/

## 5 October 2025

And in general [*Lermontov*](https://t.me/kino_voice/941) is an astonishing journey through time to what does not change with time.

From the first frames the picture envelops you in the texture of the era and the place, literally letting you touch a way of life and of thinking. We slow down together with the static camera, which does not hurry after the characters’ movements but records the overall picture almost impassively. Like fate, which is often woven from fatal mistakes.

In the poet’s last day before the duel there is nothing that would betray the singularity of the moment. On the contrary, this day seems to interest everyone except the protagonist. And Ilya Ozolin excellently conveys an ironic indifference to himself and the world, laconically and caustically joking against the backdrop of a village pastoral.

This film can be called a kind of antipode of *Prorok* (“The Prophet”, the Pushkin musical biopic). All they have in common is turning to the biographies of poetic geniuses. In everything else *Lermontov* is quieter, more modest, more realistic and more everyday, especially as regards the terrible moment of a senseless death. But death is not the end of the reflection, and Bakuradze places his full stop far more elegantly. Perhaps that is exactly why the film stands outside the competition: it is hard to judge the eternal truth about the senselessness of violence.

Catch it in cinemas from [@volgafilms](https://t.me/volgafilms) and [@k24films](https://t.me/k24films) from 16 October.

## 16 October 2025

From today Bakur Bakuradze’s beautiful [*Lermontov*](https://t.me/volgafilms/6926) is in cinemas. Following my [hot recommendation from Mayak](https://t.me/kino_voice/942) (the film festival in Gelendzhik), I also want to highlight one significant detail for everyone who has yet to get acquainted with the picture.

I mean the epilogue scene. It is a very inventively created version, by the director, of an alternative universe in which everything could have turned out differently. Pay attention to the last scene of the film, where Lermontov, in his usual manner, sets up a prank on the husband of a lady who has been playing billiards with him. Everything is arranged so that (given a certain temperament in the husband) there would be every right to challenge the poet to a duel. But that does not happen. In this case what wins is the trust between the spouses, a sense of self-worth, the humanist principles of the value of life. In a word, everything that saves not only poets but people in general.

---

## My Son: A Picture Rich in Symbols That Need Deciphering

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/moy-syn-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-10-05 (5 October 2025)
Work: “My Son” is a 2025 film directed by Vyacheslav Klevtsov.
Tags: Russian cinema, drama, festivals
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/moy-syn-2025/

The programme (largely devoted to family ties) opens with the film *My Son* (*Moy syn*). It is the feature debut of director Vyacheslav Klevtsov. The leads are Yulia Snigir, Leon Kemstach and Pavel Tabakov (who presented the film together with the crew).

The picture, designed in a minimalist, cold way, is rich in symbols, and you need to go and see it ready to decipher them. Before us is a successful lawyer who has lied herself into a corner with the whole world and with herself: at first she lies even to her psychologist. Her son is someone else’s son. Her home is an eternal dusty building site. Her appearance is a mask that she managed to take off too late. Yulia Snigir looks extremely convincing in this angular vacuum, without arousing a drop of sympathy in the audience. Her heroine, only on losing her son, realises that she has lost herself. She is convinced of it when she is also rejected by an admirer blind to her sins. And bribery and bought verdicts make an excellent background.

As one of the film’s key young characters says: “Our generation weeps for the sins of yours.” The conflict of fathers and children is resolved here in something of a draw. In the words of the creators, “the heroine finds strength in the ability to experience emotions”. Where the young generation finds its strength is for the viewers to decide.

---

## Ingrid Olerinskaya on the Second Season of Ira

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ira-2-sezon-intervyu-olerinskaya/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-09-12 (12 September 2025)
Work: “Ira” is a work  Alim Beschokov, Sergey Notarius.
Tags: series, interview
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ira-2-sezon-intervyu-olerinskaya/

Filming of the second season of [*Ira*](https://t.me/kino_voice/71) is a wrap!

Taking up an [invitation to the set from Norm Production,](https://t.me/kino_voice/825) I asked Ingrid Olerinskaya about the heroine and the surprises of the coming season.

What is impossible to imagine your day on set without?

*Without coffee, without my phone, because a heap of work questions keeps pouring in and the chat never goes quiet, and without my facial expression. Which quite often coincides with Ira’s.*

What have you taught Ira, and vice versa?

*For me this is the first role where my heroine gets pregnant, then gives birth to a child, and has a great deal of interaction with children. All of that I taught Ira, because I have 3 nephews. I have brought them up since they were small, you could say. Ira, on the other hand, taught me endurance. I am a tough little person as it is, let us say, of iron temper. But in this case, of course, the volume of work on set makes you pull yourself together and hold on to the last.*

Do you think Ira will make a good mother?

*Ira has every chance of becoming a good mother. Despite her relationship with the world, which we remember from season 1, in season 2 there is nevertheless a transformation and an acceptance of the situation and of her current status. And, of course, love and maternal feeling are there one way or another. I think it will develop and prevail.*

Which moments on set are the hardest and, conversely, your favourites?

*The most uncomfortable and infuriating moment in acting is the enormous days when I am the only one talking in the frame. On the other hand, it is also a buzz, because not everyone can do that. I pray this skill never goes anywhere. And the biggest buzz, of course, is all of Ira’s fantasies. Most of them, let us say. There is always a little magic moment there, with costume changes, with costumes, with make-up. I think it is really cool, especially when you then watch it in the context of the whole series, it is very funny. I especially like it where I portray some men. There was a sultan, a sheikh in season 1. Thomas Edison. And in season 2 there will be, I will tell you a secret, a fantasy cornet, my favourite funny character.*

What would you like to pass on to the viewers of the second season of *Ira*?

*When watching season 2, just pay attention to the script, the dialogue, the humour and in general the interesting construction and shooting. Non-linear, as if made up of flashbacks and fantasy. I think it is an interesting move; I believe in our team and I believe that the second season will be even cooler than the first.*

---

## F1: The Plastic World Has Won After All

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/f1-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-09-09 (9 September 2025)
Work: “F1” is a 2025 film directed by Joseph Kosinski.
Tags: blockbuster, sport, Hollywood
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/f1-2025/

[*F1*](https://t.me/kino_voice/874), of course, masterfully takes your breath away at certain moments, but at the same time reminds you that the plastic world has won after all.

The picture has a mass of merits: Brad Pitt, who has lost not a drop of conviction in the role of the cool rebel; the camerawork in the racing scenes, edited so that you want to unlearn how to blink; an inspiring story with driving dynamics. And the rules of motor racing are explained in the most native way possible, so that we think in the same terms as the characters. All this adds up to a wonderful attraction that genuinely fits the title of the main blockbuster, but there are a couple of “buts”.

At the beginning the film seems to do, in racing slang, a lap to warm up the tyres. We are introduced to the main characters, who do not particularly arouse sympathy (and by their nature simply do not need it), and the future conflict is outlined (Brad Pitt’s character versus everyone). All this warm-up time I, as a viewer, am in the passive position of an observer rather than a participant in what is happening, because there is nobody for me to latch onto through empathy: the heroes are declared as script functions, not fully fledged personalities.

The film’s sterile studio quality has made the character descriptions schematic, as if skipping the stage of emotional make-up and immediately clarifying for the viewer who is responsible for what. Sonny Hayes is a cool guy with character who will get on everyone’s nerves but will not betray anyone. The young driver who has to acquire wisdom, not just swagger. The team leader who is in crisis, but Hayes will save everyone. The gifted engineer from whose single exchange of glances with Hayes we predict a romantic line.

Perhaps it is precisely this technical precision of the schemes that work in blockbusters that became the key to the film’s success with audiences. But I would have liked to get more sincere impressions from the viewing, rather than rational observations.

---

## Old School: A Quality Mockumentary with a Great Set of Characterful Personages

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/oldskul-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-09-05 (5 September 2025); updated: 2025-10-19
Work: “Old School” is a 2025 series directed by Aleksandr Zhigalkin, Evgeny Shelyakin.
Tags: series, sitcom, comedy, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/oldskul-serial/

## 5 September 2025

After 5 episodes, [*Old School*](https://t.me/kino_voice/665) (*Oldskul*) is in excellent form: a mockumentary sitcom with a school accent could not have been better.

It is especially pleasing that even the unshakeable monolith Maria Pavlovna develops as a character. I had expectations that for the whole series she would be (very funnily for the viewers) bending the world to her will (if only because “old school rules”, as the song over the closing credits goes). But in fact we see concessions to her granddaughter, a crisis of age-related self-identification and many other purely human things you would not expect from a conservative maths teacher. Cool, let the series keep breaking stereotypes.

P.S. The caretaker is a genius

## 29 September 2025

The most unexpected discovery of the series [*Old School*](https://t.me/kino_voice/871)

Maria Pavlovna has surprised again. It turns out she ignores the caretaker not because she is uninterested in romantic relationships, as might have seemed the case with a pedantic maths teacher. But because the caretaker simply ~~likes gooseberries~~ is not her type!

And also because the neighbour on Thursdays, it turns out, really does come round not only “to help about the house”.  And here I suddenly synchronised with Taisya Kalinina’s character, for whom accepting this state of affairs required some separate inner work...

And joking aside, here is a vivid example of how the series teaches you to see living people in ~~a dry maths teacher~~ teachers. That is cool!

## 19 October 2025

[*Old School*](https://t.me/kino_voice/922) has come briskly to an end. The series held its quality bar steadily throughout the story, with the sole exception that in the last couple of episodes the lines for the coming season began to take shape rather too briskly. But that is forgivable, because of course one wants to keep watching these characters)

The result is a quality mockumentary with a great set of characterful personages, consistent humour and the ability to reach a completely varied audience. A phenomenon of sorts: 30 million views, mind you.

P.S.: If the last episode is an advertisement for what life looks like after a course of antidepressants taken to the end, then it has succeeded.

---

## Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears: An Atmospheric Look at 2003 from 2025

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/moskva-slezam-ne-verit-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-09-04 (4 September 2025); updated: 2025-10-17
Work: “Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears. It's All Just Beginning” is a 2025 series directed by Olga Dolmatovskaya, Zhora Kryzhovnikov.
Tags: series, musical, remake, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/moskva-slezam-ne-verit-serial/

## 4 September 2025

From the first episode of the new [*Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears*](https://t.me/kino_voice/860) (the series sequel to the Oscar-winning 1980 film) it is noticeable above all that this is not an exact reconstruction of that same 2003 when the trio of heroines first meet, but rather an atmospheric look at it from our contemporary 2025.

Perhaps that is the effect of the specifics of the musical genre, in which there are always many conventions even without leaps in time, and with them all the more so. Hence the asynchronous details: for example, in 2003 the characters of Tina Stojiljković and Ivan Yankovsky dance in the “dry fountain” in Muzeon park, which in fact only opened in 2013.

Of the Soviet source film, the main reference points remain in the form of the heroines’ characters and their firm friendship, but in everything else it is a new story. From Zhora Kryzhovnikov’s signature style come the long-awaited jump cuts, the agitation and the cheerful anger of the heroines. On first viewing the series seems something between *The Boy’s Word* and *Kombinatsiya* (“Combination”, the series about the 1980s girl band), the two previous high-profile projects from Wink (the Russian streaming service), in the first of which the musical inserts worked 200%, while in the second they rather replaced dialogue in places (which is sometimes more interesting to listen to, after all).

Since the fate of the heroines emerges rather schematically over the episode, the most touching things for me were the signs of the times: a recognisable pre-Sobyanin marshrutka (minibus), bus stops plastered with ads, screaming eclecticism in clothes. And the pop-culture artefacts and prices stood out in particular:

- *Terminator 3* and *Lara Croft* are on at the cinema, the Tolkienist movement is in its prime, and the girls run off to the casting for *Fabrika zvyozd* (“Star Factory”, the Russian pop talent show). It makes you want to shed a tear.
- A hamburger at McDonald’s costs 17 roubles. For an order of two cheeseburgers, fries and ice creams you would have to pay 160 roubles. So that such prices do not hurt so much, you can imagine they are simply in today’s Belarusian roubles.

The only thing not yet obvious is whether the project will stay rather on the side of fairy-tale cuteness or defect to realism (especially as regards the part with the heroines 20 years later); I will keep watching to find out.

## 11 September 2025

I liked the second episode of *Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears* so much that I am ready to forget all my doubts [after watching the first](https://t.me/kino_voice/870).

Moderate use of musical numbers suits the series very well. In the second episode there is only one such scene, but it is brilliant (literally and figuratively), a genuinely cool music video inside the film. Anastasia Talyzina and Andrey Burkovsky in this number combine comedy, sincerity and the demonstrativeness of their attitude to each other, important for an inserted number that takes place, as it were, in the heroine’s thoughts. The key difference of the musical scene this time: it does not retell part of the plot (as was the case with Ksyusha’s unhappy job) but complements the heroine’s emotional background without affecting the sequence of events in the series’ world! Cool, vivid, intelligible, unobtrusive.

And the definitive acting triumph goes to Masha Milash: her heroine is the most characterful and tangible, it seems to me, and following her is a great pleasure. The second episode is mainly hers in screen time, so the creators’ bets on this heroine are probably high. She truly sets the mood of what happens, whether feeding the American a pack of lies or taking the sweetest historical re-enactor, played by Andrey Maksimov, for a ride on an emotional rollercoaster: cruel in both cases, but funny. I want to believe that things will work out with the Tolkienist after all, and that Masha, in classic fashion, will ask the American where strength lies.

## 19 September 2025

I keep finding that the new [*Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears*](https://t.me/kino_voice/882) reveals itself for the better with every episode.

The third episode again has only one fully fledged musical number, unexpectedly not with the heroine, and one more half-musicalised scene with the central characters. As they say, modest and tasteful, and most importantly meaningful, with a dramatic foundation beneath the musical wrapping. I hope this side of things stays on track to the last episode.

As a whole the events of the episode are in a state, as they say, of in progress ❌ The girls have already understood something about their relationships, but have not yet had time to come to terms with that information, and keep travelling along the rails laid in advance. Ksyusha could have got away with the same status too, were it not for her husband, who arrived and brought with him the chilling atmosphere of the phrase “the groom has come”. Perhaps the final scene on the balcony is a moment rhyming with how, in the original film, Alentova’s heroine fell asleep in tears in the worst of all possible situations, and after a cut we saw a completely different life of hers years later.

## 27 September 2025

After watching episodes 4 and 5 of the new [*Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears*](https://t.me/kino_voice/905) back to back, I understood the feelings of the 90 million viewers who generated the Soviet film’s phenomenal box office. This is how the [sources](https://www.culture.ru/materials/257558/istoriya-odnogo-filma-moskva-slezam-ne-verit) describe that frenzy:

> “After the premiere of *Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears*, huge queues formed outside cinemas, with people waiting for the box offices to open. Screenings began early in the morning and went on late into the night, and visitors came to the film several times”

I too immediately wanted to rewatch these two episodes as soon as they ended, although I never wanted to rewatch the Soviet two-part film that way. The feeling of belonging to a time in which such a transformation of the heroines’ fates takes place provokes a very strong response, of course. You begin to understand the Soviet cinemagoers, and especially the women among them, 100%, and to believe in a miracle within your own era.

The musical numbers in the new episodes are better than ever. Ksyusha’s transformation into a businesswoman I personally find easy to believe, like any cinematic convention that nonetheless has a right to exist. Even Katerina’s transformation into a factory director, incidentally, was received with scepticism in its day: she could not have risen like that entirely without outside help, people said; again I quote a [source:](https://moskvichmag.ru/kino/rovno-45-let-nazad-v-etot-den-proshla-vsesoyuznaya-premera-filma-moskva-slezam-ne-verit/)

> “*Moscow* could easily have been withdrawn from distribution and ended up on the shelf. The film was criticised by both critics and the authorities, and the label ‘vulgar melodrama’ was one of the mildest accusations. Objections were raised both to the ‘explicit scenes’ and to the very story of a woman’s success. Poor Katya from the provinces could not have made such a career in the USSR, that was the general verdict”

It is especially pleasing that there is no gulf in quality between the two parts of the series; I will only miss the young versions of the heroines. On the other hand, the Tolkienist lawyer played by Andrey Maksimov is in place, and his line with Masha will definitely remain the most interesting for me.

## 3 October 2025

In the second part of the new [*Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears*](https://t.me/kino_voice/919) I am separately pleased that my favourite among the male characters has grown up the most handsomely.

Andrey Maksimov was treated gently, and 20 years have only benefited his character’s looks; well, they certainly did not get worse. Which cannot be said of Ivan Yankovsky’s character, who in age did not seem to differ much from the Tolkienist student, so this paradox of ageing is beyond me. And, of course, of Andrey Burkovsky, who, though he was the oldest of all, has been aged far too harshly (apparently so that it would be easier for Olya to leave him for Ruzil Minekaev).

The logic of the ageing (for which, on the whole, great respect to the make-up department) remains a mystery, but I am pleased that my taste did not let me down.

## 17 October 2025

In the finale of [*Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears*](https://t.me/kino_voice/927) I can understand and accept everything except the resolution of the line with Masha and Artyom (who seem to have got rid of their alcoholism).

It hurt me as a fan (they are my favourite characters). The reason for the break-up, to my taste, is completely untenable, and I cannot understand Masha’s logic at all. To me their situation looks (the only one of all the couples!) like “live and be happy”. With mutual work on themselves, of course, but basically without problems!

The other heroines’ lines seem more logical to me: they could, of course, have been handled differently or more interestingly, but the existing outcome raises no questions either. On the whole, the finale noticeably echoes the start of the series: the friends, as in the good old days, are their own only hope, and the whole world stands against them. Some things, as they say, do not change.

---

## If Cats Disappeared from the World: How the Author’s Connection to Cinema Is Felt in the Book

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/esli-vse-koshki-v-mire-ischeznut-kniga/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-08-31 (31 August 2025)
Work: “If Cats Disappeared from the World” is a 2012 book by Genki Kawamura.
Tags: books
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/esli-vse-koshki-v-mire-ischeznut-kniga/

Since I have already seen the mind-blowing [*Exit 8* (highly recommended](https://t.me/kino_voice/842)), I became interested in the book by its director Genki Kawamura, *If Cats Disappeared from the World*.

In the plot, the hero learns of a terminal illness and is already preparing to say goodbye to life, but gets the chance to make a deal with the devil and receive a day of life for every thing that disappears from our world. I read the book in literally a day and am very pleased. Not least with how the author’s connection to cinema is felt right in the text. For example:

- The “devilish double” whom the hero meets is, judging by the description, dressed in the image and likeness of Tyler Durden from *Fight Club*. He wears a Hawaiian shirt and sunglasses, while the hero keeps to a classic office style. This seems to be the best way to visualise the contemporary devil in a text.

- The hero’s beloved lives and works in a cinema. I am not even hinting at *Inglourious Basterds*; it is enough that the object of romantic interest is connected to cinema as personally as possible. Incidentally, the hero’s close friend is a film geek working in a video rental shop. No hints at Tarantino, again.

- At some point the hero reflects on whether everything happening to him could be transferred to the screen. A truly director’s thought.

- In the characters’ dialogue, films from *The Matrix* to *Now Is Good* are quoted (or mentioned) very unobtrusively but quite often (the latter figures as “the film in which the dying heroine writes out 10 things she wants to do in time”, but we know what is meant). The hero is quite well watched!

- At some point the devil proposes that all films should disappear (in exchange for a day of the hero’s life). Knowing that the author of the book is a director, following the character’s decision in this case was as gripping as it gets.

---

## Exit 8: An Adaptation That Surpassed the Notion of Adaptation

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/vykhod-8-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-08-24 (24 August 2025)
Work: “Exit 8” is a 2025 film directed by Genki Kawamura.
Tags: horror, thriller, adaptation
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/vykhod-8-2025/

I must confess: I have an unbearably poor sense of direction; mastering a new route is always a great ordeal.

All the more interesting for me was the film [*Exit 8*,](https://t.me/provzglyad/4614) already acclaimed at Cannes. I recognised myself on screen: how many times have I wandered the underground like that.

This is an adaptation of the game of the same name, which seems to have surpassed the notion of adaptation as such. The hyper-immersion in the unreal atmosphere of the underground, from which the hero cannot get out, is a real find by director Genki Kawamura

The character’s wanderings through the labyrinths of his own conscience and memories do not turn into melancholy reflection but create tension through the screen. The horror elements, the thriller mood and the gamified structure of what happens work together so precisely that a quite palpable claustrophobia, mixed half and half with a bout of anxiety, comes over you. *Exit 8* turns the viewer into an accomplice, as if the fate of the hero depended on our attentiveness too. It is for exactly this kind of gripping experience that the film is worth seeing in a cinema.

In cinemas from 28 August thanks to [@provzglyad](https://t.me/provzglyad). Do not miss it, a real thriller on the eve of autumn weekdays with their eternal metro rides.

---

## Breathe: It Does Not Much Matter How the Inquiry Ends

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/dyshi-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-08-15 (15 August 2025); updated: 2025-10-03
Work: “Breathe” is a 2025 series directed by Anna Kuznetsova.
Tags: series, drama, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/dyshi-serial/

## 15 August 2025

This summer, series about doctors are showing how dangerous and risky this profession is, one for the genuinely strong in spirit.

On the one hand there is [*Khirurg*](https://t.me/kino_voice/799) (“The Surgeon”) with Sergei Gilev’s long-suffering (but wonderful) character; on the other, [*Breathe*,](https://youtu.be/j_KRCRf7tr0?si=dhb5Xz-7NQL8ERc7) (*Dyshi*) a series of stunning power that you watch with trembling hands and your breath knocked out of you.

The first episode came out today; I [wrote](https://t.me/kino_voice/674) about it from Pilot (the Russian series festival) and am still under the impression, which is also a recommendation of sorts. One can feel differently about the heroine, Lera, but watching her is absorbing, because before us is the type of a living, troubled person, not a stock doctor meeting the classic notions of the profession, and that is both pleasing and frightening. Together with the frenzied rhythm of the action, the director’s warmth towards the characters, felt through the screen, and the delicate subject matter, the result is something inimitable.

## 23 August 2025

The second episode of [*Breathe*](https://t.me/kino_voice/818) puts all the viewer’s notions about the series in their proper places.

First and foremost, of course, they concern Lera. It turns out she manages to grab the medical record at the right moment, to convince a traffic cop of her innocence and to manipulate her children. This is not surprising, we knew she was an imperfect heroine, but it helps get rid of idealisation and unnecessary regrets **\*️⃣** It is cool when the foreground is held by a character whose likeability you sometimes have to doubt: it adds a further opportunity to reflect on the given theme.

And the updated poster seems a success to me in this respect: the patients’ lives are, of course, in her hands, but first of all, is her own?

## 6 September 2025

With every episode [*Breathe*](https://t.me/kino_voice/841) seems to make it harder for the viewer to choose a character to trust and empathise with.

Thanks to episode 4 introducing Lera’s younger children into the complex equation of the plot as well, it became clear that the story is not about obstetrics or medical backroom intrigues at all. It turns out that, as with Anna Kuznetsova’s [*Intermission*](https://t.me/kino_voice/291) (*Kanikuly*), behind the screen of a private story on a subject that seems narrow at first glance hides a universal, all-human drama. All the more interesting, because in this case predicting the ending is genuinely impossible.

## 3 October 2025

The final episode of [*Breathe*](https://t.me/kino_voice/873) confirms: in this story it does not much matter how exactly the inquiry ends, whether the child survives, or even who gets the late Motoruev’s car.

Far more significant is the path the characters have travelled over the course of the events shown: this is the very truth we were striving towards for 8 episodes, and it turns out to be not nearly as grim as it might have seemed at first. These are merely the consequences of a chain of choices made, which, on close observation, are quite possible to understand.

In this respect the series has much in common with director Anna Kuznetsova’s feature [*Intermission*](https://t.me/kino_voice/291). There too the emphasis was not on the event driving the plot but on the transformation of its participants. There is (almost) nothing interesting in a youth theatre competition in itself, but in how the adults and teenagers changed during it, there very much is.

It is separately pleasing how absolutely every character, young and old, gets a coherent personal ending. It is from their sum that the finale of the series is made up: ambiguous and non-static, like life itself, but with a gap for air, which everyone who has watched will definitely have needed.

---

## Cherry Dream at a39: A New Gogol Center Has Appeared

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/vishnevyy-son-teatr/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-08-11 (11 August 2025)
Work: “Vishnyovy son” is a 2025 stage production directed by Oleg Glushkov.
Tags: theatre
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/vishnevyy-son-teatr/

“A new Gogol Center has appeared!”, I thought in the first minutes of *Vishnyovy son* («Вишнёвый сон», “Cherry Dream”) at a39 (the Moscow theatre).

And really, it turned out to be a superb piece of work in terms of combining Chekhov’s original *The Cherry Orchard* with contemporary stage design. I had missed this since the production of *The Misanthrope* at the Gogol Center (the Moscow theatre closed in 2022).

While watching, you feel that the production is, as it were, speaking the same language as you, without forgetting its source, and that is worth a great deal. Everything from the design and costumes to the music and the fit between the actors and their roles is simply a 100% hit. I have a weakness for the use of techno music in theatre, there is nothing I can do about it, but how apt it turned out to be here: the sound of the breaking string that we deserve. And “The Winner Takes It All”, sung towards the end, is, whichever way you look at it, the most concise and laconic musical embodiment of Lopakhin’s tragedy (at first slyly disguised by director Oleg Glushkov as a dramedy).

As for the cast, it is very, very convincing. I want to rewatch every line of Ranevskaya as played by Serafima Goshchanskaya, every monologue of Petya Trofimov as played by Sergei Kirpichonok, every affectation of Dunyasha as played by Elizabeth Damsker and, especially, every scene of Lopakhin as played by Ilya Ozolin. I am ready to shower the theatre’s company with compliments endlessly: every one of these guys is simply inimitable, and the sooner they start being cast more in our films and series, the better (colleagues, take note!)

And for now we await Ilya Ozolin’s big dramatic role in Bakuradze’s [*Lermontov*](https://t.me/kino_voice/760): after he lived (my tongue will not say “played”) Lopakhin on stage, my expectations have grown.

---

## The Surgeon: A Finale Broken Down into Pluses and Minuses

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/khirurg-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-08-04 (4 August 2025); updated: 2025-08-30
Work: “The Surgeon” is a 2025 series directed by Ilya Ermolov.
Tags: series, drama, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/khirurg-serial/

## 4 August 2025

And in general [*The Surgeon*](https://youtu.be/Rq1AtLQneY0?si=vvuSDuGoID0MIPmu) (*Khirurg*) is a wonderful story about a rare type of hero who can be described as “*a bad good man*”.

A transplant surgeon who wanted to distance himself from the terrible reality of how organs are obtained ended up a victim of his own indifference. He is an excellent doctor and father, and means well, but a bad husband and a cruel man, and that is his problem.

Sergei Gilev looks perfectly contradictory in this role: combining toughness with sincerity, he creates a hero who evokes empathy but not pity. Though I am probably on his side anyway, because the other characters (except the daughter) are mostly just bad people.

I hope this story steers towards a finale where *bad good people* also deserve relative happiness.

## 8 August 2025

The fifth episode of *The Surgeon* works as a great development of the long set-up we were given [in the first four episodes](https://t.me/kino_voice/799). The method of narration changes too: no more flashbacks, if you look closely.

It is pleasing that Yulia, Marina Vorozhishcheva’s heroine, comes to the fore: it is not often you see a promotion from “damsel in distress” to a fully fledged protagonist; now she is a subject, not an object (if only briefly, yes). This is especially important at the moment when the first loop of the surgeon Sergei’s storyline seems to be complete: what the hero would do next without Yulia is not very clear. Gilev, by the way, is still magnificent. Three episodes remain to sort out all the problems and enjoy the acting (and it really is a joy to the eyes and the soul)

## 30 August 2025

The finale of [*The Surgeon*](https://t.me/kino_voice/799) puzzled me, so I will break it down into pluses and minuses:

👆A happy ending for Sergei, his daughter and her suitor. Vera seems to have ended up satisfied too (this heroine’s soul is probably a mystery)

👆Unambiguously closed storylines for a multitude of characters (which, for such a number of them, is rather a rarity)

👆Genuinely convincing (for the most part) performances

👇Overly schematic endings; in such cases I always argue that adding an episode would have been a good idea (for example, to reveal Batyr’s plan and whether or not Sergei was involved in it)

👇 So Vera is a rat twice over? Men would do better to be on their guard with her, otherwise there is a high risk of going to prison for their misdeeds. In general, a slight demonisation of the female character took place.

👇The first half of the series is noticeably stronger than the second, in plot, in dialogue and in dynamics. A pity that such a drop occurred; the story had very great potential indeed.

---

## A Trip to the Sun and Back: The Terrifying 1990s You Take for a Fairy Tale

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/puteshestvie-na-solntse-i-obratno-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-07-25 (25 July 2025); updated: 2025-08-13
Work: “A Trip to the Sun and Back” is a 2025 series directed by Roman Mikhailov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, 1990s
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/puteshestvie-na-solntse-i-obratno-serial/

## 25 July 2025

Having watched 4 episodes of [*A Trip to the Sun and Back*,](https://youtu.be/hjmw4RrrEZ8?si=clI46UKOtfK36oeq) (*Puteshestvie na solntse i obratno*) in a row, I not only immersed myself in the atmosphere of the genuinely terrifying 1990s (which, though we are tired of them, are as good as can be here), taking it for a fairy tale, but also made 2 interesting observations:

**1️⃣** Ruslan, the fairy-tale-ethereal protagonist played by Oleg Chugunov, was truly born lucky. Over the first episodes we see how in the 1990s his crew of 4 lads seems to dissolve into thin air. One was killed in prison, the second became a junkie, and what will happen to the third is not yet clear. Ruslan, as if at crossroads marked by stones with inscriptions like “go left and you will find death”, very successfully fits into the right turns and comes out of the water dry, out of the fire alive, and so on. By the standards of the era’s setting, such luck is easily taken for a fairy-tale miracle.

**2️⃣** I do not know why (all right, I do know, but I will tell you in a separate post), but in atmosphere the series reminds me of the credits of the project [*Deti peremen*.](https://t.me/kino_voice/303) (“Children of Change”) The same hypnotic feeling of watching a vanishing world over which the foot of cruel reality is already raised, ready to trample it all. Only, if in the credits it is a combination of shots like a family chronicle, in the series it is impulsive attempts to live a young and vivid life in a stale vacuum unfit for anything living at all. Terrifying and impossibly recognisable.

## 30 July 2025

The fifth episode of [*A Trip to the Sun and Back*,](https://t.me/kino_voice/780) as happens with the best episodes of series, simply demands a checklist of the beautiful things seen:

- Ruslan’s trip to St Petersburg, utterly Balabanovian and in the best traditions of *Brother*, where, as usual, all the strength lies. Except that he introduced himself as a student rather than a clerk. Except that they did not issue him Danila Bagrov’s sweater.

- A card-game scene in the spirit either of Guy Ritchie or of the forthcoming project [*Poker for Us*.](https://t.me/kino_voice/668) A wonderful attraction of reality in the middle of a fairy-tale narrative.

- The inimitable feeling of fully understanding the emotions of Vitya, the young crime boss played by Ivan Ivashov, who delivered an impressive monologue about a broken future and the forced repetition of his parents’ fate on the ruins of his hopes. For me he is the real protagonist of the episode.

It seems there is more and more of the second element than the first in the series’ magical realism, and watching this is unsettling.

## 6 August 2025

The sixth episode of [*A Trip to the Sun and Back*](https://t.me/kino_voice/789) is the penultimate one, slowing the pace a little in order to show more expressively what happens when the past inside your head does not get on with the present outside it.

The madness quietly spreading across the screen seems to hint that Ruslan has now arrived at a real crossroads rather than a fairy-tale one ➖ Either choose his own time, unsettled and shelterless as it is, or remain forever in the bright memory of childhood with a bride from fairy-tale books, like the boy Bananan “in the sheltered world of dreams” (from the film *Assa*), and, as Shpalikov wrote, “where mother is young and father is alive”. Here the father, though physically alive, is not quite alive in spirit, as if a “former person” of a departed era. The same, however, can be said of the mother, who has lost her bearings in the new world. Everyone has lost them, really: just consider the rehearsal of funeral speeches at the New Year table.

If earlier the finale seemed to promise a bright resolution against all odds, now it rather frightens: if only Ruslan’s choice turns out not to be ruinous.

## 13 August 2025

[*A Trip to the Sun and Back*](https://t.me/kino_voice/802) has ended.

The last episode has, perhaps, absorbed the whole spectrum of emotions the characters lived through over the season. It was frightening, eerie, hopeless, inescapable, bright and sad. The finale keeps you in suspense better than any thriller: thanks to the blurring of genre, it is genuinely impossible to predict what exactly will happen and how irreparable it will be. It is a great piece of work to make the resolution gripping without losing the harmony set by the previous episodes. Such an ending makes you feel sincere gratitude to the authors: the characters deserved nothing else.

Of course, because of the plot twist with Laszlo, who came in handy in the criminal schemes, the thought of Balabanov’s Danila will not leave you. Also, it seems, a bit of a holy fool, but he found his place. St Petersburg belongs there too.

And the scene in the train vestibule both horrifies and delights. After everything he has been through, Ruslan could have perished there or been born anew. How good that it was the latter.

---

## Neyrobatya: A Modern Fairy Tale with a Balance of Kindness, Charm and Humour

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/neyrobatya-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-07-15 (15 July 2025)
Work: “Neyrobatya” is a 2025 film directed by Vitaly Dudka.
Tags: comedy, Russian cinema, family
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/neyrobatya-2025/

There are films about which it is appropriate to say: “good stuff!”

[*Neyrobatya*](https://t.me/kino_voice/754) («Нейробатя», “Neuro-Dad”) is that very film. It is simply some kind of celebration, judging by its balance of kindness, charm and humour. Director Vitaly Dudka described it at the premiere as a “modern fairy tale”, and that is entirely fair. *Neyrobatya* is very reminiscent of my dearly beloved [*Legends from the Past*,](https://t.me/kino_voice/569) (*Legendy nashikh predkov*) where the present day mixes with little miracles, and (unexpectedly!) of *Kiberderevnya* (“Cyber Village”, the comedy series). Incidentally, Sergei Chikhachev is here too, as a colourful village resident) Also among the references: *The Shawshank Redemption*, *Fargo*, [*Yura dvornik*](https://t.me/kino_voice/5) (“Yura the Janitor”; that we respect)

The hero, Grisha Besov (Denis Vlasenko), is a cool robotics engineer who dreams of becoming part of a start-up but cannot because of a black mark on his biography in the person of his father, who is in prison. It is at precisely this moment that this very father appears in his life, but no longer in the most conscious state. To sort out the situation and start a new life, Grisha desperately needs to find his father’s stash of the money plundered over his entire thieving “career”. And since only the father knows its location, Grisha connects his consciousness to gadgets, and from there a chain of their small, lyrical adventures unwinds.

It would be no exaggeration to say that *Neyrobatya* is the perfect option for a good time with loved ones and family. The film makes you laugh at the level of lines (dad’s slang is something indescribable), at the level of the situations the heroes get into, and visually: the mockumentary from prison with *The Office* vibes will definitely amuse you. In cinemas from 17 July, not hinting at anything, but warmly recommending.

---

## Sober Village: A Documentary on the Edge of Comedy and Tragedy

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/trezvoe-selo-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-07-11 (11 July 2025)
Work: “Sober Village” is a 2025 film directed by Yulia Sergina.
Tags: documentary, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/trezvoe-selo-2025/

I want to add a couple more words about [*Sober Village*](https://t.me/kino_voice/733) (*Trezvoe selo*), because the project touched my heart with its cinematic quality and its balance on the edge of comedy and tragedy. Life really is the best screenwriter.

This is one of those documentaries that capture in real life things that seem fantastical until you run into them yourself. In the plot, the heads of the Bashkir villages of Kopey-Kubovo (the melancholy Rafimir) and Dyurtyuli (the proactive Lyaysan) take part in the “Sober Village” competition, together with 52 other villages. The winner, who over six months organises community leisure in their village and reduces alcohol consumption, will receive 5 million roubles for the annual budget (the usual budget of these villages is 1 million). And all the village heads badly need it: now the sewage system breaks down, now the local alcoholics start brawling so that the neighbouring houses complain, now a bridge collapses altogether and there is no money for repairs; all hope rests on this prize.

And here I want to describe the main hero in more detail. Rafimir, who heads Kopey-Kubovo, is simply the spitting image of Michael Scott from the series *The Office*, in the best sense. It is hard to believe, but their sincere naivety in striving to improve the life of the collective of fellow villagers (read: a big family) coincides 100%. And it is expressed in words, facial expressions and actions so similarly that it seems Steve Carell sometimes drew the raw material for his character from Rafimir himself. Just consider the episode where the village head, dressed up as Ded Moroz (the Russian Father Frost), goes round the villagers’ houses himself to give people and their families a holiday (recall the entirely analogous scenes from *The Office*).

And it is precisely in this resemblance, created by life itself, that the film’s main merit lies. With absolutely comic (by the standards of fiction) starting conditions, *Sober Village* touches on the far from comic problems of living people. And it is precisely this combination, I think, that can attract to the film not only documentary connoisseurs but a wider audience, who will certainly recognise familiar characters in living people whom it is easy and important to empathise with.

---

## Wild Tales: The Wildness Goes Off the Scale, Growing with Every Story

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/dikie-istorii-2014/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-07-07 (7 July 2025)
Work: “Wild Tales” is a 2014 film directed by Damián Szifron.
Tags: black comedy, anthology
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/dikie-istorii-2014/

Recently a [bot](https://t.me/CinemaChoiceBot) for finding films threw up an idea for an evening’s viewing: *Wild Tales*, a nominee for the 2015 Oscar for best foreign-language film, by the way.

The film consists of short stories, each like a mini *Final Destination* (though the endings are not so uniform). After roughly the first story you understand in what mood the fates of the characters in the subsequent plots will develop. But not to keep watching is impossible. The wildness goes off the scale, growing with every story, and the cringe (in the best possible sense) climbs out of the frame, so the title more than pays for itself. One of the stories even recalls the series *Beef*, as if anticipating its plot about road-rage showdowns.

In general, many of the problems touched on in the film can be characterised at the very least by the word “eternal”. Social injustice, aggression in everyday life, emotional abuse. In 2025 it may seem that all this is no longer so catastrophic, but the film uses hyperbole precisely in order to focus attention on human problems not of universal scale.

Be sure to watch to the end: for dessert, my favourite of all the stories, the wedding one, awaits you. I laughed myself silly at it, because the wildness of what happens is so unrealistic yet so convincing that it is impossible to remain indifferent. The problem of marriage in crisis, after all. If you suddenly remembered *Gorko!* (the 2013 Russian wedding comedy), yes, its vibes are present in the story, but prepare for humour far blacker and more misanthropic (hard to imagine, I know, but it is possible), and simply enjoy.

---

## The Ugly Stepsister: The Cinderella Tale Through the Eyes of the “Villainess”

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/gadkaya-sestra-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-07-04 (4 July 2025)
Work: “The Ugly Stepsister” is a 2025 film directed by Emilie Blichfeldt.
Tags: horror, fairy tales
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/gadkaya-sestra-2025/

I waited for the online release of [*The Ugly Stepsister*](https://youtu.be/myAwbsACdu4?si=4Tjw-SbLPsRehe1o) on our platforms, watched it and regretted not having gone to see the film in a cinema.

*The Ugly Stepsister* turned out to be a stunning mix of *The Substance*, *Marie Antoinette* and the 2021 *Cruella*, with full immersion in the atmosphere of the Brothers Grimm’s fairy tales (which is why watching on the big screen is the best choice). I always like experiments in looking at familiar stories from the point of view of a collectively condemned character, and here the choice of the stepsister from the Cinderella tale is very telling. We are used to seeing in the stepsisters only ugly exploiters of modest Cinderella, without considering the motivation of these “villainesses”. But villainy is only one facet of their nature. Having seen the story through their eyes, we begin to perceive differently both the causes and the consequences of their actions. It is very pleasing that this trend in cinema continues. And most importantly, Cinderella is still a victim too, so the story has acquired no one-sidedness whatsoever with its new lens.

Elvira, that very stepsister (but ugly? the question remains open), sincerely dreams of marrying the prince. In pursuit of happiness (and of the money her mother so badly needs) she makes colossal sacrifices in the name of beauty. So that we understand how agonising these transformations are, the “theatre of cruelty” is very aptly embedded in the film. This is a theatrical concept (by now firmly established in cinema) that puts the emphasis on the characters’ physical experience rather than on dialogue. In this sense the film really is frighteningly sparing with words. We see in detail a bloody 18th-century rhinoplasty, a no less painful eyelash extension and a literally murderous method of losing weight historically known as the “tapeworm diet”. At the same time the heroines (the world of this film is predominantly female) have no intention of talking to one another, with rare exceptions. Perhaps the only person ready to listen and to hear turns out to be the younger sister, who for the whole film seems inconspicuous and insignificant

In short, you feel sorry for everyone, because we know the finale in advance, but it is impossible to tear yourself away. I will definitely follow the future work of Emilie Blichfeldt, the director of *The Ugly Stepsister* (she even put references to *Un Chien Andalou* into the film, which is quite rare), and the roles of Lea Myren, who played Elvira, because this is a colossal piece of acting.

---

## Poker for Us: A Story That Ended Purely by Karma

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/nam-poker-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-06-20 (20 June 2025); updated: 2025-12-03
Work: “Poker for Us” is a 2025 series directed by Rustam Ilyasov.
Tags: festivals, series, Russian cinema, crime
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/nam-poker-serial/

## 20 June 2025

Fun and illegal, like gambling, the project *Poker for Us* (*Nam poker*) wins you over with stylish camerawork and crisp portraits of its characters from the first frame. Respect, by the way, for the pop-up explanations of gaming terms!

Three friends decide to open a poker club right in their own home, but the illegal business draws them in. The spirit of illicit fun is infectious through the screen, and now we are already rooting for the hapless owners of the gambling den.

The cast includes Artyom Koshman, Sasha Bortich and Pyotr Skvortsov (always glad to see him). As in *Popados* (“Busted”), the consequences of stepping onto the slippery slope for young people are declared from the first frame. But here my favourite mechanism works: even knowing the outcome, it is extremely curious to find out how the heroes came to live like this.

## 6 November 2025

The very likeable series [*Poker for Us*](https://t.me/kino_voice/925) also launched with two episodes.

I fell for it back in the summer at Pilot (the Russian series festival), and the review of the first episode was [written](https://t.me/kino_voice/668) right from there. The second does not slacken the pace either. In particular, Pyotr Skvortsov’s character, mysteriously announced in the first episode, unfolds further into full-blown madness. I have not seen the actor in this role of a completely unhinged villain for a long time, and it suits him very well, so the creators of *Poker for Us* have hit the jackpot here.

The very texture of the story about two students caught in an unhealthy scheme with an illegal casino is very absorbing, because it is done briskly, in a contemporary way and not as dramatically as it could have been with such a plot. Besides, the effect of the half-open ending announced in the first frames of the series immediately makes you want to find out how they came to live like this.

## 3 December 2025

[*Poker for Us*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1089) is over.

I am as pleased with the series as can be and will be waiting intently for news of a second season (by every parameter and every hook cast, it is essential here).

Yesterday, finishing the final episode, I became definitively convinced of the thought that nothing more plausible in terms of fatalities developing in parallel in the lives of specific people has been filmed in recent years (or I have not seen it). I do not run an underground casino, of course, but all the heroes’ ordeals from the endless cycle of problems flowing out of one another I can quite understand and share. Luckily, the story in the series ended purely by karma, so there is always hope.

Egor as played by Timofey Eletsky is the best to my taste, a very deep and, for all his deceptive exterior, touchingly sweet character. Simply a one hundred percent hit on a good man who means well and because of that sometimes does badly, and you believe it. Ruslan Bratov’s (the director of the wonderful [*Express*](https://t.me/kino_voice/52)) Javid is simply a riot too: evidently the axiom “a talented person is talented in everything” worked here. Vitya (Artyom Koshman) has a wonderful character arc with the strongest transformations, also a sheer pleasure to watch, as, incidentally, does Alexandra Bortich. In humour the screenwriters simply hit the jackpot: it is worth rewatching with a notebook and copying the jokes out into your personal collection.

In short, I can praise the series for a long time, as you can see; I hope as many people as possible appreciate it. I would not want it to end after one season without ever revealing to us the context of the video message from Koshman’s character in the first episode.

## Pilot 2025: Impressions of the Competition Pilots

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/festival-pilot-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-06-19 (19 June 2025); updated: 2025-06-21
Tags: festivals, series, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/festival-pilot-2025/

## 19 June 2025

The festival (Pilot, the Russian series festival in Ivanovo) opens with [*Konstantinopol*](https://t.me/kino_voice/622) (“Constantinople”), which, as last year, is an exemplary classical historical drama with its own advantages and shortcomings. The adventures of refugees from the Russian Empire in Constantinople in the first episode are rather of a declarative nature and, in terms of plot, fall short of the artistic elaboration of this world.

Before us is an officer who has lost his whole family and his faith in military honour, a quick-witted doctor (so far the most interesting character, played by Kirill Käro) and a “merchant” thirsting to get back the gold confiscated by the Constantinople customs officers. Tying these lines together is difficult so far, so that will be a task mostly for the most devoted fans of the genre.

## 20 June 2025

*Full House* is a story interesting first and foremost for its experimental nature. It combines a little medical drama, a little mysticism, a little procedural, a little of Bulgakov’s *A Young Doctor’s Notebook*. Not everything is smooth, but if they polish it, as the creators said, it is potentially a good thing.

The plot about a principled medical resident in the far north looks somewhat uncomfortable, exactly enough to convey the heroine’s state in a new place where there is zero trust from colleagues and bureaucracy and drinking surgeons all around. Incidentally, Pyotr Fyodorov is rather good as the latter. It will be interesting to see how his clearly drawn conflict with the heroine, played by Maria Lisova, develops. For the sake of such a clash of experience and idealism, it is probably worth waiting for the remaining episodes.

## 20 June 2025

Remember the title *Popados* (“Busted”): it is a brisk piece of crime action with new faces and already established artists. I was looking forward to it largely because of the duo of Makar Khlebnikov and Timofey Tribuntsev, and they really are wonderful here, playing father and son.

The plot structure neatly combines flashbacks with a present in which the consequences of the teenagers’ prank have already arrived. Flirting with the criminal world turns into big problems for the heroes, and here one recalls *Na avtomate* (“On Autopilot”), a project that reflected substantively on the same themes. The pilot gave all its lines worthy set-ups at a good pace, so one really does want to wait for the continuation.

## 21 June 2025

With all my heart I wish the project *Bukhanka Chyornogo* (“Chyorny’s Loaf”, a pun on the UAZ “loaf” van) to find its platform and be filmed to the end: it is a real discovery among the independent projects.

The hysterically funny Lyokha, the protagonist, whom I privately dubbed “the plush gangster”, works as a waiter in his father’s coffee shop, hates hipsters with their almond-milk lattes and threatens them with a pistol over complaints about the dishes (on closer inspection it is just a pistol-shaped lighter). In his room a portrait of Sasha Bely (the gangster hero of *Brigada*) hangs on the mirror, and he himself is grotesquely stuck in the 1990s, when his grandfather Grisha Chyorny ran things. In search of past greatness he goes to his grandmother’s Karelian village, where the only thing left of his grandfather’s legacy is a UAZ van, that very Chyorny’s Loaf (my applause for the project’s resourceful title). An attempt to get back his grandfather’s Merc turns into problems, and from there all that remains is to wait for a whole season)

My [*Garazhniki*](https://t.me/kino_voice/137) (“Garage People”) of 2025.

## 21 June 2025

The southern-sunny and pleasantly naive series *Vinodely* (“The Winemakers”) succinctly declares a lately favourite screenwriting device: the collision of the working class with the aestheticising bohemia.

This time a winery is to be divided. A trio of proletarians from Chelyabinsk come to Gelendzhik for the inheritance of a relative who vanished from the radar 20 years ago (and has now died altogether). The local owners (and partners of the deceased relative), played by Andrey Urgant and Elena Podkaminskaya, are in shock. Podkaminskaya, by the way, plays the winery’s manager, no less beautifully than many years ago she played the manager of a French restaurant in *Kukhnya* (“The Kitchen”, the hit sitcom).

Standard comic situations are supplemented by wine snobbery and a mismatch, let us say, of gastronomic cultures, compensated by a romantic match) I hope the story opens up like a good wine.

## 21 June 2025

It is great that many projects at this Pilot are devoted precisely to women and their problems.

*Feyk* (“Fake”) is a wonderful illustration of complete defencelessness on the internet, and following on from that, of maximum vulnerability before people who do not believe you and judge you. A real horror in which the monsters hide not under the bed but in the comments.

A kind-hearted biology teacher (Anastasia Krasovskaya, who for the second festival in a row gets heavy scenes of violence) runs into brutal online stalking: everything looks as if she is taking part in erotic correspondence under her own name. Her identity has literally been stolen. The young woman tries to find the culprit, and this gives the proceedings a swift pace and the right nerve. It is frightening and intriguing how this story might end ⬅️

---

## The Phoenician Scheme: Wes Anderson’s Signature Style, with Exceptions

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/finikiyskaya-skhema-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-06-08 (8 June 2025)
Work: “The Phoenician Scheme” is a 2025 film directed by Wes Anderson.
Tags: arthouse, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/finikiyskaya-skhema-2025/

In Wes Anderson’s [*The Phoenician Scheme*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/5460719/) the director’s signature style, which we are used to, shows through more subtly than ever, but with exceptions.

There are no screamingly contrasting or, conversely, carefully matched colours in the film’s palette, and the absurdist humour characteristic of Anderson’s characters looks unusually unobtrusive. On the other hand, the work as a whole seems to leave the impression of a summing-up. The key theme of fragile family ties, which flows from film to film with this director, is in place. But there is not even any certainty that the family is real, and blood kinship, it turns out, is not so important. The motif of the journey, masking the characters’ inner transformation, now works not towards a reset of characters but towards a wholesale rebirth. And the amount of violence on screen, unusual for Anderson, seems to bring the picture closer to a reality that is not at all distinguished by multicoloured aesthetics and symmetry.

In this I see two patterns:

**1️⃣** The protagonist, who runs his business against every rule of economics, constantly survives deadly situations yet stays alive. This is very reminiscent of the path of Wes Anderson himself, who works by his own rules of cinema and with every new work survives the inevitable “death of the author” (Roland Barthes’s concept, according to which the author of a work loses authorial power over its meaning immediately upon publication). Perhaps that is exactly why the protagonist of *The Phoenician Scheme* constantly rephrases other people’s wording in business papers, just as viewers rephrase the message the authors put into films or texts.

**2️⃣** By the end (I do not think this will be a big spoiler) the characters seem to arrive at the absence of symmetrical and colour correctness altogether: what we see in the frame resembles the reality around us as never before in Wes Anderson. This seems to underline once again the importance of inner content rather than the outer, however beautiful, shell: a very soothing thought.

Though perhaps this is my viewer’s interpretation, made thanks to the phenomenon of the “death of the author”.

---

## License to Love: A Second Chance Is, First of All, Something We Must Give Ourselves

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/muzhu-privet-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-06-04 (4 June 2025)
Work: “License to Love” is a 2025 film directed by Anton Maslov.
Tags: drama, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/muzhu-privet-2025/

The saying that “sometimes life gives a second chance” is incomplete, and the film [*License to Love*](https://okko.tv/movie/muzhu-privet) (*Muzhu privet*, “Say Hi to Your Husband”) illustrates this very well. A second chance is, first of all, something we must give ourselves.

The best Russian film of the 2025 Moscow International Film Festival envelops you from the first frame in warmth and hope for the best. Yulia Peresild’s heroine Katerina seems ashamed to be unhappy amid the joyful newlyweds at her job at the registry office: life around her is in full swing, and her day will come (probably) when her husband wakes from his coma (5 years on from the tragedy). In parallel, Katerina’s daughter plans to rush into marriage with a promising but unloved fiancé, and her son is even trying to court a classmate of strange (if not to say absent) moral principles. It seems they all need a second chance.

Despite the utterly tragic plot, what happens on screen does not knock you off balance or make you shed tears straight away. Apparently thanks to the lightness with which Katerina overcomes adversity: she will answer the nasty old neighbour’s remark with a joke, laughing; she will look at her son’s teenage crises with an understanding smile; at work she will wink affably at the citizens in the queue. In the course of analysing the heroine, I came to the thought that such calm is given to her by certainty: her husband is stuck in a coma, and, however terrible that is, she has got used to it. The hardest part for Katerina begins with the appearance of a real choice about what to do with her life, which had seemed settled forever.

In *License to Love* there is a fleeting but important mention of a Soviet classic, *Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears*. The two films really are related by a shared mood and the display of gentle female strength in the fight for one’s own happiness. The acting in *License to Love* is top-notch too: Peresild and Vdovichenkov exist beautifully as a pair. All together, an excellent reason to drop out of reality for a couple of hours and think about the price of happiness and the number of permissible chances on the way to it.

---

## Fisher. Eclipse: Greatness in Its Purest Form

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/fisher-zatmenie-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-05-29 (29 May 2025); updated: 2025-07-18
Work: “Fisher. Zatmenie” is a 2025 series directed by Alexander Tsoi.
Tags: series, mystery, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/fisher-zatmenie-serial/

## 29 May 2025

[*Fisher. Zatmenie*](https://youtu.be/_7QB_MyZ1gI?si=t-jsRQLNmEpuN-Up) («Фишер. Затмение», “Fisher. Eclipse”, the second season of the hit crime series) pleases from the first episode: Bokov is in excellent form, Yatsenko in his role wisecracks like a god, and Starshenbaum’s heroine looks right at home in this company.

The first frames, where Bokov interrogates Fisher in prison, are as if straight out of the world of [*Autsors*,](https://t.me/kino_voice/500) (“Outsource”) and evoke a pleasant feeling of recognition (if that is intentional, cool). The exposition works like clockwork: there is a tail end of the old case, an extended (despite the episode’s running time of only 40 minutes!) introduction of new characters, and a humanising of the characteristic traits of the old ones.

Bokov, who kept saying “Sho?” (“What?”) in season 1, for instance, has acquired a little dog, naturally named Sho. I hope the doggie does not come to harm in the course of catching the maniac.

## 20 June 2025

Even in festival conditions I could not miss the new episode of [*Fisher*](https://t.me/kino_voice/631): the midpoint of the season whets the appetite for the resolution to the maximum.

Besides the magnificently worked-out plot (to my taste, more powerful than in the first season!), the series’ speech specifics are gaining momentum too. This is the most linguistically distinctive series of recent times. Outdone, perhaps, only by [*El Ruso*,](https://t.me/kino_voice/233) where the actors talked like Old Believers)

But the virtuoso use of profanity by Yankovsky’s and Starshenbaum’s characters makes you want to literally write it down and quote it. Whichever way you look at it, such speech adds a hefty dose of sincerity and realism to everything that happens, which is extremely important for this crime story.

## 26 June 2025

[*Fisher*](https://t.me/kino_voice/659) is not only breaking records on the [Kinopoisk Pro Index](https://t.me/kinopoisk_Industry/5427) but also sharply (and, like Bokov, boldly) turning off the planned plot trajectory.

Having “slipped”, as Bokov put it (I never stop admiring him) at the very end of the fresh episode, the investigation is forced to change direction sharply? One would like to hope that the outcome of the investigation will not boil down to the formula “the butler did it” and that the criminal will not be as close at hand as he now seems.

And this episode has more of Yatsenko’s character and of Fisher himself. Andrey Maksimov is an amazing actor, of course: before watching the pilot episode of [*Normalny*](https://t.me/kino_voice/679) (“Normal”), where he plays a man on the autism spectrum, I could not imagine him in the role of even a remotely positive character (not a gangster and not a maniac). And now, what do you think? I cannot perceive him in *Fisher* as a maniac: he is such a sweet, kind guy. But all this, of course, is a joke; this is how I praise stunning transformations and a 180-degree change of type.

## 5 July 2025

Meanwhile the second season of [*Fisher*](https://t.me/kino_voice/706) has decided after all to be more cruel than the first and to take my favourite character away from me.

In the sixth episode everything twists mightily around one particular character whom I had come to love over the season, and it seems it will not end well. On the other hand, over the next two episodes I will definitely have time to enjoy how well the screenwriters have brought together a heap of storylines that at first seemed disparate. Sectarians, a nasty official, local gangsters: all this turns out to be intertwined and involved in the approaching resolution.

Also, incidentally, Andrey Maksimov seems to have been lucky this season to play every facet of Fisher, and it looks very, very convincing. And most importantly, the line with his interrogations does not seem at all extraneous or foreign to what is going on in Kurortny; on the contrary, it seems to let us look retrospectively at the search for the new maniac and build our own guesses based on their (the maniacs’) logic.

## 17 July 2025

In my opinion, the finale of the series [*Fisher. Zatmenie*](https://t.me/kino_voice/619) is greatness in its purest form. Besides all manner of praise for the work itself, I will follow with great interest the future roles of Nikita Khudyakov, who played Vanya Zlobin, because in this story he showed himself to be a very powerful artist. Watching him was a real pleasure.

The resolution looks quick, rhythmic and without unnecessary preludes, but with an elegant sprinkling of devilry ➡️ For me this is the perfect outcome: I do not like detective stories where the intrigue drags on and on, forcing us to watch the investigators’ train of thought for an indecently long time; personally I find it easy to drop such viewing. To the last I wished that this would not happen with *Fisher*, and my wishes came true. I had [guesses,](https://t.me/kino_voice/725) but in reality everything is done more cunningly, literally as unpredictable as fate itself, and that, it seems, is the height of craftsmanship. I liked the detail of Zlobin’s transfer “from somewhere up north”: *Fisher* has more in common with *Autsors* than it seems.

Separately, I cannot help admiring the character posters: bamboo, a mourning ribbon, bees; a good set of details both for those who have not yet watched and for those who already know everything.

Naturally, my book of quotations did not go without additions from Bokov’s lexicon. The line about how “I don’t need to say it twice” I will remember for a long time. May this feature continue in the future, if *Fisher* becomes an anthology with an immortal Bokov from season to season.

## 18 July 2025

The more I think about the [resolution](https://t.me/kino_voice/762) of the second *Fisher*, the more additional meanings I find.

First, I read an [interview](https://seance.ru/articles/fisher-zatmenie) with the screenwriters, Sergei Kalvarsky and Natalya Kapustina. It turns out we owe the atmosphere of the series to *Assa*. ~~Those who know me are aware:~~ It is my most beloved film, but not once while watching did I catch myself making the association, and now it has hiiit me. That is what explains this convincing counterpoint that makes you suspect rot even in the sweetest character.

On the other hand, I have plenty of cultural associations regarding Zlobin, who split into twins, and that is my second point. In the few seconds they were shown on screen together, I managed to recall both Cronenberg and Balabanov. The former because of the film *Dead Ringers*, about twins who villainously swapped places at work and in life (literally, even with women). And from Balabanov, the screenplay *My Brother Died*, with its telling title and a truly Balabanovian plot. And most importantly, a resolution that quite mirrors that of *Fisher*.

---

## Other People’s Money: Dashing Crypto Crime with Two Maxim Matveevs

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/chuzhie-dengi-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-05-28 (28 May 2025); updated: 2025-06-07
Work: “Other People's Money” is a 2025 series directed by Igor Tverdokhlebov.
Tags: series, crime, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/chuzhie-dengi-serial/

## 28 May 2025

A little later, I started [*Other People’s Money*](https://youtu.be/4JuxiHkwp64?si=wXLxHfRx4WL8dGcD) (*Chuzhie dengi*), a dashing piece of crypto crime with two Maxim Matveevs (hello to *Amur*, *Mickey 17*, *Vasily* and other [films with twins).](https://t.me/kino_voice/294)

The first thing that impresses pleasantly is the camerawork. The camera flies, zooms in on the characters’ faces and on objects, dollies in and out to the rhythm of the showdowns between characters, and even films them from a hidden-camera angle. Such visual variety literally rivets the gaze: it has been a long time since I was drawn into a series precisely by the cinematography. This is a rare phenomenon among contemporary projects and therefore a winning decision.

Watching Matveev in two guises is also extremely interesting; it is especially pleasing that the long-playing one turned out to be not the self-assured personality but the modest version of the hero, capable of character transformation. Despite a plot that is absolutely fantastical in current realities, the very idea of making something about good old swindlers operating with the latest technology and bitcoin is really rather appealing. In short, every factor speaks for continuing to watch.

## 7 June 2025

It is great that [*Other People’s Money*](https://t.me/kino_voice/617) not only kept its camerawork trick right up to the finale but did not let us down in the script either.

Events unfolded in such a way that the finale brings a great deal of moral satisfaction. Behind the numerous cunning schemes with crypto and cash-outs, viewers had to choose their favourite ~~Twix bar~~ version of Maxim Matveev, and the authors did the same for an effective resolution. An understandable attitude of hatred mixed with pity arose towards Svin (“Pig”), and, though Gosha Kutsenko’s character is utterly distinctive, you do not sympathise with him that much. Alina (Stasya Miloslavskaya), of course, is not without questions, but did nothing radically bad (and, accordingly, did not deserve it).

It is as if the series, which resembles science fiction more than reality, ended fantastically fairly. And that, of course, is a pleasant rarity for the empathetic viewer.

## Den radio: A Live Look at What We Are Used to Seeing as a Film

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/den-radio-teatr/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-05-26 (26 May 2025)
Work: “Den radio” is a 2001 stage production directed by Sergey Petreykov.
Tags: theatre, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/den-radio-teatr/

Another theatrical off-topic post. This time about a production that I had rewatched as a film some 8 times.

It is *Den radio* («День радио», “Radio Day”), a show that Kvartet I (the Moscow comedy troupe) have been performing for 25 years now and that has existed as a [film](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/402979/) since 2008. The production is good precisely as a live look at what we are used to seeing in the fixed format of film. On stage the intonations are livelier and the characters more three-dimensional; I was especially impressed by Nonna Grishaeva, who seems not to have changed at all over these 25 years) By the way, every signature “*maladtsy!*” (“well done!”; put a ❤️ if you read it in that very intonation)) from Leonid Barats’s character is met with applause by the audience, and it is great to see that with your own eyes. But make sure you do not know all the jokes from the film literally by heart before you go, otherwise the wow effect is somewhat dulled

Why go to the theatre, you will ask, when there is both the film and a [television version of the play?](https://hd.kinopoisk.ru/film/45a12e6a541b9258be4d0bbd8613dae9) One nuance: in neither of these versions will you see the magnificent Pavel Maykov performing songs as the frontmen of several bands. Every musical number is an explosion of energy, comedy and artistry from Maykov and the band Bobry. It was this artist’s participation in the production that was the deciding factor for me: Maykov does not have many theatre roles, and watching him perform is always a great pleasure.
