## Outsource: The Finale, and I Have Not Enjoyed Series This Much in a Long Time

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/autsors-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-02-13 (13 February 2025); updated: 2025-03-27
Work: “Outsource” is a 2025 series directed by Dushan Gligorov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, thriller, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/autsors-serial/

## 13 February 2025

It is pleasing that practically at the start of the series year such a cool story as [*Outsource*](https://youtu.be/TznVzdJyuK8?si=3gxs6xEcgoxdVdfQ) (*Autsors*) comes out: a series with Ivan Yankovsky as Kostya, an enterprising prison warder who in the mid-1990s decides to sell victims’ relatives the chance to execute the killer with their own hands. This plot spine is surrounded by spine-chillingly terrible stories of the hero’s colleagues and other inhabitants of the town, which makes the series’ structure rich! In this respect I like this non-main poster of the series: Kostya is clearly going to stir up some volcano of consequences.

Judging by the first episodes, Yankovsky’s character serves as an infernal otherworldly force that gradually brings out in the locals hidden traits they had not even suspected, asking awkward but very simple questions and offering not the most moral but direct solutions. You can enjoy this character largely as an extension and continuation of Yankovsky’s work as Raskolnikov, only a Raskolnikov who feels he has the *right* and gives no thought to repentance.

I hope *Outsource* will set the quality bar for other projects this year too, because so far it is the strongest thing of 2025.

## 10 March 2025

How brilliantly details work in [*Outsource*](https://youtu.be/TznVzdJyuK8?si=3gxs6xEcgoxdVdfQ)!

Colleagues [noted the prosecutor’s house-warming scene](https://t.me/KingOfYantar/4469), but I was struck by the transformation of Natasha’s mother, played by Karina Razumovskaya. All the time she was giving her daughter destructive advice from the position of “the main thing is to hang on to a good man”, behaving not as a mother but as an auntie personifying public opinion, she wore her hat without taking it off: a symbol of closedness, insincerity, distance from her daughter’s feelings.

But when the irreparable happened in episode 5 (Natasha, after an abortion done on her mother’s advice, ended up in intensive care and will never be able to have children), Natasha’s mother at last took off her protective armour of coldness and demandingness towards her daughter. For the first time in the series (this did not happen even at the wedding!) she appeared before her daughter without the hat and without the swagger, even though it happened unforgivably late. A small thing, but the effect on the viewer is colossal.

## 13 March 2025

At some point [*Outsource*](https://t.me/kino_voice/449) began turning into *House of the Dragon* in the number of its intrigues, and my soul demanded an episode-by-episode breakdown.

**1️⃣** I still have doubts: does Ivan Yankovsky’s character exist at all? He is some kind of incorporeal shadow that manages to be here, there and everywhere, persuading anyone he meets with the efficiency of a hypnotist. I would not be surprised if in the end he vanished, like Tyler Durden, leaving the jailers with a pile of insoluble problems. Especially after the line “And who could do anything to me anyway?”…

**2️⃣** The poster with the women turned out to be very apt: judging by episode 6, the ball is passing to their side, and now interesting twists are to be expected precisely from the female half of the characters. Natasha’s mother has put her hat back on, though authority has, on the contrary, grown only in Natasha herself, which makes her all the more interesting to watch. In general, all the female characters here are so top-notch that, despite minimal screen time, I am ready to praise them separately, beyond my general admiration for the cast.

**3️⃣**With every week the episodes fly by faster and faster; given the number of untangled plot threads, in the remaining two episodes an ultimate resolution awaits us with answers to all the questions at once (and answers that are surprisingly simple, as always with Yankovsky’s character). Literally on the principle of “seven troubles, one answer”.

## 21 March 2025

The seventh episode of [*Outsource*](https://t.me/kino_voice/461) seems to have been squeezed too much (in both running time and events), and on the whole looks like a quiet break for both sides of the conflict to prepare their strategy. Perhaps such swiftness is needed for the inevitable approach to the terrible (no doubt it will be exactly that) resolution, but as a viewer I would of course like this story to continue endlessly.

**1️⃣** The women, as I thought, have taken the situation into their own hands. And, surprisingly, the most harm turned out to come from the mothers, Natasha’s and Roma’s. The first brought into the house a cutthroat worse than our main characters: the prison governor. As a result he overheard Natasha’s revelations about the money, which she had for some reason (Lord, after all her mother’s abuse and the story with the abortion?!) actually brought there. And the second was so impressed by Volkov’s warnings about “the old prostitute” that she stashed her son’s money away for good, nobody knows where (I suspect that in her simplicity she might have handed it to that same Kostya Volkov “for safekeeping”).

**2️⃣** Kostya Volkov’s daughter, it seems, does have a soul after all. If Ivan Yankovsky’s character sniffs out that his daughter is now lying to him too (and he has already figured everything out from the suitcase and the dirty boots), it will be interesting to see what fate befalls her.

**3️⃣** Speaking of Volkov. There was so little of him in this episode that I am more and more convinced he never existed at all. Nevertheless, in favour of his existence is the prison governor’s order to deal with Volkov. I think that will be the main attraction of the final episode: who ends up dealing with whom.

**4️⃣** The prosecutor’s wife underwent a very interesting character transformation in this episode. I always had a special kind of sympathy for her, and now, for the brilliant self-organisation of the prison staff’s wives, I respect her even more. A pity only that, it seems, it will lead to roughly nothing.

## 27 March 2025

*Outsource* is over. I have not enjoyed series this much in a long time (since *Give a Show!*); to put it briefly, it is simply something else (I am as pleased as Mila Ershova in this still). And at more length, here are a few thoughts:

- I kept hoping that Volkov did not exist, but the creators did something cooler and made him immortal! I do not remember when I was as glad for any film character as when Volkov turned out to be alive. (All right, it is simpler: either the convict doctor gave the wrong recipe for the cocktail, which is why he laughed so hard at the end of the episode, or the prison doctor got it mixed up, or the potion simply worked on the gravely ill, and Yankovsky’s healthy character survived it).

- By the way, I am also glad that Volkov did not carry out the final shooting with his own hands: that would have gone against his character. And now it is also clear what happened at Volkov’s previous job and why he was transferred: obviously his former colleagues also failed his uncomplicated test of their mettle.

- Hooray, they showed, if only for a few seconds, the collapse of our friends’ business because of the abolition of the death penalty. On the one hand, as the memes say, it is gratifying: the death penalty went away together with the people who made it an instrument of profit. On the other hand, what else, if we hypothetically continued the series, could prison warders sell to the powerful after the abolition of the death penalty? Demand creates supply, as we know, so inventors like Volkov will probably never die out.

- The women, as usual, are on fire. In this episode specifically the heroines of Mila Ershova (her heroine’s walk with the Raffaellos has already become a meme) and Darya Kotreleva (a spectacular escape from everyone gave her heroine perhaps the happiest resolution). It is very good that all the female characters, though they were supporting ones, received in the finale some clear full stop or trajectory of future development; supporting heroines do not always get that attention.

- It is good that the story has partly come full circle: now Kostya Volkov will go off to a new job at another penal colony and stir things up there. This is even better than a standard finale: now a second season of this story is definitely not needed (unless in anthology format).

And what do you think of the finale?

---

## Home: Yulia Peresild in the Lead and Practically Only Role

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/on-i-ona-2025/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-02-12 (12 February 2025)
Work: “Home” is a 2024 film directed by Evgeny Korchagin.
Tags: Russian cinema, science fiction, thriller
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/on-i-ona-2025/

In cinemas from tomorrow: [*Home*](https://youtu.be/lQVg1ro2eyk?si=Y4lKk62IULGr9HNV) (*ON i ona*, “ON and Her”), with Yulia Peresild in the lead and practically only role. The thing is, the second main character is a disembodied artificial intelligence built into the house that the heroine, Ksenia, has rented for a holiday somewhere by the sea. Ksenia herself has the most direct connection with AI: she developed an entire smart voice assistant for decision-making, but her ungrateful employers, alas, did not appreciate it and sent Ksenia (as an unwanted employee) off on this very holiday. But a happy, harmonious holiday in a super-smart house turned into something between a horror film, a psychological thriller and a science-fiction drama.

This film is hard to describe without spoilers, so I will break it down into pluses and minuses:

👆 The film has an extremely apt theme. In a world where AI can generate the faces and voices of people who do not exist, and where for many some ChatGPT or other serves as an authoritative adviser, it is always useful to reflect on the flip side of technological blessings and on the importance of the human being.

👆 The metaphorical, chamber nature of the statement: thanks to the extreme conventionality of what happens, the inner conflict of Peresild’s heroine comes to the fore and remains truly central throughout the story.

👆 Yulia Peresild’s performance. Spending 90% of the time on screen alone without a partner and staying convincing is a great skill, and the plots of contemporary cinema do not offer many opportunities for it.

👆 The finale, which remained a mystery to me in the good sense of the word. Usually I do not like resolutions that leave me not understanding why the hero decided as they did. But here, watching the heroine’s (rather misanthropic) decision, I felt a pleasant curiosity.

👇 The extreme conventionality of everything that happens is the very plus that turns into the main minus. It seems that for the absolute majority of viewers the technically perfect world, saturated with the most modern gadgets, in which the heroine lives may seem a parallel universe that arouses no sympathy whatsoever.

---

## The Enchanted Tinderbox: As Fresh as Can Be Against the Stream of Fairy-Tale Films

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ognivo-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-01-27 (27 January 2025)
Work: “The Enchanted Tinderbox” is a 2024 film directed by Alexander Voitinsky.
Tags: Russian cinema, fairy tales
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ognivo-2024/

January weekends are given to us to catch up on everything we did not get to over the holidays, and yesterday my choice fell on [*The Enchanted Tinderbox*](https://youtu.be/TtUQSMUcVws?si=N_SikwDt3BFLJYFO) (*Ognivo*)

This picture looks as fresh as can be against the rest of the stream of fairy-tale films. First, it is important to note that of Andersen’s original text only the tinderbox itself remains, as a magic object in the hero’s hands: there are no dogs with enormous eyes, no witch, no real soldier. Instead there is a usurper, a coup d’état, conspirators, a road buddy movie, time travel and a rascal who pretends to be a soldier to get out of prison (in short, phenomena closer to us than the pure magic of the original text).

Second, the lead is the wonderful, vivid, charismatic Roman Evdokimov. While watching I realised that this is exactly the kind of fairy-tale hero we are missing: a kind character who keeps messing up, gives in to temptations and his own selfish interests; you cannot expect anything of him, which makes him all the more interesting to watch right to the end. Roman himself talks about this in an [interview with colleagues at Kinopoisk](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4010173/); I recommend it as a great companion to the film!

Third, there is no love story here at all! Usually our hero performs heroic deeds only on the way to the princess he wants to marry. In *The Enchanted Tinderbox* kindness comes from humanity and compassion, not romantic interest. I have nothing against heroes motivated by feelings, but how pleasant it is to see the plot develop differently)

These factors add up to an inventive plot in which every twist invigorates with its unpredictability, and give a unique type of fairy-tale hero who goes not by the logic of the “positive character” (like Emelya or the Troubadour from recent adaptations) but against it, as a comic version of “that power which eternally wills evil and eternally works good” (Mephistopheles’s words in *Faust*). For this, *The Enchanted Tinderbox* is so far my favourite contemporary fairy-tale adaptation.

---

## Robert Eggers’s Nosferatu: The Most Well-Made and Successful Remake

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/nosferatu-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-01-24 (24 January 2025)
Work: “Nosferatu” is a 2024 film directed by Robert Eggers.
Tags: horror, remake
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/nosferatu-2024/

Robert Eggers’s [*Nosferatu*](https://youtu.be/9H7bQkAfHyo?si=C2rcOjhc4mKoikCM) seems to be the most well-made and successful remake I have seen. I enjoyed every minute of the film, and here is why:

- The remake is exactly twice as long as the original, but it shows in more detail the cause-and-effect links, the characters’ motivations and other half-tones barely perceptible in the source film, and my viewing experience benefited from this. Sometimes articulating certain facts in dialogue is not chewing over the obvious but widening the context

 - Eggers’s film popularises the story of Nosferatu, which until now mostly interested a limited circle of insiders. Now the reminder that light conquers darkness is in plain view for everyone again.

- Nicholas Hoult is the perfect Hutter. I have heard opinions that he is bland in this film, but that is precisely the perfection: his character is the real victim of this Nosferatu story, deprived of the right to decide his own fate in roughly the first scene, so being “bland” is what the logic of the character requires.

- Lily-Rose Depp is an extremely strong actress in terms of physical performance. It is precisely the bodily aspects of her acting that gave this whole mystical story a kind of anchoring in physical reality, where the evil force is anything but a ghost.

- Nosferatu’s new look (and peculiar speech) is an excellent find. The 1922 Nosferatu evoked only fear. In his new guise the vampire evokes a range of mixed emotions and reminds us that nothing human is alien to evil. But let us not forget that this does not stop it from being evil.

---

## Squid Game: Types Instead of Names, and an Imperfect End to the Franchise

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/igra-v-kalmara-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-01-18 (18 January 2025); updated: 2025-06-29
Work: “Squid Game” is a 2021 series directed by Hwang Dong-hyuk.
Tags: series, thriller, Korean cinema, analysis
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/igra-v-kalmara-serial/

## 18 January 2025

The first season of *Squid Game* was largely an attraction: both at the plot level, where deadly games among the poor entertained the elite, and at the level of the viewer’s perception: the series’ vivid symbol-memes lodged in the memory for a long time (while its twisty finale, in my case at least, was practically forgotten)

The second season is not rich in such entertainments, so it plays differently. We are introduced into the action very unhurriedly, without being reminded, meanwhile, of some important details forgotten over several years. It is not vitally necessary, but personally I would have preferred not just to assume in general terms that Seong Gi-hun intends to stop the games, but to recall in detail (since the games themselves have been pushed back all the way to the third episode) how things ended there.

And, most importantly, the second season has lost the lightness of a reality show while increasing its moral analysis of what is happening. Now we do not simply watch from the outside a hero who has got into a fix, but are given his optics from the start: after all, we too have already “played these games” when we watched the first season. Hence an even greater temptation to transfer the events of the series onto our own realities and even fewer opportunities for escapism while watching. And the finale, cut off essentially for the formal division of seasons, embarrasses rather than intrigues. In short, it is all rather specific and an acquired taste, and how many have acquired it will be shown this year by the figures for the third season (which will no longer have the advance credit of such gigantic expectations).

## 29 June 2025

Ask yourself how many characters from any season of [*Squid Game*](https://t.me/kino_voice/381) you remember by name? Well, Seong Gi-hun. Well, the Front Man. If you remember anyone else, you are surely a member of the series’ fan club.

Most likely you do not, and yet everything is clear without the names and the viewing goes on. This is the manifestation of an interesting industry case.

The trick is that the casting of the actors for the roles in *Squid Game* is special. We do not get to know each of them in detail; we have neither the time nor the opportunity to remember this crowd by name, or even by number (which in itself is a very winning device for an international project, but again, apart from 456, whose number do we remember by heart?) The secret is this: each of the actors is a very clear-cut type turned up to the maximum, recognisable without a name from episode to episode.

It is precisely this typification that is one of the keys to the project being talked about for 4 years. We remember the characters as “that vile junkie rapper”, “the kind old lady”, “the mummy’s-boy weakling” or “the greedy old man”, and that is enough for us to understand one another and to remember the events of the previous season far better. The credit for this effect goes to the actors’ types and the work on how they are expressed. It is great that genuine know-how can be found in such a mass-market product.

## 29 June 2025

On the whole, the third season of [*Squid Game*](https://t.me/kino_voice/710) is a decent, if not perfect, conclusion to the main part of the franchise (not counting the future American *Game*, of course).

The final opposition of 8 adult men and a baby girl seems a great device, hinting to the viewer at whom, in the authors’ opinion, the future belongs to. What bothers me in this whole nobly built construction is that neither the organisers of the games (the same kind of adult men) nor the main consumers of the games, the so-called “VIPs”, have gone anywhere. And the two girls (222’s daughter and Seong Gi-hun’s daughter), having come into such money, may sooner or later become “VIPs” themselves. In a word, some kind of deceptive catharsis took place.

But that does not bother me as much as the secondary storyline with the collective search for the island. I have probably not felt like this since reading *The Master and Margarita* at school, when from one chapter of Woland’s Moscow escapades to the next you suffer through the text about Yeshua. Only in Bulgakov all this is justified, significant and equally valuable (and, growing a little beyond a schoolchild’s optics, you understand that). Whereas here this storyline appeared, completely unproductive in terms of any influence on the resolution. It is made almost solely to turn one game that fits perfectly into one season into two seasons, through a side plot. I sincerely did not appreciate such a doubling of the plot and hope that in future seasons (they are inevitable) they will manage to focus on exploring human nature in extreme circumstances.

## A Real Pain: An Unassuming but Insanely Talented Film

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/nastoyaschaya-bol-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-01-10 (10 January 2025)
Work: “A Real Pain” is a 2024 film directed by Jesse Eisenberg.
Tags: drama, tragicomedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/nastoyaschaya-bol-2024/

I do not know how your first working day went, but I, whatever that may mean, ended mine by watching Jesse Eisenberg’s *A Real Pain* with Kieran Culkin.

Joking, actually I had been waiting for the film [since the trailer](https://t.me/kino_voice/216). I am always interested in what Eisenberg does, and after the Golden Globes I sped up my viewing: I had to understand what Culkin had done to beat our own Yura Borisov)

In the end I am impressed. I do not remember when I last saw anything as well put together, harmonious and compact as *A Real Pain*. Despite its modest running time of an hour and a half, the film fits in reflections on the subtlety and complexity of family ties, attempts to understand the phenomenon of collective grief/guilt, and the search for a cultural identity from which the heroes were thrown out before they were even born. That sounds rather tragic, but the film is also rich in life-affirming irony, which lets you examine these serious themes without excessive dramatisation.

Culkin and Eisenberg are a treasure in their own right. From the first minute you believe they are brothers, but radically opposite ones. At the same time the declared contrast is not a template but credible, deep and realistic. You believe such people can exist, can be brothers and can turn up somewhere among us. Culkin’s award is completely deserved, and it is gratifying that he got it. The only question is that his role is really a lead rather than a supporting one, but that is another problem.

And the costumes subtly underline the brothers’ evolution during their journey  In the first half of the film Eisenberg’s character prefers a restrained blue, and Culkin’s a rich burgundy. Further on, the difference in their characters is declared: Eisenberg wears an orderly check in the same shade (the character has a steady job, is married and is raising a child), while Culkin wears blurred, chaotic blotches of random shape (he, without spoilers, also leads a rather chaotic life). And in the last minutes of the film the heroes seem to have accepted each other, grown close again and swapped a little of their best qualities, so that Eisenberg is in the rich burgundy and Culkin in the restrained blue. It does not catch the eye, which makes it especially gratifying to discover, like the whole film: unassuming, but insanely talented.

## One Day in Istanbul: A Sweet Picture, but Not a Very Ambitious One

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/odin-den-v-stambule-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-01-05 (5 January 2025)
Work: “One Day in Istanbul” is a 2024 film directed by Avet Oganesyan.
Tags: Russian cinema, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/odin-den-v-stambule-2024/

These New Year holidays I did not rewatch any of the classic Kvartet I (the Moscow comedy troupe), but I did get through their new film [*One Day in Istanbul*.](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/5379163/) (*Odin den v Stambule*) A writer, a producer, an official and a doctor come to visit a billionaire friend of theirs in Turkey (no, this is not the start of a joke). It turns out the latter has died, so the meeting of friends on the booked yacht will now be a somewhat unusual one.
The picture is sweet but not very ambitious, so I will break it down into pluses and minuses:

👆The traditional Kvartet I humour: black, absurd and simple all at once. The performers are still on top form, and the jokes in their signature style give a pleasant feeling of recognition

👆I will single out separately the funny (and not very kind) jokes about Alexander Tsypkin

👆The chamber quality of the action and the richness of the visuals. In our winter greyness it is always pleasant to spend time with a film full of shots of sun, sea and resort bliss.

👆An unexpected finale that refreshes your impression of the film

👇New male characters and (for reasons of the new ethics) female ones attached to the main foursome not quite to the point. It is not quite clear who they are or what their presence adds to the story and the humour

👇 A detachment from a reality in which everything can be googled in a second. For example, one of the comic situations is built on the heroine not knowing her favourite writer by sight (although she adores him so much that she carries his paper book around with her, so why not google what your favourite writer looks like?)

## Zigzag of Success: Ryazanov’s Small and Terribly Well-Made New Year Picture

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/zigzag-udachi-1968/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2025-01-04 (4 January 2025)
Work: “Zigzag of Success” is a 1968 film directed by Eldar Ryazanov.
Tags: Soviet cinema, comedy, New Year
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/zigzag-udachi-1968/

By the way, on the subject of advertising as a marker of an era. In the original *The Diamond Arm*, released in April 1969, Gaidai unobtrusively inserted a promo for another 1968 comedy, less well known today as a traditional Soviet New Year film but no less wonderful. I took a screenshot of the advertising poster that briefly becomes visible when the smugglers’ car drives away from the pier at minute 23)

[*Zigzag of Success*](https://youtu.be/rjeWVIBUbuE?si=wFq9nsKcptyLawNq) (*Zigzag udachi*) is a small and terribly well-made New Year picture by Eldar Ryazanov, which really did come out just before New Year in 1968. A young photographer (Evgeny Leonov, in the role of a little man with his vices) dreams of a camera of his own and, taking a chance with money from his photo studio colleagues’ common fund, buys a lottery ticket. What follows is an utterly comic struggle between the personal and the public within one particular workplace: imagine a mix of *Garazh* (“The Garage”, Ryazanov’s satire), the series *The Office* and the pre-New Year bustle in which everyone is trying to be happy, and you get roughly this film.

I watched it precisely thanks to the poster inside *The Diamond Arm* and enjoyed it enormously! Every type in the photo studio collective looks as convincing as can be, the characters’ problems are utterly familiar (some want to get married, some to get a flat), and the humour really is inventive, the kind we are used to from the best examples of Soviet cinema. In short, if you want to watch something charmingly New Year-ish from the Soviet era but not the usual mainstream fare, take a look at *Zigzag of Success*: Gaidai would not steer you wrong.

---

## First Issue: The New Glossy Magazines Are Telegram Channels

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/pervyy-nomer-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-12-05 (5 December 2024); updated: 2025-01-06
Work: “First Issue” is a 2024 series directed by Klim Kozinsky.
Tags: series, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/pervyy-nomer-serial/

## 5 December 2024

A checklist for watching the series [*First Issue*:](https://youtu.be/ufgnauYcWiQ?si=BWPAGlTg2Q4gR_ZS) (*Pervy nomer*)

- Make sure it has been long enough since you watched the series *The Thaw*, because here Evgeny Tsyganov got exactly the same role (only instead of the cameraman Khrustalyov it is the writer Inozemtsev), and you may get bored

- Make sure it has been long enough since you watched the series *Besprintsipnye* (“The Unprincipled”), because the chronotope of Moscow for the rich is the same here, and you may get bored

- Make sure you have no experience of working in contemporary Russian media, otherwise you may not believe the details of newsroom life on screen, where half the editorial staff walk out in a single day on principle (and presumably pay their living costs with those principles too)

- Make sure you are not watching the series *Give a Show!* in parallel, because there will be an inevitable urge to compare two stories about the backstage of the media

- But at the same time! Leave yourself time to watch the credits (they are gorgeous here) and pay attention to the supporting characters: there are wonderful characters from Denis Vlasenko, Lukerya Ilyashenko, Pavel Derevyanko and Egor Koreshkov

## 6 January 2025

I have finished watching the series [*First Issue*](https://youtu.be/ufgnauYcWiQ?si=xGj0P38j9EWSlEaa) and am amazed at the irony that befell it. The plot is supposedly devoted to glossy magazines: there is a magazine that has to be ~~resurrected~~ relaunched, editors and publishers, media, God forgive me, holdings, and potent newsroom ratting…

But what it actually turned out to be about is that the new glossy magazines are Telegram channels, influencers and their blogs and blog-lets of various calibres. Everything alive, active and intrigue-creating in the series happened on the internet: the magazine’s fate was made up of what was leaked, which interviews were taken, which posts were written and which stories were posted. And the magazine seemed to be just a decoration on the table at which everyone sat down to discuss completely different things.

If this effect was intended on purpose, that is cool!

P.S.: Of all the characters, my love in this series is Lukerya Ilyashenko’s heroine. What a dark, hypnotic, wicked charisma she has, how good she is in the roles of traitresses, schemers and witches. She first charmed me in the series *Happy End* and once again in *First Issue*. I waited for her appearances on screen more than for anything else.

## The Thaw: Not Everyone Was a Protagonist, but Everyone Lived Their Own “Thaw”

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ottepel-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-11-29 (29 November 2024); updated: 2024-12-14
Work: “The Thaw” is a 2013 series directed by Valery Todorovsky.
Tags: series, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ottepel-serial/

## 29 November 2024

Series have had to change, after all, in moving from television to streaming)

I was watching *The Thaw* (*Ottepel*), a classic of our series full of dreamy nostalgia, by Valery Todorovsky (by the way, put a 👀 if you want a more detailed opinion of the series).

And then I come across a shot with a whole newspaper column devoted to one of the main characters. Naturally I hit pause, I want to read it all! But no such luck: it quickly turns out that the text here is one paragraph, copied and pasted as many times as needed to fill the space.

Of course, the series was shown on television back then, and it never occurred to anyone that somebody would pause it and start studying the whole text. And yet it seems that in contemporary series of a similar level you will no longer find such small harmless bloopers (they will all be big and hurtful ones, yes; just give us a freeze-frame to examine)

## 14 December 2024

Valery Todorovsky’s *The Thaw*, about filmmakers of the 1960s, had long been on my watch list, but the final push came after watching [*Namedni* 1961)](https://youtu.be/BB7A6w7f1uY?si=1xpb-a1pS1gxwamQ) (Leonid Parfenov’s documentary chronicle of Soviet life). I wanted to prolong my immersion in the era. And [here](https://t.me/kino_voice/313) plenty of 👀 reactions came in, so I owe you a detailed review of the series!

To convey how thoroughly, vividly and in detail this story immerses you in a world of its own in every aspect, I will give one example that I liked (and, most importantly, one without spoilers). When watching/rewatching, pay attention to the nameless passer-by who witnesses the naked performance of the girl offended by Evgeny Tsyganov’s character at the very beginning of the first episode. After this moment a whole era will pass in the series, but you will remember this passer-by: Egor Koreshkov’s character looks at the seated girl with such surprise, with a viewer’s curiosity. He is a true wordless witness of the era, since we never even learn his name. But he will make a second appearance, in the very final scene, and it will be emphasised specially so that we notice.

In parallel with the characters we followed, this lad will also live his life, which stays off screen, and will also say goodbye to the Thaw in his own way (I will not retell the final scene). This is us, the viewers, who entered the story because it began vividly and left it a little different, having absorbed everything we saw from the outside. And feeling through the screen such depth in working with an era, in which not everyone was a protagonist but everyone lived their own “thaw”, is a very valuable emotional experience.

## Children of Change: Three Paths, Raves, Vodka and IT, Adjusted for 1995

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/deti-peremen-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-11-21 (21 November 2024); updated: 2026-01-30
Work: “Children of Change” is a 2024 series directed by Sergey Taramaev, Lyubov Lvova.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, 1990s
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/deti-peremen-serial/

## 21 November 2024

“Russia”, as the [song](https://music.yandex.ru/album/17719679) went, “has three paths: raves, vodka and IT”. That (adjusted for 1995) is what the series [*Children of Change*](https://youtu.be/7RAPJDHKWik?si=xbQKsxySIgZ68O-Y) (*Deti peremen*), which launched today with two episodes, is about.

What is fresh in the exposition: an unusual family of a mother and three sons by different fathers (our “three paths”, a great opening). What is familiar: the ubiquitous 1990s. Perhaps such a prominent series should have been released at some distance from *Daring* (*Likhie*), which also lays claim to being a family saga in the middle of hard times, but let us watch the competition!

I think the series will not get lost, because at the start we have:

- Charismatic and distinctive representatives of opposite worlds. Viktoria Isakova as Flora, the mother of three lads, passionate about life no matter what. And Timofey Tribuntsev as Zhigalin, the unhinged, infernal leader of an organised crime group who does evil on an unearthly scale

- Contrasting types of young people: a philosophising gangster (Slava Kopeikin, tormented by Hamletian questions), an anarchic artist (Makar Khlebnikov, so far my favourite of all the sons; he draws film posters, mind you) and the youngest son, who has not yet shown himself in any particular way (perhaps, in this context, thank God; he will stay in one piece longer), Khetag Khinchagov

- The supporting cast: the wonderful Alexander Yatsenko, Artyom Bystrov and Lev Zulkarnaev (somewhere in the series, they say, he will recite poems of his own composition!)

- An interesting dramatic engine in the mother’s ignorance of what her eldest son does. She will, of course, have to find out that he is a gangster, but what happens then is the intrigue. That is what we keep watching for.

## 30 January 2026

[*Children of Change 2*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1038) started straight off at a gallop

The first episode obviously implies a certain number of events left off screen; there is room here for flashbacks, which I hope we will see over the season. That would be a harmonious link between the “before” and “after” of all the characters, for whose understanding some context is needed, literally from Flora (Viktoria Isakova in heroin chic) to Genrikh (the endlessly many-faced Sergei Gilev).

What is striking, though, is how the new season immediately divides the characters into those who managed to reassemble themselves and survive in hard times, and those who stayed themselves and therefore did not make it into the future. Perhaps this will become the key theme of the season: to give up a part of yourself and live on, or to stay true to yourself but perish.

## Chef: Principled Kai, Who Has an Ember Instead of a Heart

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/shef-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-11-19 (19 November 2024); updated: 2024-11-26
Work: “Chef” is a 2024 series directed by Mikhail Raskhodnikov, Evgeny Puzyrevsky.
Tags: series, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/shef-serial/

## 19 November 2024

Well, I really did watch 6 episodes of [*Chef*](https://t.me/kino_voice/297) (*Shef*) in a row (yes, the cunning [@fridaytv](https://t.me/fridaytv), the Pyatnitsa channel, held back the 7th and 8th all the way until Sunday; they did promise to bring it to the boil!) And it really was good.

Our initial expectations were justified thanks to the story of principled Kai (who, contrary to his name, has not a splinter of ice instead of a heart, as in *The Snow Queen*, but an ember). Off the top of your head you cannot name other contemporary heroes who could utter the words *“I’m not going anywhere, because this is my home, and anyway, why should I?”* (episode 2). Denis Prytkov delivered his second stunning role of the year (the first was [*Ona takaya klassnaya*](https://t.me/kino_voice/182), “She’s So Cool”), and it is simply a celebration.

As the story developed, the focus spread to other characters, or rather heroines: the women working in the prison colony’s kitchen. There is nothing complicated in this part; the mechanism of a team getting used to a new manager (our Kai) is a traditional part of any film about the path to a dream, overcoming everything on the way to the goal and success. But the main advantage of this part lies in its proportion and transparency. The prisoners do not reform in 5 minutes, dazzled by the greatness of the chef who has fallen on their heads, but keep showing their character until the respect of each of them is won. And despite the modest running time, Kai’s achieving mutual respect with each of the heroines is shown, spoken and dramatically justified (and not, may the series *Kombinatsiya* forgive me, played out as a silent scene to cheerful music instead of a convincing speech by the hero against that background). Things are fine with the music too, where it is present and needed: Dayte Tank (!) plays, and that I respect.

Towards the finale Pyatnitsa pulls a trump card from its sleeve and turns episode 7 into what it does best. Yes, yes, into a reality show. Well, with such material it would be a sin not to wrap it in its favourite packaging. And that is good too. We have got to know Kai and his new team from the prison kitchen well enough. Now we can step back and look at it all in the third person. And from what angle this series will serve us its dessert episode, we will see on Sunday.

## 26 November 2024

I thought for a long time about how to understand the finale of the series [*Chef*](https://t.me/kino_voice/301). Then I realised it reminds me of this photograph: beautiful and at the same time chaotic, but worth looking at anyway.

On the one hand, in the finale, as in the whole series, everything fits screw to screw, the drama works and passions run high. The kind of content I do not speed up, because the dynamics are wonderful as they are) Prytkov is superb, the other characters’ images have fully opened up and come alive by the finale, and all the scenes with the opening of the restaurant are executed with filigree precision.

On the other hand, for all my love of the series, I began to notice its craftedness: the little seams needed to move the action, coincidences in the characters’ fates that try to pass for cinematic conventions. It seems too conventional, both the twist with the medical record forgotten in his own pocket and, even more so, Kai being jailed for a year. Good in script terms, but is Kai not too clever a hero for that?

While I was thinking, I read an [interview](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4010300/) by colleagues at Kinopoisk with Denis Prytkov (that is where the photo comes from). I found no minuses; it is definitely the best companion to the series, and as proof, here is a quote (about food and about love, of course):

 *— Do you have a signature dish?*
>
**— French-style meat! That’s how I won my wife’s heart. Once, before Covid, I made her invite me over. I spent my last money on groceries and went to cook at hers. Sadly, I didn’t stay the night, but the dish, as history has shown, worked.**

## Give a Show!: The Best Series of 2024

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/dayte-shou-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-11-18 (18 November 2024); updated: 2024-12-25
Work: “Give a Show!” is a 2024 series directed by Dmitry Litvinenko.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/dayte-shou-serial/

## 18 November 2024

I began to fall in love with the series *Give a Show!* (*Dayte shou*) back at Pilot (the Russian series festival), and [wrote about it](https://t.me/kino_voice/131) back then. But I was afraid that, as often happens, after a brisk start the plot would begin to sag, the pace to slow and other unconvincing things to set in.

I can hardly believe that for 4 episodes now *Give a Show!* has not just kept its quality but raised it with every episode. At the end of an episode you think “well, that’s it, it can’t get any better, this must be the peak, time to brace for the fall…” Then you switch on the next one and once again enjoy the powerful drama, the sharpness of the plot twists and the performances.

An especially pleasant impression is made by the mix of themes: there is the hopelessness of starting a career in the Russian media, a romantic line (Savostyuk and Krasovskaya, bravo; I have not believed in a pair of characters this much in a long time), corruption, the underbelly of show business and anything else you like. I describe it as if we had a new “encyclopedia of Russian life” before us (as Belinsky called *Eugene Onegin*), but why not? All the more so since the talk-show format around which this whole whirl takes place can truly be considered an encyclopedia of life in the country over the last 20 years, if not more.

## 25 December 2024

The finale of the series [*Give a Show!*](https://t.me/kino_voice/300) fell perfectly in December, when it is time to choose the best, and for me it really did become the best series of 2024!

It has been a long time since I watched any serious drama with such involvement and tension, because usually in these heavy genres some lack of credibility always catches my eye and spoils the whole impression. Here everything worked, from the first episode, seen back at Pilot, to the last, which repaid each of the characters entirely according to their karma. As I always do with favourite projects, I recorded my detailed impressions as a voice message, and here I will leave a couple of points worth taking from this series into the next year:

- Oleg Savostyuk is pure acting power and one of the best characters I saw in 2024. Truly, if it were not for Lev Zulkarnaev and his character in *Ona takaya klassnaya* (“She’s So Cool”), it would have been a triumph with no alternative

- Russian series have begun to venture (and very successfully) into the territory of the media backstage. We saw *Give a Show!*, and after it came *First Issue*. If this is a new language for talking about the surrounding reality (besides fairy tales and the 1990s), it will be interesting to follow

- Black humour is our everything, and it seems there will only be more of it in Russian projects

## The Apprentice: The Eternal Plot of “Thou Shalt Not Make Unto Thee Any Idol”

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/uchenik-voskhozhdenie-trampa-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-11-12 (12 November 2024)
Work: “The Apprentice” is a 2024 film directed by Ali Abbasi.
Tags: biopic, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/uchenik-voskhozhdenie-trampa-2024/

[*The Apprentice*](https://youtu.be/o023dg0Zbgw?si=MAOpVNqTpRSKONyv) is so formal that its main characters remain objects that arouse neither sympathy nor empathy, only the desire to observe from the outside (but for no more than two hours). That is what makes the film good: on either side of a neutral position it is easy to slip into sympathy or antipathy towards the characters, and with active politicians there is a risk of spoiling the whole film. At the same time, do not think the performances are anything other than one better than the next: Trump as played by Sebastian Stan creates a literally documentary effect, and Roy Cohn as played by Jeremy Strong outdoes everyone involved with his naturalness.

But the neutrality of the narration and the documentary-style performances do not provoke the emotional response one might count on before watching: well, at least indignation, say, that personalities like these get their hands on money, or on the contrary inspiration, the motivation to “attack and deny” too, as the characters recommend. Taken as a whole, the picture resembles Ouroboros, the mythical serpent devouring itself from the tail. The ring structure of the plot, combined with the mirroring of the main characters, leads us through one turn of a spiral that will probably never be broken. So watching such a film means getting a slightly better feel for the eternal plot of “thou shalt not make unto thee any idol” (except, perhaps, of yourself)

---

## Intermission: On the Courage to Taste the Whole Spectrum of Life’s Emotions

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kanikuly-2023/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-11-07 (7 November 2024)
Work: “Intermission” is a 2023 film directed by Anna Kuznetsova.
Tags: Russian cinema, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kanikuly-2023/

> - I want to gobble up that mask over there.

> - The sad one or the happy one?
> - Both.

In Russian cinemas from today: [*Intermission*](https://youtu.be/GZ9ORVnK8jg?si=G-BDIysXndwCb6rc) (*Kanikuly*, “Holidays”), the winner of Mayak 2023 (the film festival in Gelendzhik). A film that has absorbed *Sto dney posle detstva* (“One Hundred Days After Childhood”) and *Dozhivyom do ponedelnika* (“We’ll Live Till Monday”), but speaks to the viewer in its own language, which is what makes it worth seeing. Take the quote I put at the top: like the whole film, it is about the courage to taste the whole spectrum of life’s emotions and to accept all the experience you are capable of living through.

In the plot, Tanya, the young head of a drama club, takes her charges, aged 3 to 16, to a children’s theatre competition in Sochi. Going with them to keep an eye on creative types, Tanya above all, is the deputy head teacher Maria Genrikhovna. And although the exposition gives you every impression that Tanya and Maria will be the ones in conflict, the story turns out to be deeper and more many-layered. And where, for the children and teenagers during the 5 days of the trip, the position of the comfortable and worthy adult is taken by Tanya, for Tanya herself that adult becomes Maria. But Maria has no such adult of her own, and that is only one facet of the tragedy of the finale, in which, it seems, nothing fatal has happened.

What I most want to note is the overall mood of the film: down-to-earth naive, recklessly funny. Sleepless nights on the road, the teachers’ humour, maximally uncomfortable but cosy lodgings, an emotional overdose from a contrast shower of feelings: as people now joke on social media, it is “just another Tuesday” on any group trip of a school club, an olympiad team or any other kind of club. I was nostalgic to the full. So *Intermission* really is a small holiday you can immerse yourself in and come out of the film, as they say, 120 minutes older.

---

## Crime & Punishment: Ivan Yankovsky Is the Perfect Raskolnikov

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/prestuplenie-i-nakazanie-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-11-02 (2 November 2024); updated: 2024-12-02
Work: “Crime & Punishment” is a 2024 series directed by Vladimir Mirzoev.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, adaptation
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/prestuplenie-i-nakazanie-serial/

## 2 November 2024

Splitting [the series based on *Crime and Punishment*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/series/5377359/) into two parts is an excellent idea.

Not only because it is fashionable in the series world right now (recall *Baby Reindeer*, with its division by meaning, or *Ya znayu, kto tebya ubil* (“I Know Who Killed You”), with literally two blocks of episodes). But also because of the semantic structure of what happens. Today we saw the exposition, the crime (even in the plural), while the punishment, as happens in life, is not only delayed but also more agonising than the crime itself (in our case 6 episodes against 4).

A very simple but effective formal device makes waiting for the second part of the series practically guaranteed. We commit the crime almost playfully together with Raskolnikov and his Devil from Dostoevsky’s metaverse; it seems to fall into our hands of its own accord. But the punishment will come later, when all the thoughts have been thought over, all the hypotheses put forward and all patience exhausted (all the more so given the postponements of the premiere).

There is only one question: how do I now stop seeing this structure in every series I watch along the way?

## 2 December 2024

*\*tag yourself on Monday\**.

It seems Ivan Yankovsky is the perfect Raskolnikov. Misanthropic and merciful, unbalanced and rational, majestic and degraded all at once. His portrayal is especially well suited to the finale that [*Crime & Punishment*](https://youtu.be/RchRWY4waQI?si=xzvvRm0keRfB1SiJ) received in Vladimir Mirzoev’s directorial reading (no spoilers, but the resolution is a curious one).

After watching all 10 episodes of the new *Crime & Punishment*, it becomes obvious that the on-screen madness and devilry around the crime itself are absolutely necessary and appropriate. And just as appropriately they disappear towards the end of the story (or rather jump from Raskolnikov onto Luzhin, Svidrigailov and other characters; incidentally, all the supporting performances are utterly outstanding).

And here a great moment of talentedly deceived expectations arises, leading to an impressive resolution. The series pretends that everything is heading towards what we expect: Raskolnikov and Sonechka off to penal servitude, that sort of thing. But no such luck. And it is for this final surprise, when it would seem nothing is left for sudden twists, that the series is definitely worth watching to the very end.

---

## The Highway: The Poster, the “Spiral of Silence” and a Finale Everyone Decides for Themselves

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/trassa-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-31 (31 October 2024)
Work: “The Highway” is a 2024 series directed by Dushan Gligorov, Konstantin Statsky.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, thriller
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/trassa-serial/

Halloween is an exquisitely chosen date for the finale of *The Highway* (*Trassa*))

Over 10 episodes the story has established itself as a succession of utterly mind-boggling horrors that befell several characters. So as a horror for the pumpkin feast it is perfect)

But I want to dwell separately on the current poster, which makes the whole content of the project clear at a glance. Here we have the heroine in a stifling noose made of the highway, near which all the madness happens.

On the one hand, clearly, circumstances are strangling the heroine; she is literally risking her life trying to save her daughter. On the other, allow me to turn to media theory (there it is, dear thing, it came in handy in adult life). It has the concept of the “spiral of silence”: a situation in society and the media in which a person is less likely to voice their opinion on an issue if they feel they are in the minority and that retribution or isolation threatens them for that opinion. The silence twists in a spiral through the years, and you get the situation in the series: decades-long abuse of defenceless people by sick freaks. An astonishingly accurate hit with the poster, bravo!

Whether the heroine managed to break the “spiral of silence” and the chain of violence in the finale, each viewer decides for themselves. In my opinion she did not, but it turned out fair, and such a cruel outcome even pleased and surprised me)) Those who have watched it, what do you think of the finale?

## Daring: Every Chance of Standing Alongside Brigada

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/likhie-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-24 (24 October 2024); updated: 2025-09-18
Work: “Daring” is a 2024 series directed by Yuri Bykov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, crime
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/likhie-serial/

## 24 October 2024

The series [*Daring*](https://youtu.be/ZZsPnO0dr4A?si=HgfimuYLnzc-InsK) (*Likhie*, “The Dashing Ones”, a nod to the “dashing 90s”) has every chance of standing alongside *Brigada* (the cult 2002 gangster series) as a saga of equally epochal sweep about crime and the people who are drawn into it (not) of their own will.

*Daring*, as always with Yuri Bykov, sets out the characters’ initial motivation very intelligibly. Artyom Bystrov’s character, Pavel, a simple taiga gamekeeper who makes a living from honey, finds that in 1991 there is nothing to live on, while at the same time his former fellow villager is buying a whole flat in Khabarovsk. A thirst not even for a beautiful life but simply for one that is not humiliating takes hold of the hero, and from then on he is ready to take the word of the fellow villager promising the same “well-paid job”. Naturally, such a job implies nothing good.

The story is very well constructed, made up of two stories developing in parallel, in the present day and in the 1990s. On the one hand, we do not even have to wait 16 episodes to understand where, 30 years later, our protagonist’s son (his main accomplice from the first episodes) has ended up. On the other, the inserts of the present let us not simply watch silently, yet again, the deeds of bygone days in the 1990s, but see the delayed consequences of that time, which now seem invisible. A series I will be watching closely to the end.

## 18 September 2025

The opposition of father and son Likhovtsev in the second episode of the continuation of [*Daring*](https://t.me/kino_voice/893) is constructed as convincingly as possible.

Since the start of the season, only the very worst has been coming out in Zhenka, even if with good intentions (the “help” with his younger brother’s screw-up, for example). The character turns out to be somehow rotten, insincere, two-faced, even by the standards of those around him. Either the psyche of a child immersed in bloody business from childhood could not take it, or he simply absorbed the worst of the atmosphere of his time, but the result is plain to see. I admire Egor Kenzhametov in this role. A curious coincidence that he also played the younger brother of Yura Borisov’s character in the film *Byk* (“The Bull”): in that role Egor, on the contrary, had to stay clear of the harshness of character, while here he goes all out.

In contrast to him, the father, Pavel Likhovtsev, oddly enough, seems brighter. It is astonishing how, with so much blood on his hands, the character managed to preserve (or at any rate to be able to remember) a sincere, bright love for his wife and some sort of value system. Artyom Bystrov’s performance in this role was wonderful from the start, but now it acquires some new importance.

## The Alien: Simple Science Fiction That Could Really Have Happened

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/prishelets-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-24 (24 October 2024); updated: 2024-12-24
Work: “The Alien” is a 2024 film directed by Ivan Sosnin.
Tags: Russian cinema, science fiction
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/prishelets-2024/

## 24 October 2024

Yesterday I was at the premiere of Ivan Sosnin’s [*The Alien*](https://youtu.be/REDTP-7B_jU?si=e16bmSzMvAlBXeQa) (*Prishelets*). The film, as always with this director, instils faith in the best and charges you with kindness, and sun and bright colours break through the impassable Russian snows on screen.

Lyosha, a young man (everyone in the village thinks he is strange, but that is not so at all), is impatiently waiting for aliens to arrive: he draws crop circles, tunes the radio equipment in his house, picks up signals and, in general, lives for his idea. In the end he does meet an alien woman, and of course that opens his eyes to life.

The science fiction here is simple, without the tiresome profusion of special effects. It is exactly how an alien might appear in an ordinary village, in the snowy Russian landscapes familiar to us. Such a deliberate avoidance of special effects makes the science fiction sweet, close, inspiring the feeling of a story that could really have happened.

The protagonist, played by Maxim Stoyanov, could not have been any different. It is a wonderful performance, a combination of vulnerability and defencelessness with a righteous anger at a world that promises people like Lyosha nothing good. Stoyanov’s physicality also works for the character: on the outside he looks like a mighty giant, but inside, as we see, he has a very fragile world, which the actor manages to convey. After *The Alien* I looked at this actor with new eyes; that is one of many things to thank the film for.

And also: in Ivan Sosnin’s films even villains get a chance at something better and, without meaning to, set out on the path of good. The film’s finale is proof of that.

In cinemas from today: a warm recommendation to go with your loved ones and share the bright emotions of a worthwhile film.

## 24 December 2024

In my colleagues’ and my [year-end selection of films](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4010434/) at Kinopoisk I, as has become the custom, answered for kindness and talked about [*The Alien*](https://t.me/kino_voice/269). Ivan Sosnin’s new film is striking not so much for its thought about people’s non-acceptance of their neighbour (usual for the exposition of this author’s stories) as for the language chosen to convey this problem:

> In the hands of the kindest Russian director, Ivan Sosnin, the cruel axiom “man is a wolf to man”, to a track by Mujuice, turns into a gentle but intelligible reminder: “man is an alien to man”.

If in 2022’s *Dalyokie blizkie* (“Distant Close Ones”) contact was made on Earth, by driving a few thousand kilometres in a van and talking heart to heart, in 2024 a whole sci-fi with an ambiguous finale is being launched. That is precisely the reason that makes any summing-up of 2024 impossible without *The Alien*, a snowy, chamber story that, in fact, concerns everyone.

## Yug and Ira: The Voice-Over as a Lifestyle Podcast About the Hero’s Life

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/yug-i-ira-zakadrovyy-golos/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-21 (21 October 2024)
Tags: series, Russian cinema, analysis
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/yug-i-ira-zakadrovyy-golos/

**How do you make the story of a 14-year-old lad or a 30-year-old single woman interesting?**

(More precisely, the stories of the series *Yug* and *Ira*)

> For those who have not watched them:
>
> *Yug* (“South”), 2024: Ivan Sosnin’s dramedy about a 14-year-old boy who sets off to look for his father all over Russia
>
> *Ira*, 2023: the story of a 30-year-old woman (Ingrid Olerinskaya) whose personal life has not worked out.

Use a voice-over! The screenwriter of both projects, Alim Beschokov, by all appearances, applies this device with pleasure)

In general, a voice-over is used in cinema either as the subjective voice of the hero telling the viewers something himself, or as the objective voice of a third-person narrator who does not take part in the action and comments from the outside.

In *Yug* and *Ira* the voice-over always belongs to the protagonist, which means it shows hidden aspects of their inner world. Literally a non-stop lifestyle podcast about the hero’s life)

The trick is that a voice-over usually voices details left off screen, the things we do not see. But in these series the voice-over often duplicates scenes shown on screen and doubles the effect. For example, in *Yug* there is a scene where the hero goes to buy a new SIM card: we see this on screen. And in voice-over Yug tells us how he went to buy it and why. Visually we see the situation in the third person, but we learn by ear how he lives through it in the first. So the chances of growing close to Ira or Yug become much higher thanks to this device.

---

## A History of Russian Film Festivals: From the 1935 Soviet Film Festival to Kinotavr

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/istoriya-rossiyskikh-kinofestivaley/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-15 (15 October 2024); updated: 2024-10-30
Tags: festivals, film history
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/istoriya-rossiyskikh-kinofestivaley/

## 15 October 2024

**1️⃣** **Part ⅕. The second-oldest**

Where did film festivals come from in the first place?
It all began with European film clubs in the 1920s; then came curated screenings with a programme lasting several days, and then, with the arrival of sound film in 1927, the process sped up many times over. So in 1932 the world’s first film festival took place: Venice. It appeared as part of the Venice Biennale, an international art exhibition held since 1893 (the same age as cinema!). There was no competition yet, but at the second festival in 1934 it appeared: the main award was not yet the Golden Lion but the Mussolini Cup (yes, cinema was the most important of the arts for the most varied regimes).

And this is where we arrive at the second-oldest film festival: the Russian one! Or more precisely, the Soviet Film Festival in Moscow. 1935, the Udarnik cinema, an international competition, the opening film *Chapaev*. On the jury: Sergei Eisenstein, Vsevolod Pudovkin, Alexander Dovzhenko. The preconditions for its emergence: political hostility to the regime in Italy at the time and the 15th anniversary of the Soviet film industry, which was celebrated everywhere in January of that same year.

Unfortunately, neither of the first two film festivals flourished for long. Venice went underground for the whole of the Second World War and returned to its flagship status only in 1946. And the Soviet Film Festival in Moscow was never again held in its previous form. Its successor was, and remains today, the Moscow International Film Festival (MIFF). From 1959 it was held every two years, and from 1999 it became annual (who was behind that, by the way, I will cover in one of the next posts). And until 2022 it was the only Russian A-category film festival (that is, accredited by the International Federation of Film Producers Associations on a par with Cannes, Venice, Berlin and a dozen or so other major festivals around the world).

In short, with film festivals everything seems to happen not thanks to, but despite. But when has that ever bothered us?)

In the next part: who made MIFF annual, what is strange about its programme, which festival split off from the Moscow International, and much more.

## 23 October 2024

**2️⃣** **A History of Russian Film Festivals.** **Part ⅖. Changes**

So, [in the previous part](https://t.me/kino_voice/247) we arrived at the moment when MIFF became a regular Soviet film festival held every 2 years. It was an astonishing time, when Federico Fellini, Sophia Loren and Francis Ford Coppola came to the USSR just as they did to Venice and Cannes, and in 1987 the jury president was Robert De Niro. In short, MIFF grew by every measure to truly Hollywood proportions.

And so in 1988 MIFF grew so large that its documentary programme split off, taking shape as a separate (also international!) festival, at that time only of documentary film, Poslanie k cheloveku (“Message to Man”). At the suggestion of the documentary filmmaker Mikhail Litvyakov, the showcase was moved to Leningrad, held there for the first time in 1989, and its symbol (in the first photo) was named the “Kentavryonok”, the little centaur (yes, this image was hovering over the Russian festival movement even before Kinotavr appeared!). Message to Man is still actively held, now including experimental and fiction film and animation too. Kinopoisk has a wonderful [article](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4006929/) with a more detailed history of the showcase and unique photos (I was especially struck by the shot of Leni Riefenstahl receiving an award in 2001)

Meanwhile MIFF began to stall: the collapse of the country, crisis and social upheaval do nobody any good. In 1998 it could not be held at all because of financial problems. In 1999 the post of president of MIFF was taken by Nikita Mikhalkov (something tells me no such post existed before), and since then the festival has been held annually. Let me remind you of the context: in 1999 Mikhalkov is a triumphant figure with *Burnt by the Sun* already behind him (the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film and the Grand Prix of the 47th Cannes Film Festival) and the internationally shot *The Barber of Siberia*. So there is no need to be surprised at the magical disappearance of the financial problems, all the more so since various researchers describe the Mikhalkov of that period as a rather effective manager ([I relied](https://t.me/kino_voice/107), in particular, on the book [*Istoriya rossiyskogo blokbastera*](https://books.yandex.ru/books/JZRDAukA), “A History of the Russian Blockbuster”).

In short, MIFF survived hard times for the second time in its history, but on the horizon other major Russian film festivals had already appeared: Kinotavr and Okno v Evropu (“Window to Europe”). Where they came from and how they differed, in the next part!

## 30 October 2024

**3️⃣ A History of Russian Film Festivals. Part ⅗. Why Kinotavr Is Called That**

So, MIFF survived, and Kinotavr and Window to Europe appeared. Let us look at them in more detail.

Kinotavr did not appear at once. Its prototype, the Festival of Unsold Films, [took place](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/3374283/) in Podolsk in 1989 on the initiative of the businessman (if one may call him that; the man has an interesting biography) Mark Rudinstein. The thing is, in the raging perestroika the amount of auteur cinema rose sharply, but cinemas did not buy it, because the new market economy needed crowd-pleasers rather than art films. So a multitude of films arose that had no chance of reaching cinema screens and audiences. And then Rudinstein stepped in and gave these films and their authors a chance. The authors’ jubilation motivated the businessman so much that he decided to stage a bigger film festival by the sea, in Sochi, of course. Only the unwanted auteur films were not fit for such a scale.

The festival held by the sea in 1991 acquired a programme of two parts: one for audiences (“Cinema for Everyone”) and one for critics (“Cinema for the Chosen”). [They say](https://kinoart.ru/texts/mezhdu-banditami-i-skrepami-kak-rodilsya-kinotavr-etalonnyy-rossiyskiy-kinofestival) that because of this someone joked that it was turning into “some kind of centaur” (*kentavr*). And the film critic Alyona Bokshitskaya corrected: “Kinotavr!”, giving the festival its name. That is how it would exist for the next 30 years, becoming the symbol of a whole film era. By the way, the post of “festival president” (and we remember who holds it at MIFF) appeared precisely at Kinotavr, and it was held by Oleg Ivanovich Yankovsky. It sounds honorary, but it had a thoroughly practical purpose: state sponsorship needed someone whom officials would be happy to receive in their offices and not send away empty-handed. For Kinotavr’s first ten years this scheme with Yankovsky worked, but then something stalled, and the question arose of selling the festival.

In its early days Kinotavr had an international programme (as, in principle, did all the festivals mentioned above). And in 1993 the festival Window to Europe was launched in Vyborg: the oldest national film festival in Russia, focused specifically on Russian cinema. A festival with a surprisingly calm history, it outlived Kinotavr and exists to this day.

In the next part: the rebirth and death of Kinotavr, and lots of film festivals with one-word names

---

## El Ruso: A Series About Simple Truths in Complex Argentine Settings

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/el-ruso-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-08 (8 October 2024)
Work: “El Ruso” is a 2024 series directed by Sergey Mokritskiy.
Tags: series, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/el-ruso-serial/

The whole of [*El Ruso*](https://youtu.be/fSM0IunUOGI) is out: a series about simple truths in complex Argentine settings.

As I [wrote](https://t.me/kino_voice/131) after Pilot (the Russian series festival), I was interested in watching the concept of Balabanov’s “city as an evil force” at work, so I switched on the third episode without hesitation. And then the fourth, the fifth, the sixth… And every time the story stopped at a moment after which it was impossible not to keep watching. Not a single boring filler episode. Not a single abandoned storyline. All the little knots tied over the course of the story were untied clearly and in order by the finale, and, what is valuable, not as a soulless cut of each character in turn but as action as distinctive and stirring as the whole series.

The idea of the importance of love and of human treatment of one another against all odds can be framed in different ways. But in the case of *El Ruso*, surrounded by Old Believers’ chintzes and the criminal neon of night streets, it took shape not as a tedious, hackneyed moral but as a skilfully drawn line, triply underlined by the finale. And thanks to the structure (served by the sets, by the performances, which do not overshadow one another, and by certain cinematic conventions) the series draws even those who are usually ready to stop themselves at any second into genuine binge-watching.

It seems this is the case where a series fits in everything, for every taste, without dropping anything along the way. A rarity and a pleasant discovery.

## Wolfs: When the Wolves Are Fed and the Sheep Are Safe

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/odinokie-volki-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-09-29 (29 September 2024)
Work: “Wolfs” is a 2024 film directed by Jon Watts.
Tags: comedy, crime
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/odinokie-volki-2024/

The film **Wolfs** (released in Russia as *Odinokie volki*, “Lone Wolves”) is the case where, as the Russian saying goes, “the wolves are fed and the sheep are safe”: both in the plot and in terms of the picture’s artistic merits.

An unpretentious comedy about the clash of two criminal fixers in the persons of George Clooney and Brad Pitt shows its ironic tone from the first frames. These peculiar cleaners of the criminal world are at first cramped in the format of a chamber TV play set in a luxury suite, which gives their disagreements an even pettier character. And then (instead of the gun hanging on the wall) the duo is invaded by the revived corpse of a hapless zoomer (played no less brilliantly by Austin Abrams).

And everything in their small night-time adventure is grotesque, hyperbole and exaggeration. The fixers’ industry turns out to be too small, with one nurse, one HR person and one Albanian gang between the two of them; the difference between the generations is declared too vividly, where our zoomer tries to reflect on his feelings while the fixers hurry him for information on the job. That is why the humour works for any audience, and the overly blissful happy ending (our stern wolves let the lad go unharmed) is spoiled, perhaps, only by a crumpled final scene with a meaningful silence. But although I do not like open endings, I am still pleased with the film.

In short, a great thing for an evening, whatever people say about it! If you like this kind of film, I have 2 more recommendations. First, Ilya Naishuller’s film [*Nobody*](https://youtu.be/bZOHmDYCo2I?si=U7jLBklli8ErVW3b), with Bob Odenkirk and no less criminal fun. Second, a Russian analogue: the series [*I snova zdravstvuyte*](https://youtu.be/c1E9atEi7mw?si=iDRjBvpeX20bi2J4) (“Hello Again”, the first 2 seasons). Merzlikin as the fixer, Vlasenko as the zoomer, pleasant humour and bits of Russian reality as a bonus)
