## Kombinatsiya: The Story of a Band from the Inside Out

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kombinatsiya-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-09-14 (14 September 2024); updated: 2024-10-26
Work: “Kombinatsiya” is a 2024 series directed by Nikita Vlasov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, music
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kombinatsiya-serial/

## 14 September 2024

In the series [*Kombinatsiya*](https://youtu.be/F4R5Et6LW9w?si=yU3aIVrIbDV7kMa7) (“Combination”), about the producer of a cult girl band of the late Soviet years, a lot did not work, as my colleagues write. But I was especially surprised by a malfunction in one particular mechanism.

The friendship of Tanya and Alyona, the band’s singers, is sold to us through exactly the same mechanism as in *The Boy’s Word* with Maratik and Palto (“Coat”), right down to the physical resemblance. Dark-haired Tanya, like Maratik, is a street hooligan and tearaway who unexpectedly comes from a well-off and quite philistine family by late-USSR standards, while fair-haired Alyona is simply Andrey-Palto at the start of the action: for everything good (and musical) and against everything bad. And so they met, went from hatred to love in express mode and found noble friends in each other, which we are supposed to understand from a series of scenes with an exchange of barbs, knowledge (of life or of books, it does not matter) and some displays of female solidarity. A perfect idyll of Palto and Maratik, who practised push-ups, speaking English and singing “Sedaya noch” (“Grey Night”, the Laskovy May hit) and topped it all off with borscht.

And such a mechanism for depicting a nascent friendship is very good: it shows the outstanding traits of both heroes (or both heroines) and helps the viewer warm to and grow attached to them. The girls’ performances as a duo are top-notch too, especially Elizaveta Bazykina’s; she is a sheer pleasure to watch, really! But for me a complete repetition of the mechanics of characters from another series instantly breaks the emotional ties with what is happening on screen and kills the intrigue. And their place is taken by the uncanny valley effect (and sadness at such a confluence of circumstances).

## 20 September 2024

By the third episode of *Kombinatsiya* (very touching and at the same time energising for achievement) I finally understood why the project still appeals to me.

As a viewer with a producer’s background, I am grateful that at last we are shown the story not of singers hired to show their faces and sing lyrics written for them to music written for them, but of the producer who runs all this, and a little of the composer who creatively drives it. These are people without whose work the band really would not have existed, the concerts would not have been organised and Moscow would not have been conquered. Of course, in reality they were and remain off screen, but how pleasant it is, at least in an artistic reimagining, to look at the story of a band from that very inside-out side where Shishinin has to strike deals with everyone and Okorokov has to write the music.

Of course, bands differ, and singers can be the authors and ideologists of a band, but in *Kombinatsiya* the case is different and the priorities in the story are, quite rightly, different. And where we have the wonderful series *Korol i Shut* (“The King and the Jester”), about singers who are also the band’s founders, there should also be a good series about a band with a different background. Thank you, *Kombinatsiya*, for that!

## 26 September 2024

In the new, fourth episode of *Kombinatsiya* there is categorically too little of my favourite character, the composer Vitaly Okorokov, played by Vladimir Kanukhin. In my view, this is the subtlest and deepest figure of all, and every appearance of his on screen is apt and fitting.

On this subject I recommend an [interview](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4009440/) by colleagues at Kinopoisk with the actor: it is the most pleasant and calming interview I have ever read!

## 26 October 2024

The finale of *Kombinatsiya*, of course, noticeably adds to the series the ambiguity for which it was already distinguished all along. Behind the grandiose story of the band’s revival after Apina’s departure, the stories of the individual members (except, perhaps, Tatyana Ivanova) get even more lost, and especially that of Shishinin with his sad end.

The last episode, alas, was overtaken by the curse of many final episodes of Russian projects: it turned into a quick cut of resolutions for each storyline. By the list: Apina’s solo career, launched; Ivanova’s crisis, over; Shishinin’s binge, finished; the new band, assembled; the murder, committed. On the other hand, there was a minimum of music-video scenes, which earlier replaced dialogue, plot development and much else besides. And here there simply was not enough time to talk something through, and that, of course, is a noticeable imbalance.

**\*️⃣** But in the end the series still did its job: it gave a little of what I call “angry energy”, when you want to follow the hero and push through any obstacles; it gave aesthetics, because the image really is beautiful; and it gave additions to my playlist, and for that I am grateful.

---

## Yuryev’s Island: The Magic of Cinema in Action

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ostrov-yureva-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-08-25 (25 August 2024)
Work: “Yuryev’s Island” is a 2024 film directed by Aleksandr Barshak.
Tags: Russian cinema, festivals, road movie
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ostrov-yureva-2024/

The magic of cinema in action

I am talking about [*Yuryev’s Island*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/5451180/) (*Ostrov Yuryeva*): I managed to see it at the premiere screening of the Budem Zhit (“We Shall Live”) film festival, and I honestly had unusually pleasant impressions. In the plot, an unenterprising Muscovite, having celebrated his 32nd birthday, suddenly becomes fixated on the idea that in a past life he was the sailor Yuryev, who almost discovered a new island but died without recording the discovery. The hero heads for Vladivostok by train (yes, it is a road movie), meets a *gopnik* (a street tough) there, and from then on the pals are inseparable on the way to their discovery.

Despite a complete absence of budget (before the screening the creators shared that they had shot the film for 5 years practically for food), the picture is very interesting. Solid craftsmanship comes to the fore, and it creates a feeling of magic. Everything is simply done as it should be, and it works: the actors are convincing, the script, despite the utmost realism, is inventive and generous with unexpected turns, and the direction does not press on the viewer.

Take, for instance, the reflection of the best traditions of Soviet cinema of the Stagnation era: a hero shut up in his inner world and running away from problems, unable to decide on anything, reproachful but loving women (I felt it while watching, rushed to rewatch my Kinopoisk colleagues’ [video essay](https://youtu.be/1aDB1TksfUU?si=VzWODF2mUNkMlRVX) about the era, and was convinced).

Or the Gospel motifs: there is a moment in the film when the hero preaches a sermon to fishermen from a boat, becoming an utterly Christological character.

Also, and this is especially valuable for me, part of the action takes place in Vladivostok, which our filmmakers (for reasons unknown to me) rarely visit, and they should. I have long wanted to visit this city, and that is exactly where I plan to spend my holiday!

And you, if you see it in cinemas or at one-off screenings somewhere, be sure to go.

---

## Morozko: The Opening Credits as the Quintessence of the Story

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/morozko-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-08-14 (14 August 2024)
Work: “Morozko” is a 2024 series directed by Yulia Lysova.
Tags: series, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/morozko-serial/

Speaking of credits again. I want to tell you about what is, in my view, the best Russian series of the first half of 2024: [*Morozko*.](https://youtu.be/OXVxBLnxk50?si=3l6Kr99P34ORrUh3)

I will begin my account precisely with the series’ opening credits, because they are, in my opinion, the quintessence of the story. Hypnotic in everything, from the rhythm and the frenzied collage to the music playing behind them, they seem to anticipate each of the series’ features. *Morozko* is:

- A plot based on the real story of the series’ creator, Yulia Lysova: the credits use real photographs, letters and drawings. Yulia, by the way, [wrote](https://t.me/jlisova/1202) on her channel about how it all came together, and there is a lot of interesting material about the series there in general!

- Incredible (really, you will not get bored) plot twists. Everything rushes, races and sometimes glints with neon, like the elements in the credits.

- A feeling of authenticity. You sense that behind every element of the story there is a personal experience, trauma or memory, which Aglaya Tarasova and Nikita Efremov convey brilliantly.

- Harmony of form and content: for example, in the first episode the heroine says that all she has left of her family is photographs, and we immediately see a selection of them in the cool format of the credits

In short, in these credits everything is as in life: something ran past and you did not manage to appreciate it and regret it, while something else lodged in your memory forever, though at the moment it did not seem special. I fell in love with *Morozko* about 30 per cent for them alone)

---

## House of the Dragon: Seasons Two and Three, Episode by Episode

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/dom-drakona-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-07-16 (16 July 2024); updated: 2026-08-10
Work: “House of the Dragon” is a 2022 series directed by Clare Kilner, Geeta Vasant Patel.
Tags: series, HBO, fantasy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/dom-drakona-serial/

## 16 July 2024

As gripping and good-tensely the fourth episode of *House of the Dragon* was, the fifth turned out just as incoherent and empty, collapsing the whole rhythm of the narrative, which had been gathering pace over the season.

The only thing I enjoyed watching was Daemon slowly going mad, while his place as “the reckless guy who is interesting to follow” is taken by one-eyed Aemond. Only in the fifth episode even he was boring to follow. Let alone Alicent’s attempts to make contact with sulky Cole or with the council in its full male line-up (Rhaenyra has the same problem, but at least she has Mysaria now).

## 24 July 2024

A couple of words about episode 6 of *House of the Dragon*.

The stale rhythm of the previous episode is livened up a little, but still not enough for a situation called “the season ends in 2 episodes”. Sad as it is to admit, the storyline of Daemon’s conversations with his own conscience has become for me that very place in the series where I want to speed up or skip. I expect that these synchronous torments of the hero and the viewers must be justified by a triply impressive resolution (and meanwhile I console myself with memes).

Alicent, as was to be expected, got what she fought for. But her dismissal was far less epic than the situation with Larys Strong: he and Aemond delivered the best dialogue of the whole episode, if not the season. I watched with great pleasure this high-speed mid-air change of shoes, in which Aemond outdid Larys himself, and that takes some doing. It remains to look forward to what the revenge of the humiliated and insulted Larys will be like.

But Rhaenyra’s whole role in this season seems to be reflected in the scene of a knight’s (failed) attempt to tame a dragon. Rhaenyra stands to one side and watches, mostly in silence. But the slap delivered to a tiresome courtier and the “gifts” sent to King’s Landing bring back the days of the Rhaenyra who could be rude to noble ladies and break up Daemon’s clash with Otto Hightower by flying in on a dragon. I hope that for the rest of the season we will be watching exactly that heroine.

P.S. Even before watching episode 6 I learned from a colleagues’ post that it would have a certain scene that our domestic streaming services would have to cut. Deep down I hoped it would finally be Daemon with Daemon in Daemon’s hallucinations) But the whole episode I eyed every pair of characters with suspicion. Lady Jeyne Arryn and Rhaena? Okay, I am ready. Daemon and Viserys? Go on, they are hallucinations, we have seen all sorts there already. But the creators outdid my imagination; it was unexpected, I respect it

## 30 July 2024

The seventh episode of *House of the Dragon* is at last brisk, eventful and spectacular (things are heading for the season finale, after all).

The episode’s main merit, of course, is the abundance of meme-worthy moments. Starting with the stream of Targaryens of varying degrees of purity arriving at the Blacks’ castle (this shot was nicely [joked about](https://t.me/FBChu/40714) in the wake of [Durov’s post](https://t.me/durov/339) about his sperm donation) and ending with Daemon suddenly seeing a goat in the castle corridors (obviously both as his own reflection and as a reminder of the scapegoat Blackwood, executed by him relatively undeservedly). And Aemond, of course, has learned nothing from life, so he once again ran into Vhagar’s unmanageability. I hope he will not kill any more of Rhaenyra’s children with such careless driving.

A segment that is claiming permanent status this season, which cannot but please: “The most epic mid-jump change of shoes”. This time we admire the young Lord Tully, who did not merely outplay Daemon but literally destroyed him morally, because the self-proclaimed king consort could not have imagined such a thing.

And the sulker of the seventh episode (no, Criston Cole did not take part in the action), Alicent, simply went off into the forest, so I am already mentally preparing for hallucinations like Daemon’s in the castle. However, such a shift of balance between the two heroines towards the end of the season looks very harmonious: as feeble as Rhaenyra began this season (gaining resolve not without Mysaria’s help), so shattered will Alicent (very probably) end it.

By the way, what was the moment with Mysaria in the previous episode about, if in this one everything is as if nothing had happened? I worry about their relationship no more than about my own, of course, but I would like to see a continuation)

## 6 August 2024

**The finale of season two of *House of the Dragon*!**

From experience I approached the viewing with fairly lowered expectations. Perhaps that was for the best, because I came away from the episode with a very pleasant impression: it is still a positioning of forces, but with painstakingly thought-out surprises, intrigues and set-ups for new storylines. A breath of fresh air after such a stuffy season.

Of course, what freshened up this episode were all the scenes in Essos. Watching the fight between a Lannister and the admiral Lohar in a mud puddle, I had a very pleasant feeling of returning to the universe of *Game of Thrones* (it sounds very strange, I understand, but such are the associations). They showed the intersection of two worlds, fresh faces, mores, the comic surprise of the admiral being a woman (and one of certain tastes at that), and it was she who surprised our Lannister (who had come to hash things out with serious men).

Remember how I hoped that our long-suffering watching of Daemon’s hallucinations would be justified by something super epic? And so it happened! Quite unexpectedly Daemon was granted a brief recap of 8 seasons of *Game of Thrones*, was filled with it and realised his place in the universe. This insert was so sudden, so different even in visual style from the rest of the series, that at first I did not believe my eyes. Nevertheless, *HotD* took a big step towards Winter, war and the other horrors the descendants of the protagonists will face.

The suffering from Daemon’s storyline ended, and the suffering from Rhaena’s storyline began) Over a few scenes with her in this episode I was more bored than over the whole of Daemon’s line in the season. But such, evidently, is the path to a dragon (or a mountain wyrm, if you believe some analyses): I can only hope that Rhaenyra’s children stay in one piece too and that the dragon finally ends up in the right hands (and that we will not see any more of this running about the hills).

Finally, into the permanent segment of the episode’s outstanding dialogue go Rhaenyra and Alicent, who has come to her senses after her mini-retreat. Rhaenyra, as someone who has already tried to come to terms and has more than once compromised her own moral principles, effectively declares: “you are no longer a sister to me”. Both as a viewer and dramatically I understand this; too high a price has already been paid for Alicent’s intransigence: Rhaenys killed, Jace mortally offended, the lives of false Targaryen bastards sacrificed (and such marginal figures as Ulf admitted to the castle). I remembered [one of the episodes](https://music.yandex.ru/album/6820951/track/107996163) of our episode-by-episode marathon *V predydushchikh seriyakh* (“Previously On”) about the first season of *HotD*. The hosts there assumed that Rhaenyra and Alicent would certainly come to an agreement. Now we have been shown that, alas, they twice failed to agree. And failing to agree is also a result and a resolution for a season.

## 3 July 2026

Judging by its first two episodes, the new season of [*House of the Dragon*](https://t.me/kino_voice/170) looks eventful.

And although from the first scenes it makes no such impression at all, it quickly corrects itself. That very feeling of “wait just a little longer and it’s about to start”, of which we had our fill over the first two seasons, quickly gives way to “whoa, that too?”. If possible, of course, it would be good to balance the rhythm of the action somehow, but maybe that is actually a strategy.

At the start of the season, do not misunderstand me, the storylines of the secondary characters were a little tiresome. Even in the second season they looked rather recently introduced, and at the start of the third they provoke mild bewilderment: is this what we gathered for? Although, once again I will try to rationalise it for the showrunners: if it is a plan to lull our vigilance before a succession of cool twists, it worked perfectly (not counting that for the first half of the opening episode I almost physically fought the urge to stop watching).

## 11 July 2026

As for the original [*House of the Dragon*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1620), it is pleasing so far, albeit with rather unoriginal ideas

To film the phrase “heavy is the cap of Monomakh” (the Russian equivalent of “heavy is the head that wears the crown”), the series slowed its pace considerably, practically locking the episode’s action within the four walls of the royal castle. It turns out that the long-awaited “after” of Rhaenyra taking the throne instantly turns into “so much for all that talk”.

I was amused by the concisely shown chain of searches for the state treasury, or at least for the nobleman responsible for it. Anyone who has had the good fortune to work in an even slightly corporate environment knows this situation: the project is old, more than one team has changed while working on it, and then comes the moment when the successors discover in horror that there is neither documentation nor any staff who possess the information.

So it was with Rhaenyra: she got neither onboarding nor a welcome pack, only worries and rats.

## 23 July 2026

A few remarks along the way while watching [*House of the Dragon*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1635)

- Sulkers do not change. Especially if they are knights. Especially if it is Criston Cole. Thus predictable storylines (because of the stupidity of what happens) form around him, whose outcome is a surprise only to the characters who happen to witness it all, not to the viewer.

- Psychological rebirths do the Targaryens good. Especially the one-eyed ones. Especially if there is a witch with a powerful moral compass nearby. One of the most interesting storylines is now developing around Aemond Targaryen. Around him, too, there is a heap of conspiracy theories (up to his possibly becoming the leader of the White Walkers who appeared to Daemon in his vision at the end of the second season). All these theories are unconvincing, but they are telling as a symptom of the audience’s interest in the character.

- If the history of the Targaryens had developed a little differently, perhaps their totem animal would have become cats instead of dragons. In any case, thank you to the fifth episode for this sweet detail.

- New characters who are introduced straight away with a voluminous context and a personality worked out in the script are superb. Ormund Hightower is the main proof of this (unlike some characters whose only reason for taking up screen time is an inferiority complex in the absence of a dragon). On the whole, by the middle of the third season a feeling forgotten since *Game of Thrones* began to be felt while watching, that of a three-dimensional, densely populated world, and it is pleasant.

## 10 August 2026

And in general, the finale of season 3 of [*House of the Dragon*](https://t.me/kino_voice/1652) is greatness.

If we operate with comparisons to *Game of Thrones*, it is at least the same level, if not superior. We were shown everything:

- a magnificent battle scene (with the detailed horrors of war)
- attempts at wise diplomacy (which, as in life, nobody appreciated)
- the despair of a queen as the only real hostage of power
- a comedy on the edge of madness (does the cry “I'm alive, imbecile” ring any bells?)

The multi-genre nature of this episode provokes real admiration. The screenwriters provided a multitude of emotional attractions, brilliant performances from at least 3 actors (in my subjective opinion, the performers of Rhaenyra, Gwayne and Aegon distinguished themselves here) and an extremely brisk pace (viewers of the season know that not every episode deserves praise for this). In a word, watching the season for this episode alone is more than worth it; the resolution before a two-year pause is wonderful in every sense.

---

## Inside Out 2: The Device Remains, but No Meanings Have Been Added Around It

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/golovolomka-2-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-07-09 (9 July 2024)
Work: “Inside Out 2” is a 2024 film directed by Kelsey Mann.
Tags: animation
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/golovolomka-2-2024/

I watched the second *Inside Out*. An unpopular opinion is coming (which is not rare for me, though usually in the positive direction), but first some praise.

It is great that they not only kept the trick of all these emotions coexisting but added new ones. Anxiety, of course, is ferociously like the real thing, and Disgust provoked quite palpable disgust. The jokes really are funny and original. And it is pleasing that, together with Riley, the seriousness of the problems the film touches on has grown up: we were shown a panic attack here, if you please.

But it is still predictable and boring. It is extremely hard (for me personally) to empathise with a dazzlingly white, healthy and socialised teenage girl from a complete, well-off and prosperous family living in a developed country. She goes through her growing up without any outside upheavals that would make watching precisely her emotions and moral ideals especially valuable (they are still valuable and important, like any emotions, but they have no cinematic twist). She gets no more and no less traumatic experience than any standard teenager. Actually no, less, because in the finale she is taken into the best girls’ hockey team (and what goes on in the heads of the girls who did not make it??)

And what goes on in the heads of orphans? And what goes on in the heads of teenagers with chronic illnesses? And how do Joy and Anxiety share the console when a teenager’s relatives die? And how is Anger held back in those for whom dyeing a strand of hair red is not enough to be accepted?

I would have liked to ponder possible answers to such questions after watching the expensive and long-awaited sequel to a story with a very original formal device at its heart. But the device remains, and no meanings have been added around it.

---

## Pilot 2024: The Picks I Will Definitely Be Watching

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/festival-pilot-2024-izbrannoe/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-06-27 (27 June 2024)
Tags: series, festivals, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/festival-pilot-2024-izbrannoe/

I did not finish talking about Pilot (the Russian series festival in Ivanovo), and for it to let me go, I have to finish) Here is a selection of the picks I will definitely be watching.

***Teoriya bolshoy lzhi*** (“The Big Lie Theory”)

A wonderful story about the harm and benefit of lying: over the pilot episode they were definitely in equal proportion. If *Ona takaya klassnaya* (“She’s So Cool”) had not been in the competition, all my sympathies would have gone to this series. The characters here have to lie to make money, lie to keep relationships (or build new ones); in short, lie so that, paradoxically, their conscience does not torment them. All this, naturally, is done very funnily and originally, so I sincerely recommend it: in my view, this is where Pilot’s best script was.

[*Give a Show!*
](https://youtu.be/3sRut1jp4Ww?si=ZRl8LRYJAnL1o2NF)
As I wrote for our piece on Kinopoisk, “an attraction of unprecedented vileness”. Not because the series is bad, but because Miloš Biković plays a pop king who has lost his moral compass (and drags everyone he meets down with him) far too convincingly. But I will follow this series for the stories of Pasha Goncharov (very well played by Oleg Savostyuk from *Snegir*, “The Bullfinch”) and Vera (Anastasia Krasovskaya). They were side by side on screen for only a couple of seconds, and that in a flashback, but you already want to watch them as a pair as much as possible.

And with Pasha’s storyline I feel the utmost empathy and recognition. Everything shown about his internship on a big talk show, working 25/8 for 0 roubles, is the pure truth from the life of novice journalists. Out of personal interest in this story I will be watching the series for sure.

***[Chistye](https://youtu.be/ozXtd9w4wg8?si=wIiRqmT09H_P4Gcn)*** (“The Clean Ones”)

A series that was announced as an erotic thriller ended up interesting me for something completely different. I have a modest guess that it will be like *The Boy’s Word*, only with heroines instead of heroes. We are presented with several young women in a borderline state and in the most dysfunctional conditions, and from there they have options for how to live with it (or die). And by the finale we will surely sit with our mouths open, roughly as when we watched the fate of Palto, Adidas and Maratik in the finale of the aforementioned *Word*. And it is as something that may unexpectedly astonish me that I will watch *Chistye*.

***[El Ruso](https://youtu.be/TUicVx3jLSw?si=oZ0lgoaXQbF7-vKg)*** (this is not a trailer but a rather interesting commentary from the creators about the series, I recommend it)

I do not yet fully understand whether I will watch the series seriously, but since there is doubt, I should write about it. I am attracted by the Balabanovian idea of “the city as an evil force”, which is present here, and by the declaration of the importance of human dialogue against all odds. And from its very first frames the series enchanted me with the painted chintzes of the Old Believers’ costumes and a tension akin to the one that arises when watching a horror film: everything seems fine, colourful and bright, but you feel a chill. So it is enticing.

---

## Baby Reindeer and I Know Who Killed You: One Device, but There Is a Difference

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ya-znayu-kto-tebya-ubil-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-05-22 (22 May 2024); updated: 2024-05-22
Work: “I Know Who Killed You” is a 2024 series.
Tags: series, analysis, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ya-znayu-kto-tebya-ubil-serial/

## 22 May 2024

**A new trend in series**

In my last post I talked about **Baby Reindeer**, one of the strongest film impressions of the year, not least because of how the narrative changes in the middle of the series. It turns out the story is not about the woman stalking the protagonist at all, but about an episode of abuse he lived through before that, so *Baby Reindeer* does a complete U-turn in genre and from a sometimes awkward dramedy turns into a thriller about the human psyche at various stages of suppression (a special episode, twice as long as the others, is devoted to this).

“Phew, a heavy series,” I thought, and went on to watch **I Know Who Killed You** (*Ya znayu, kto tebya ubil*)

And what do you think? Right: in the very middle the series turns around and from a gripping spectacle with chases, shoot-outs, scandals and intrigues becomes a classic drama about an orphan girl who piece by piece reassembles her unrealised life with a family lost forever.

The device is the same, but there is a difference, of course:

In *Baby Reindeer* the break in the middle of the series masterfully deepens the issues, adds a heap of new aspects to our understanding of the characters and heightens the intrigue

In *I Know Who Killed You*, in my opinion, the change of genre worked to its detriment: it brought with it a change of protagonist (and I had come to watch Yatsenko for all 8 episodes), and moved the tragedy from the plane of Hamlet’s “to be or not to be” to the scale of Reels about working through psychological trauma in adolescence, which to an adult (not yet in the role of the parent of a teenager) seems not entirely interesting

## 22 May 2024

At the same time! *I Know Who Killed You* has a heap of indisputable pluses

1) Alexander Yatsenko’s inimitable, simply outstanding and whatever-else-you-like acting: he is simply magnificent in this series, touching and cruel, cowardly and decisive, funny and indifferent, empathetic and manipulative, including with the viewer; he simply left no chance not to admire him

2) A most unexpected and equally pleasant reference to *Cargo 200*: Agniya Kuznetsova moves into Yatsenko’s house as a live-in nanny, declares from the doorstep that nobody should pester her because *her fiancé is serving in the paratroopers*, and then for 6 episodes watches *a man with unprocessed trauma keeping a kidnapped little girl in a locked flat*. Only a little was missing for a complete hit on the blind old woman with her signature line “we’ve got flies”…
At the same time I am terribly glad that in the universe of this series Kuznetsova’s heroine’s fiancé apparently came back alive and well, because in the second part of the series she is already a happy mother of many children.

3) The vibe of the series of my childhood, in particular *I vsyo-taki ya lyublyu* (“And Still I Love”): a real soap opera with betrayals, lies and broken lives, and above all a change of heroine in the middle of the series
Do not judge me too harshly, that happened too, and I liked it more than *Papiny dochki* (“Daddy’s Daughters”) and *Ranetki* put together

---

## Tantsuy, Seledka!: Why It Is Our Aftersun

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/tantsuy-seledka-solntse-moe/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-04-26 (26 April 2024)
Tags: Russian cinema, comparison, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/tantsuy-seledka-solntse-moe/

**Why [*Tantsuy, Seledka!*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/5134592/) (“Dance, Seledka!”) is our [*Aftersun*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/4948281/)** (released in Russia as *Solntse moyo*)

(no, not only because the heroine rummages through her father’s video cassettes for the whole film))

here is a checklist of similarities:

- a daughter’s last journey with her father: it does not matter that in the case of *Seledka* this journey is literally a last journey to the morgue, while in *Aftersun* it is a trip to a resort. What matters is that these are the last hours in her father’s company

- the soundtrack: really, never mind that “Under Pressure” has turned into Malikov’s “Do zavtra” (“Till Tomorrow”) in our version; the feelings of irreplaceable loss (but with hope for the future) are the same

- the carpet: in *Aftersun* that sad carpet, bought in Turkey on holiday, passes to the heroine as an inheritance, while in *Seledka* a traditional Soviet carpet, practically taken down off the wall, is used to wrap the corpse of Pavel Maykov’s character

- the cassettes, and my traditional passion for finding references to *Assa* in everything: we all remember that *Aftersun* is built on rewatching tapes, while in *Tantsuy, Seledka!* the heroine receives a cassette her father recorded especially for her, and he even says an introduction at the start of the tape. If you have had a really lousy day, he says, you have to dance. We do not hear what is recorded on the cassette after that (that is how the plot goes), but for some reason I am sure the tape would have had the song “Chudesnaya strana” (“Wonderful Country”), to which Drubich’s heroine sat sadly in someone else’s coat at the end of *Assa*. Otherwise, what else would you listen to when things get really bad and you have to dance

---

## The Giant Ants of Novosibirsk: A Graphic Novel That Lulls Your Vigilance

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/gigantskie-muravi-novosibirska-kniga/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2023-12-16 (16 December 2023)
Work: “The Giant Ants of Novosibirsk” is a 2023 book by Vitaly Terletsky.
Tags: books, comics
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/gigantskie-muravi-novosibirska-kniga/

i not only talk but sometimes write too (and not only about films but about books as well!)

for example, with colleagues from Kinopoisk and Bookmate we put together the [book highlights of the year](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4008810/), and I gave my vote almost without hesitation to the graphic novel I had just (at the time the selection was being compiled) read, by Vitaly Terletsky and Evgenia Chashchina, *Gigantskie muravyi Novosibirska* (“The Giant Ants of Novosibirsk”):

> Stas, a 22-year-old unemployed man, tells his friends in the minutest detail about his childhood memories: the giant ants of Novosibirsk. Only Stas is from Kirov and has never been to Novosibirsk. Around this conflict between memory and facts, in an elegant chaos, flash the adventures of the Decembrist Muravyov-Apostol, love, sculptures of giant dinosaurs and the search for one’s own “self”. And the protagonist himself resembles Solovyov’s Bananan from *Assa* dropped into the world of the film *Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind*.
>
> Cinematic and escapist, but far from as lightweight as it seems at first glance, Terletsky and Chashchina’s graphic novel lulls your vigilance with rainbow watercolour. And for its finale it offers a hard choice (one that has gained relevance in the last couple of years) between soul-saving but false memories and looking hopeless reality in the face. And, it seems, for the hero the choice is obvious.

before settling on my recommendation for good, I also thought about Alexei Ivanov’s *Broneparokhody* (“Armoured Steamers”); I sincerely recommend this book (which is also in our selection!) no less than *The Giant Ants*; it definitely made my top book impressions of the year)

but *Broneparokhody* lost to *The Ants* on one subjective criterion of mine, code-named “my jaw dropped and I had to pick it up”.

all the films and books (and pieces of music, and \[insert as appropriate\]) that I am ready to remember among the best (both of the year and of my life) must make me feel roughly like that, otherwise the road to the podium is closed) and my tastes are peculiar, so completely unpredictable things sometimes meet the subjective criterion, but that is another story...

in general I have been reading Terletsky for a long time, and I strongly recommend not only the fresh novel but also such time-tested (and reread) things as *Russkie obedinyayutsya s krokodilami i napadayut na Evropu* (“The Russians Join Forces with the Crocodiles and Attack Europe”) and *Padenie Yeltsina s mosta* (“Yeltsin Falls off a Bridge”); here, it seems, the titles themselves are the best recommendation

## Year of Birth: A Solovyov-Style Farce and a Finale with Many Interpretations

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/god-rozhdeniya-2023/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2023-11-14 (14 November 2023); updated: 2023-11-14
Work: “Year of Birth” is a 2023 film directed by Mikhail Mestetskiy.
Tags: Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/god-rozhdeniya-2023/

## 14 November 2023

yes, I have finally seen *Year of Birth* (*God rozhdeniya*)! I adore films like this: when, watching the second half, you simply switch off and pick your dropped jaw up off the floor, because you cannot even guess what will happen in the end. Filipp is an absolute Bananan with his room of magical escapist artefacts, and the plot itself is also rather Solovyovian, combining vulgar everydayness with an unimaginable farce from a parallel universe (by the way, ever since I saw Solovyov’s influence here, I immediately remembered the head of the boy Bananan in *2-Assa-2*, cut off from its owner and sewn onto a market sunflower-seed seller, so now this connection cannot be unseen)

separate respect for the song “Allo, Marina”: jokes aside, it is literally our version of “I’m Just Ken”! making people go crazy over a song by ~~Ryan Gosling~~ Yura Borisov before they have even seen the film is an excellent move)) I, for one, fell for it; only Yandex Music knows how many times I have relistened to it (and will again)

and on the whole, I simply strongly recommend going to see the film; it is almost universal, and everyone will be able to find something of their own in it thanks to an understandable plot about the difficulties of unconditional love (not for nothing is Eldar Kalimulin an absolute copy of Joseph Gordon-Levitt from *500 Days of Summer*) and a finale with many interpretations: I counted 3 of them… but those are spoilers! So I will tell you about my versions of the finale’s interpretation in the voice message below

## 14 November 2023

A bonus post! (almost like [*Bonus-trek*](https://music.yandex.ru/album/14629532), “Bonus Track”, heh-heh)

do you know why the song “Allo, Marina” begins with the line “*I live without feeling my trousers under me*”? I have found an explanation)

no, it is not just an allusion to Mandelstam (whose poem begins “We live without feeling the country under us”).

telling Filipp the truth about Soplya, his father (formerly Kostolom, “Bonebreaker”) specifies that he gave Soplya his trousers so that he would have something to lie in in the coffin. And it is Kostolom who turns out to be the character who, after Soplya’s death, lives “without feeling his trousers under him”: he becomes disillusioned with life, betrays his dream, his ideals and any creative aspirations. this can explain both this character’s bitterness towards his son and his disillusionment with life

I have not analysed the rest of the song’s lyrics, but if you have theories, leave them in the comments))
